Newcastle appoint Jaissle - what should fans expect?

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 18:32:43 GMT

Matthias Jaissle has signed a four-year deal with Newcastle United until 2030

Matthias Jaissle has quite an act to follow at Newcastle United.

"It won't be easy to succeed Eddie [Howe]," a source said.

Just like Newcastle's moves to sign young players from the continent, there is an element of risk with this appointment as the club bring in a manager who has never coached in the Premier League before.

German Jaissle delivered success in Saudi Arabia and Austria - with Al-Ahli and Red Bull Salzburg respectively - but this will be the first time he has sampled life in one of Europe's top five leagues.

He becomes the Premier League's second-youngest current head coach, at 38, and his first competitive game is against Liverpool on Sunday, 23 August.

In the statement announcing his appointment on Wednesday, Jaissle said it was an "incredible honour" to become head coach of "one of the biggest clubs in European football".

"My teams are built on togetherness, hard work, intensity and a passion to improve every single day," he added.

"I believe there is enormous potential within this squad and throughout the football club.

"I give my complete commitment and total energy to bringing further success to Newcastle United."

There has been no time to waste since Jaissle arrived at Newcastle's pre-season training camp in Spain at the weekend.

"He will try to understand the culture, what Newcastle means to the community, as soon as possible," added a source.

"That's what he will live by."

Howe certainly set the standard.

The Englishman took charge of a side in relegation trouble, kept them up, then went on to end Newcastle's long wait for silverware by winning the EFL Cup in 2025 - and also qualified for the Champions League on multiple occasions.

However, last season was a bruising one domestically - Newcastle finished in 12th place - and Howe watched Alexander Isak, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon leave within a year.

Newcastle are set to lose a fourth key player too, with captain Bruno Guimaraes heading to Arsenal.

They need a progressive manager to start a new cycle following Howe's decision to step down - and build on what he did at the peak of his reign.

Effectively, Jaissle's remit will be to develop players and outperform clubs with bigger wage bills. And Newcastle's squad should expect him to be just as demanding as his predecessor in training.

"We did lots of small-sided games to keep the intensity high and if someone had not been giving it their all, he called them out on it," said former Salzburg midfielder Zlatko Junuzovic.

"He's not afraid to address things head-on."

Jaissle has quickly had to get to know a new set of players, but he will encounter a group who are already used to similar principles from their time under Howe, as well as new young signings who are eager to learn.

He also brings with him a group of coaches and analysts who will look to quickly get his message across.

Al-Ahli defender Merih Demiral knows that better than most.

"Looking forward to going to training every day was so important," he added. "They paid great attention to every detail and always made sure we were fully prepared.

"Matthias has built a really strong team around him and they played a huge role in our success."

Jaissle and his staff will be working with a squad whose average age has dropped significantly this summer.

However, the German will still rely on experienced heads such as Dan Burn and Fabian Schar in the dressing room.

Jaissle, a former defender with Hoffenheim, was a few months younger than Junuzovic when he took charge of Salzburg in 2021.

But he did not shirk in telling the midfielder he would find it difficult playing alongside the younger players in the side.

Jaissle challenged Junuzovic to improve and earn his place in the starting line-up, and "kept his word" when he did.

"He understands the players' language," the former Austria international said.

Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes

Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer

It is a little telling that Red Bull Salzburg have not won the league since Jaissle departed following his second successive triumph three years ago.

The Austrian club have not reached the Champions League knockout stage, either, since doing so for the first time ever under Jaissle in 2022, even if they were ultimately hammered 8-1 on aggregate by Bayern Munich in the last 16.

Jaissle went on to show an ability to adapt at Al-Ahli with a different profile of player, winning back-to-back Asian Champions League titles.

As much as his aggressive side pressed high, and got the ball forward quickly, they also had solid defensive foundations and no other team conceded fewer goals in the Saudi Pro League last season.

Such a balanced approach will be needed if Jaissle is to succeed in the Premier League, which is a different beast altogether, as he will soon find out.

But Newcastle's new boss will certainly back himself.

"The best way to describe him is his mentality," said Turkey international Demiral.

"Even if we were losing 2-0 or 3-0, he never lost his belief. He always believed in his players and prepared us with the same mindset in training.

"This is one of the main reasons why we managed to come back and win so many matches."

It's a very different league, and challenge, but Newcastle will hope it's a sign of things to come.

Jaissle's predecessor Howe had similar principles in terms of building a side around physical intensity, pressing and direct attacks.

The German primarily uses a high-pressing 4-4-2 when the opposition are building from the back.

Even when his teams are pushed into more of a mid-block, they have shown an impressive understanding of when to step forward and transition into a high press as a collective.

Howe's defensive tactics should align well with the Red Bull style of pressing, which could make it easier for the players to buy into Jaissle's methods.

What Howe was criticised for towards the end of his tenure was a supposed lack of adaptability.

After joining Al-Ahli, Jaissle inherited a mosaic of superstars and less experienced Saudi players - a wildly different challenge from coaching a Red Bull club with consistency and understanding in style from youth level through to the first team.

While he retained his coaching principles, he recognised the need to platform players according to their individual strengths within that framework.

The Premier League is constantly evolving, with coaches designing new counter-measures to tactics that appear to work from one week to the next.

If Jaissle is going to succeed in the Premier League, that agility will be a vital asset.

After deadly Kyiv strike, Ukraine warns interceptor shortage is costing lives

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 18:19:51 GMT

At the Kvitneva railway station near Kyiv, workers lift white body bags from the pockmarked platform and carry them to waiting ambulances.

Shoes, glasses and some pieces of clothing mark the spot where eight people were killed during Russia's latest massive aerial attack on Ukraine.

Overnight, Moscow fired 115 drones and 24 ballistic missiles. Most of the drones were shot down, but Kyiv's depleted air defences did not intercept any of the missiles.

Twenty-one people were killed and dozens more were injured.

The latest Russian barrage destroyed storage and logistics facilities - from online retailer warehouses to a postal sorting centre.

In Kvitneva, it is not clear if the target was the railway itself or the warehouse beside it, which was also hit and was still smouldering hours later. Down the road, another warehouse was still ablaze more than 12 hours after the attack.

The attack started just after midnight, with very little warning. It was one of the most intense nights of bombardment Kyiv has endured in recent months.

Nearby, Anastasiia Dudley's house was almost totally destroyed but she and her mother survived – shaken but unharmed.

Anastasiia has lived through years of war - but Wednesday was her "scariest night" since the start of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022, she says.

She looks up at the precariously leaning walls of her house, which she says was hit by a drone a few hours before missiles struck the warehouse and the station nearby.

"You see two floors - the first and the second, but it was a three-floor house with a roof," she says. The building's top floor has been sliced off. "So no roof, no third floor, and extensive damage on the second floor. It's pretty unstable".

Ukrainians have lived through four-and-a-half years of war, but now air defences are increasingly vulnerable, resulting in dozens of deaths at a time.

For years, Ukraine has relied on US supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

But the US has used many of its stockpiles during its war with Iran and is reluctant to give up more. After initially offering Ukraine the license to make Patriots in early July, last week President Donald Trump denied the US had agreed to "give away that kind of technology".

Yet without them, Ukraine's skies are wide open.

"Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Last week, following another deadly attack in which only one out of 27 missiles was shot down, he warned that a shortage of interceptors "encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives".

On Wednesday again Zelensky made a direct link between the delays in supply and the "horrific casualties and destruction" witnessed regularly across Ukraine.

"Quite literally every single day, the lives of people here in Ukraine depend on the decisiveness of our partners in Europe and America," he said later, adding he had spoken to Nato chief Mark Rutte about getting interceptor missiles.

Ukraine has an undisclosed number of Patriot systems, but it is the Patriot interceptor missiles which are in short supply.

It takes at least two to bring down each incoming ballistic missile and the system has a range of around 160km (99m), so effectively placing units can be difficult.

Russia, meanwhile, uses on average between 20 and 30 ballistic missiles each time it carries out large-scale strikes on Ukraine.

Ukrainian military expert and former intelligence service officer Ivan Stupak says the lack of interceptors left Kyiv in a situation comparable to having a supercar in the garage but no petrol.

"Imagine you own a Lamborghini but have no fuel," he tells the BBC. "You have one of the best cars in the world, but you can't drive anywhere... The situation with Patriot is similar. The systems are there, but there are no interceptor missiles."

A lack of Patriot missiles leaves the whole country exposed – including the valuable Patriot systems.

"Now the question is how to protect the systems themselves from being destroyed," Stupak says. "Because they could very well become priority targets for the Russian Federation.

"Until we receive more interceptor missiles, these systems need to be relocated or concealed somehow so the Russians cannot detect and destroy them. Right now they're extremely vulnerable."

At the railway station as the medics leave the scene, another team moves in quickly to repair the power lines above the track so services can resume. This is the rapid recovery and clear-up Ukrainians have become all too familiar with.

But they know their skies can still light up with deadly force at a moment's notice. Countering that threat and keeping people here safe can depend on decisions about production and distribution of interceptors made many miles from Ukraine's borders.

No misconduct case for officer who shot Chris Kaba

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 18:13:52 GMT

The Met police officer who shot Chris Kaba will not face misconduct proceedings, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has said.

Sgt Martyn Blake shot the 24-year-old in Streatham, south London, in 2022 after Kaba tried to ram his way past police cars. Blake was cleared of murder following a trial in 2024.

A decision was made in January to pause any proceedings involving Blake until a law change relating to the use of force in misconduct cases was introduced and its impact was clear, the IOPC said.

Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the IOPC's decision brought an end to "almost four years of uncertainty" for Blake, calling the accountability process for police officers "disgraceful".

In June the use of force test in such cases changed from the civil law test to the criminal law test, meaning actions that did not amount to a crime should not amount to misconduct either.

Referring to Blake by his cypher NX121, Rowley said: "Today's decision finally brings to an end almost four years of uncertainty for NX121, his family and the wider firearms command, with all the considerable worry and stress that has brought.

"We also recognise the profound impact on Chris Kaba's family, who continue to grieve their loss."

He added: "Since NX121's unanimous acquittal by an Old Bailey jury, and in the absence of any evidence that he failed in his duties, we have been clear and consistent in our view that he should not face a misconduct hearing."

The commissioner said the decision "must be a milestone moment" to reset the police accountability system.

"No police officer is above the law, but we have been clear the system holding police to account is broken," he said.

"Your life being on hold for four years or more as you go through multiple accountability processes is a disgraceful way to treat brave men and women. I also see the profound effect these cases routinely have on officers' families.

"Criminals are held to account once by the courts - officers can be held to account four times through criminal, misconduct, civil and inquest processes that span years. That cannot be right."

Amanda Rowe, IOPC director of engagement, said they had "always sought to avoid any unnecessary delays" in Blake's case, but said it was right proceedings were paused until the impact of new legislation was understood.

"Having considered both our policy and the representations from the Kaba family and Sgt Blake, we have today notified them of our decision to withdraw disciplinary proceedings," she said.

A coroner will now decide whether an inquest will take place into Kaba's death.

The IOPC's decision was criticised by the Justice for Chris Kaba Campaign and the charity Inquest, with both groups calling it a "blow" to Kaba's family.

Temi Mwale, from the Justice for Chris Kaba Campaign, said the decision sent a "dangerous message", and Deborah Coles, from Inquest, said it signified that "police can act with impunity".

Paula Dodds, chairwoman of the Metropolitan Police Federation, said the IOPC had made "the right decision".

"Police officers are of course – and rightly – highly accountable for their actions. But the officer has sadly suffered years of legal scrutiny following this incident," she said.

"We are pleased this has all now concluded and that the officer can continue to serve the public without this hanging over him."

A spokesperson for the Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, said: "It is right that the IOPC have independently assessed the full circumstances of the case.

"The mayor is clear that all lessons from this case must be learned for the benefit of the police, families and communities impacted."

In a statement, City Hall Conservative Leader Susan Hall AM welcomed the news.

She said: "This disgraceful investigation should never have begun in the first place.

"The mayor and the ideologically captured IOPC are failing our police officers, not least our firearms officers, every day by refusing to provide the political and organisational support to the brave men and women who put themselves in harms way to keep us safe."

She said the officer had been "let down at every stage and heads must roll".

Woman arrested after four stabbed in central London

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:34:52 GMT

A 47-year-old woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden in central London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were taken to hospital after emergency services were called to reports of a stabbing in Endell Street at about 12:30 BST.

The force said two men remain in hospital with injuries not thought to be life threatening or life changing while the other two have been discharged.

The woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault. The Met said it was believed to have been a mental health-related incident.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports.

"While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental-health related incident."

He added a "visible police presence" would remain in the area while evidence was gathered.

Crowds looked on as London Air Ambulance landed in nearby Trafalgar Square as part of the emergency service response but the victims were all transported to hospital by road.

A cordon that started at High Holborn and covered the St Mungo's homeless centre on the street has now been removed.

A spokesperson for St Mungo's said they "could not confirm whether anyone from St Mungo's is involved at this stage".

"Our thoughts are with everyone who has been affected by this distressing incident.

"We are working closely with emergency services on site," they added.

Officers had been seen speaking to people before they entered the centre.

Arjan Gjorga, who manages a fish and chip shop on Endell Street, said a woman had "started stabbing random people".

The 48-year-old added: "We saw this lady after a few minutes being arrested – the police responded immediately."

Another witness, who did not want to be named, said they saw the stabbings take place outside the Shaftesbury Theatre before the woman made her way down Endell Street.

The witness, who wanted to remain anonymous, said: "We noticed she stabbed three people with scissors by the theatre then she came down here and the police were here."

An employee at a nearby barber shop said they helped one of the victims call the police after they had been stabbed.

The worker, who wished to remain anonymous, said: "One of the victims ran into the shop to call the police.

"He was traumatised, he was panicked but the police turned up very quickly."

El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:04:16 GMT

The tremors from Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate primary will have been felt hundreds of miles away by the Democratic Party leadership.

In a year in which Republicans appear to be facing significant electoral headwinds, Democratic primary voters have taken a chance on a left-wing insurgent, raising the stakes in a Senate race in November that could decide overall control of the upper chamber.

The question is whether the way El-Sayed has electrified the party base and tapped into their anger will work on general election voters. And whether an unabashedly left-wing Democrat can win in a swing state.

The party establishment, which had backed his opponent, will hope so.

Primary results across five states on Tuesday were a snapshot of the mood of the American electorate three months before the midterm elections.

Here are four key takeaways from the results.

Abdul El-Sayed's victory on Tuesday night in Michigan's contentious Democratic primary race for Senate was hardly a surprise. He had led by a comfortable margin over congresswoman Haley Stevens for weeks.

While the final projected result was much closer than those surveys had suggested, again raising questions about modern polling accuracy, it doesn't diminish the shockwaves the victory of the former Michigan health official is sending throughout the Democratic Party.

El-Sayed, the child of Egyptian immigrants, ran on a left-wing platform with the backing of such liberal stalwarts as Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Stevens had the backing of Democratic leadership in Washington, an established record as an elected official in Michigan and deep financial pockets, including $32m from Aipac - the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Outside groups favoured her over El-Sayed by a margin of nine-to-one.

None of it mattered.

In debates and on the stump, El-Sayed proved to be the more gifted candidate, and Democrats seemed open to his policies, including government-sponsored health insurance, efforts to lower drug costs, higher taxes on the wealthy and campaign finance reform.

His campaign refrain - "money out of politics, money in your pocket" - has been a common one among left-wing candidates this election cycle.

This sets up a general election contest against former Republican congressman Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed. It will provide perhaps the most dramatic, high-stakes test of whether a left-wing candidate can win a general election race in a true battleground state.

Given the narrowness of El-Sayed's primary victory, he has considerable work ahead if he wants to unite the party before November's vote.

While El-Sayed did well with higher-educated liberals, he'll need to win over the lower-income voters who backed Stevens in Detroit and in more rural areas. These are voters whose preferences the pre-election polling did not seem to adequately reflect.

If El-Sayed loses to Rogers, it would be a major blow to Democratic hopes of retaking control of the US Senate given a Republican hasn't won a Senate race in the state since 1994.

If he wins, however, it could provide left-wing Democrats with proof of concept for why a left-wing candidate for president in 2028 could be more successful than the kind of establishment centrists the party has nominated in recent contests.

And with Michigan's position as a key early state on the Democratic presidential primary calendar, the state will have an outsized say in who the party's nominee will be.

Stevens was the highest-profile Aipac-backed candidate to lose on Tuesday night. In lesser-watched races, the results were more mixed.

Elsewhere in Michigan, Democratic Socialist Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar, who has been an outspoken supporter of continued US support for Israel. He became the latest party House incumbent to be ousted in the primaries.

William Lawrence, who has called for an immediate end to US arms sales to Israel, defeated two centrist Democrats in a House of Representatives district in Michigan that is likely to be a key electoral battleground in November.

If the mood of the Democratic voters has soured on pro-Israel politicians in Michigan, and in previous races in New York and Colorado, that was not the case in the Missouri and Washington results.

In Washington, congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who supports military aid for Israel, easily turned away a left-wing challenger. She is one of the few Democratic incumbents in districts Trump won in 2024 - and will be a prime target for Republicans in November.

Meanwhile, in a solidly liberal Missouri district, Wesley Bell denied a comeback bid from Cori Bush, a founding member of the "squad" of left-wing congresswomen. Two years ago, he unseated her in part because of her criticism of Israel.

While most of the contests on Tuesday night were intraparty primary fights, there were a couple of notable votes that could provide evidence that the overall mood of the electoral continues to tilt toward the Democrats.

In Missouri, voters overwhelmingly rejected a ballot measure that would have made citizen-backed amendments to the state constitution more difficult to enact.

In recent years, such citizen-driven efforts have been used to push Democratic initiatives that had no chance of passage in the Republican-controlled state legislature. They include protecting abortion rights and raising the minimum wage.

Meanwhile in Kansas, voters rejected a ballot measure that would have have required the state's supreme court justices to stand for election. At the moment, they are appointed by the governor and a commission of lawyers.

In 2024, the state high court had ruled that the right to abortion was protected by the Kansas constitution - a decision Republicans said was out-of-step with the will of state voters.

Both efforts were pushed by state Republicans and, in both cases, the proposals were easily defeated.

It was largely a good night for Trump-backed Republicans, who earned a few victories in their primaries.

John James won Michigan's Republican nomination for governor despite being heavily outspent by his wealthy opponent. Trump not only endorsed James but appeared on stage with him last week.

In Kansas, Republicans opted for the Trump favourite for governor amidst a crowded field. And in the Washington state race to replace outgoing Republican congressman Dan Newhouse, Amanda McKinney, the president's pick, also finished first.

The 71-year-old Newhouse, who is retiring, was notable for being one of the last two remaining House Republicans to have voted to impeach Trump after the 6 January 2021 riot at the US Capitol.

Given that this is a reliably conservative district, McKinney is a favourite to defeat her Democratic opponent in November, which would likely move House Republicans further to the right. It's the latest bit of evidence that old-line establishment Republicans like Newhouse are a vanishing breed.

But Trump didn't get it all his own way.

In Michigan, Thomas Smith defeated Trump-endorsed Amir Hassan, a former law-enforcement officer who also appeared on stage with the president, despite Smith having dropped out of the race last month while remaining on the ballot.

Charli XCX on lying, Love Island and life post-Brat

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 15:46:34 GMT

"Was that the truth, or was it a lie?"

This is the question posed by Radio 1's Jack Saunders to Charli XCX about an answer she gave in their last interview.

The Apple singer previously told the presenter that she hadn't started making any new music - when in fact she was putting the finishing touches to her new album, Music, Fashion, Film.

"Yeah, it was a lie," says Charli.

"I'd finished the record pretty much," she tells Saunders during a special performance at the BBC's Maida Vale studios.

"So I was just lying to your face basically.

"I knew when I said yes to Reading and Leeds it was going to be about this next album."

But why do artists feel they need to keep their plans under wraps, and is there pressure to do so?

Released in July, Music, Fashion, Film follow's Charli XCX's huge hit album, Brat.

The record became a cultural phenomenon, used in Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign and even resulted in Collins English Dictionary updating its definition of Brat.

So why keep her much anticipated follow-up quiet?

Publicist Josh Moss tells BBC Newsbeat that at the early stages of a campaign, artists won't be giving much away.

"What people don't realise is that there's so much planning and strategy that goes into an album roll out," says Moss, who has represented artists like Maisie Peters, Bruno Mars and SOMBR.

"At a time where attention spans have shortened, artists want to sustain excitement pre and post release.

"One of the best ways to do that is through drip-feeding information."

So is it all just harmless fun, or is this a case of artists being more cautious?

Maria Veronese runs media training company Mediapro and says Charli XCX's method may not be a surprise to her fans.

"She's fun, she's Brat and it's what we expect of her really," says Veronese.

"It's what her fan base loves her for."

She says a lot of people who use media training, do so because they're nervous about saying things they don't want to.

"We just help them go through all of those scenarios.

"Talk about bridging techniques, and what they can say instead of things they don't want to say, so we're not telling them to lie."

During her interview with Jack Saunders, Charli XCX also discussed the process of getting the album cover together for Music, Fashion, Film.

It contains a black-and-white photo of Velvet Underground musician John Cale, fashion heavyweight Marc Jacobs, and film director Martin Scorsese.

"I will say it was an absolute nightmare," says the singer.

"We were really down to the day before that deadline and you know, they're busy guys," she says.

"I felt it was one of those moments where I was like this is a once in a lifetime moment, this is probably never going to happen again.

"It was really sweet and overwhelming."

And she wanted this album to feel like something new and different.

"The way that Music, Fashion, Film sounds was like a very sort of deliberate response to the way that Brat sounds.

"They're sort of polar opposites."

After the overwhelming success of Brat, does Charli feel like she can have a 'normal' life?

"I can't just sort of go home and like unplug and be like a different person," she tells Saunders.

"Apart from when I'm watching Love Island.

"I will say, that is my one time where I'm like, I'm actually off now.

"I'm not thinking about fonts or whatever."

But she wouldn't want things to be any different.

"I love the life that I have, I wouldn't change it for anything else."

See the Sun like never before with most detailed images yet

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 15:01:33 GMT

Scientists using the world's most powerful solar telescope have captured the surface of our Sun in new, unprecedented detail.

Images and footage show "whirlpools" of activity that it has not been possible to see before.

It is the Sun's magnetic field being twisted and moved by the motion of hot gas.

That constant swirling is a driving force behind bursts of energy from the Sun, creating so-called space weather, that can disrupt Earth's power grids and satellites, and could even injure astronauts.

"The Sun is the source of that energy and of all of that space weather," explained Dr David Boboltz from the US National Solar Observatory (NSO).

Capturing more detailed pictures of our solar system's star will help in responding to that weather, he said.

"To figure out and eventually predict space weather, we want to understand the physics of the Sun, all the way down to the smallest scales."

The findings, published in the journal Nature, were made possible by the Inouye Solar Telescope - a facility built on a high peak in Hawaii, where clear blue skies are free of dust.

Zooming in on the Sun's surface, the team captured a detailed view of swirling vortices.

NSO astronomer Dr David Kuridze, told BBC News: "These twisting motions are creating magnetic energy, which can build up to produce those large-scale explosions."

The term for what the scientists have discovered on the Sun is "Kelvin-Helmholtz instability".

The phenomenon happens when fluids - in this case hot gases - slide past each other and cause small disturbances to grow into spiralling vortices. In the ocean, it helps explain how ripples become giant, powerful waves.

Dr Friedrich Woeger, also from the NSO, explained that finding it on the Sun's surface not only explained the dynamics behind space weather, but even why the surface of the Sun is so hot.

It shows how energy is transported upwards.

"Once there's enough energy wound up in the higher layers, it can then be released, as a flare or what's known as a coronal mass ejection," he said.

Boboltz added that, as well as the practical need to understand and protect ourselves from space weather, the new findings were a reminder that the Sun is a "unique laboratory".

"It's our closest star," he said. "And it can help us understand some very basic laws of physics.

"The first experimental proof of Einstein's general relativity came from solar eclipse observations.

"So simply for human knowledge," he added, "we need to have experiments like this".

'I feel unsafe', says powerlifter over racism row

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 14:32:33 GMT

Belgian champion Sonita Muluh is of Cameroonian descent

A powerlifter who alleged she was subjected to a racially motivated act that she says led to her disqualification from an event has said she "does not feel safe" when competing.

Belgium's Sonita Muluh was attempting a record 334.5kg squat at the Powerlifting Championships in Lithuania in June when Ernestas Kusinas - a 'spotter' who helps to ensure the validity of an attempted lift - touched the weights with his knee.

Muluh was disqualified and not allowed to reattempt the lift by judges, who ruled on a separate technical infringement.

But police in Lithuania have launched a criminal investigation after Kusinas later wrote on Instagram: "I am racist, and ⁠I did it intentionally."

A police spokesperson told Reuters the investigation will focus on the Instagram message and events at the championship, with a maximum penalty of two years in prison.

Kusinas told Reuters his Instagram comment was written out of anger after he was accused of racism by an unidentified social media user, and was intended not as a statement but as a mockery of the accusation.

He has been handed a lifetime ban by the Lithuanian Powerlifting Federation, and his social media accounts have since been switched to private.

"It's shocking to wake up five weeks later and it's all over the internet that he did it on purpose because of the colour of my skin," Muluh told BBC Sport.

"I feel unsafe and uneasy that this person is standing beside me with massive weight, with what can go wrong, with the amount of weight on your back.

"I was lucky when I realised [it hit his knee] and I could stabilise it. Not everyone could. It was the heaviest ever squat for a female."

A devastated Muluh initially refused to blame Kusinas for what she thought was a mistake.

"He did not reach out afterwards to apologise, but he is not obliged to. I thought it was a human mistake, that cost me a lot on the day.

"But there was no hatred [from me]. I didn't lash out; didn't curse at him. There was a video of it posted afterwards and I said: 'I hope he does not get hate.' I believed it was an honest mistake.

"And then I find out five weeks later that he said this."

Muluh, 29, also says she feels the sport's world governing body, the International Powerlifting Federation, "failed" her following the incident, and that swift action is only happening now as the story has grown.

"I feel like the federation needs to do background checks. If you are going to put my life in someone else's hands, at least make sure that person is well equipped to be able to protect me or keep me from harm.

"But they failed me [through] negligence and putting my life in danger.

"[Kusinas] doubled down in his racist behaviour [afterwards]. Only now is he saying it was a joke. There's nothing jokey about any of what he said. He put my life in danger. Nobody spots like that, with their knee.

"It's never going to feel justified... I trained through injuries just to prepare. I've put my body through a lot for this to happen. There's never going to be any real justice."

Muluh, who has won multiple accolades in the sport, went on to say she did not feel welcome at the event in Lithuania.

"I hope [the IPF] do things differently - that they consider the safety of athletes more and especially minority people. I feel that's what has been missing - we have been made to compete in places we didn't feel welcome.

"People looked down on us in Lithuania in a very disgusting way. When I competed in Poland someone sneezed in my face at the airport.

"Some black athletes are booed in competition, we have to worry about our skin colour while competing.

"Powerlifting has been a very supportive niche sport, so far. But who is standing up for athletes against racism? This situation has changed my view a lot. There's a lot of people who didn't speak out about it. A lot of big names didn't say a word about it. They didn't reach out to me. All the black athletes reached out, so we all supported each other."

Speaking to Reuters, Kusinas added he ​unintentionally interfered with Muluh's and other athletes' attempts because he was tired after his duties at the event.

In a statement the IPF said: "The IPF unequivocally condemns racism, discrimination, and hateful conduct in all its forms. Such behaviour has no place within the IPF or the global powerlifting community.

"We acknowledge and commend the Lithuanian Powerlifting Federation for its prompt and decisive response to this matter, including its immediate action to permanently ban the individual from participation within the federation.

"In addition, the IPF will co-ordinate with the relevant IPF commissions, the IPF safeguarding officer, and the IPF Championships Team to identify opportunities to strengthen the recruitment, screening, accreditation, and oversight of volunteers supporting IPF events.

"The IPF remains steadfast in its commitment to equality, inclusion, integrity, and fair play. Racism, discrimination, and hate have no place in our sport."

Following Kusinas' lifetime ban by the Lithuanian Powerlifting Federation, it said in a statement: "We would like to address the situation that unfolded on socal media. We reviewed available information relating to Ernestas Kusinas and were deeply shocked by the views and activities addressed publicly which contradict the principles we stand for.

"The federation takes full responsibility for addressing this matter."

The serial candidates standing against Farage in the Clacton by-election

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 13:44:39 GMT

A record number of candidates are standing in next week's Clacton by-election, but some names on the ballot will be more familiar than others.

As the main parties are not standing against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, the 33 other candidates on the ballot are either from smaller political parties or are standing as independents.

Eight of these names have already appeared on multiple ballot papers elsewhere in the UK however, including Reclaim Party leader Laurence Fox and satirical candidates Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the serial candidates who have decided to stand in Clacton, how they have fared in previous elections, and whether they have ever won enough votes to save their £500 parliamentary - or £10,000 London mayor - deposits.

The Clacton by-election takes place on 13 August, and because there are a total of 34 people contesting the seat it means people in the constituency will be casting their votes on what is understood to be the longest ballot paper in British electoral history.

There are eight candidates standing against Farage who, including the current race in Clacton, will have made at least three attempts to be voted into Westminster or to become London's mayor.

They are: Rejoin EU candidate John Stevens, Social Democratic Party leader William Clouston, Reclaim leader Laurence Fox, independent Joseph 77, Count Binface, and three candidates from the Monster Raving Loony Party - leader Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap.

UK electoral law does not prevent a registered political party from fielding more than one candidate in a parliamentary by-election. Each candidate must have a valid nomination and be authorised by the party's nominating officer.

Nigel Farage has previously stood in seven parliamentary contests since 1994, and successfully became an MP for Clacton in the 2024 general election.

Parliamentary candidates do not have to be from the area they want to stand in to appear on the ballot, but they do have to be nominated by 10 people who live in the constituency.

A £500 deposit is also required to validate their candidacy, which they only get back if they achieve more than 5% of the vote share.

Mayoral elections have stricter eligibility rules. For example, in London candidates must either live, work or be registered to vote in the capital, or rent or own a property in the city. They must also get at least 10 nominations from each London borough and at least 10 from the City of London, and win more than 5% of the vote share to have their £10,000 deposit returned.

Howling Laud Hope, the leader of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, has previously stood in 37 parliamentary elections since 1983.

Real name Alan Hope, the party leader challenged David Cameron's seat when he was elected prime minister in 2010, and stood against former prime minister Theresa May in the 2017 general election.

He gained his highest share of the vote in the 2011 Leicester South by-election, which was held by Labour. Hope finished last of five candidates, with 553 votes, or 1.6%.

He has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 37

Deposits lost: 37

Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, whose real name is Nick Delves, has previously stood for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 13 parliamentary contests.

He stood against former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer in the 2024 general election, but his highest share of the vote came in West Derbyshire at the 2001 general election, when the Conservatives held the seat. He finished fifth of six candidates with 472 votes, or 0.9% of all votes.

Like Hope, he has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 13

Deposits lost: 13

Tom Darwood, who stands under the name Joseph 77, has previously contested seven parliamentary elections.

The strongest of those runs came in Southend West in Essex at the 2019 general election. He received 574 votes, or 1.2%, in a seat held by the Conservatives.

Darwood has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 7

Deposits lost: 7

Count Binface is the satirical alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, who has previously stood in four parliamentary elections and two London mayoral elections.

As Count Binface, Harvey has been on the same ballot as two sitting prime ministers during a general election - Boris Johnson in 2019 and Rishi Sunak in 2024 - and separately stood as a different character, Lord Buckethead, against Theresa May in Maidenhead in 2017.

In 2023 Count Binface stood in the Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election after Johnson resigned as an MP, and in June this year he stood against now prime minister Andy Burnham in the Makerfield by-election.

His best parliamentary result came in the Richmond and Northallerton vote against Sunak in the 2024 general election. He gained 308 votes - 0.6% of the total share - and finished sixth out of 13 candidates.

He has not previously won enough votes to get back any of his deposits.

Previous attempts: 6

Deposits lost: 6

Baron Von Thunderclap - real name Peter Berry - is the third Official Monster Raving Loony Party candidate on the ballot. He previously stood in six parliamentary elections.

The Clacton contest is his first parliamentary by-election however, and his first parliamentary race outside Mid Sussex. His strongest turnout was during the 2001 general election, when he received 601 votes, or 1.3% of the vote share. He finished fifth out of five candidates and the Conservatives held the seat.

He has never won enough votes to get back a £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 6

Deposits lost: 6

Former Conservative MEP John Stevens, who is standing for the Rejoin EU Party, has previously appeared on the ballot in four parliamentary elections.

His best result came as an independent in Buckingham in the 2010 general election, when he challenged then speaker of the House of Commons John Bercow. The main parties do not usually stand against the Speaker in a general election, and Stevens finished second of 11 candidates with 10,331 votes, a 21.4% vote share. Farage also challenged Bercow for the seat that year and came third.

It means Stevens is the only Clacton candidate to have stood against and won more votes than Farage in a parliamentary contest. Stevens also gained enough votes to qualify to have his deposit returned.

Previous attempts: 4

Deposits lost: 3

William Clouston, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, previously stood in two parliamentary elections.

His best result came in Hexham, Northumberland, in the 2024 general election, when Labour gained the seat from the Conservatives. Clouston finished last of six candidates with 1,211 votes, or 2.3% of the vote share.

He did not win enough votes in either contest to get back his £500 parliamentary deposit.

Previous attempts: 2

Deposits lost: 2

Actor turned right-wing commentator Laurence Fox, of the Reclaim Party, has previously stood in one parliamentary by-election and one London mayoral election.

His only parliamentary contest before Clacton was the 2023 Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election. Fox finished fourth out of 17 candidates. The Conservatives held the seat, while Fox received 714 votes, or a 2.3% share of the vote.

He did not win enough votes to get back either of his deposits.

Previous attempts: 2

Deposits lost: 2

For this analysis, the BBC counted previous UK House of Commons elections and elections for Mayor of London.

The current Clacton contest counts towards the three-contest threshold to be included in the analysis.

Local council elections, local and combined-authority mayoral elections, devolved legislatures, European Parliament elections and London Assembly elections were excluded.

Disney agrees deal to let TikTokers use its films and TV shows in videos

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 13:06:43 GMT

Disney and TikTok have agreed a deal which will allow creators to use clips from Disney films, including its subsidiaries, in their videos.

It means clips from hit franchises like Star Wars, Toy Story and the Marvel Cinematic Universe will soon start popping up in videos - which will also be shared on Disney's short-form video platform, Verts.

The scheme will be launched in the US before being rolled out to other countries.

Neither company shared financial details of the agreement, although it follows the collapse of a $1bn (£745m) deal between Disney and OpenAI which would have let people use its characters in AI-generated videos.

That agreement was cancelled in March when OpenAI shut down its AI video generation tool Sora, citing a decision to focus on other parts of its business.

"Today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways," said Disney's chief marketing and brand officer Asad Ayaz, following the TikTok deal being announced.

"Disney owns some of the world's biggest franchises but ownership of attention is shifting towards creators," social media expert Matt Navarra told BBC News.

"Hollywood used to market at fans - now it needs to give fans the raw materials to market with it, and that is quite a profound shift."

TikTok said its platform saw an average of 6.5 million posts relating to film and TV per day last year.

Fans like to use clips from films and TV shows in their videos, but without express permission, they would often be taken down due to copyright claims.

This makes it harder for a wide audience to engage with fan-created content around a big release.

TikTok would also benefit from the "credibility of becoming a formal distribution partner to one of Hollywood's biggest studios," Navarra said.

He added that TikTok's recommendation algorithm gives it the power to "influence which character or scene or forgotten franchise suddenly becomes very valuable again".

Disney and TikTok said a jointly-run programme would boost some creators' videos and give them access to exclusive events.

"This is a deal that repositions and recovers Disney in the UGC [user-generated content] space following the content gap left by the sudden collapse of Sora," Gareth Sutcliffe from Enders Analysis said.

But he said it was not without risk.

"There is an ongoing safety debate around TikTok under European online rules," he said.

"At a minimum, Disney will need to employ significant guardrails to curate the creator content that is selected."

Online creators and influencers are becoming more important to brands' marketing strategies.

Last year, a report from Oxford Economics said YouTube content creators contributed £2.2bn to the UK economy in 2024 and supported 45,000 jobs.

There is also a recognition that even very small influencers, who focus on niche topics, might have lower follower counts but come with a hyper-engaged audience.

Disney launched its short form video platform Verts in the US in March, with plans to expand that further around the world.

Waste workers help winner find binned €1m lottery ticket in Italy

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 12:33:43 GMT

A lottery player who accidentally binned a €1m (£857,158) winning-ticket may be the luckiest person in Italy after refuse workers found the missing slip.

The anonymous player disposed of the ticket in a shop in Bitonto, southern Italy, after checking their numbers and being told it was "non-payable".

The person only realised they threw away a winning ticket after a relative pointed out the numbers they always played had been drawn.

It sparked a two-day search through a "mountain of waste" which had been collected by a bin lorry, the head of the refuse company, Roberto Nicola Toscano, told Italian news agency Ansa.

"This story is nothing short of miraculous," he added.

Recounting the story, he said the mix-up happened because the "non-payable" message appears when the prize is too high to be paid out by the shop.

When the player returned home, their family reportedly pointed out their favourite numbers - 2, 4, 8, 10, and 51 - had been drawn.

"It was then that they realised the misunderstanding. So they all went to the shop together and discovered that the tickets had been thrown away and collected by one of our operators," said Toscano, director of SANB who handles waste collection in the area.

After the player made contact with the refuse company, the bin lorry was located before its contents were compacted for disposal.

"Luckily it was a Sunday, otherwise the load would have already ended up in landfill," the boss told Italian broadcaster TGCOM24.

The truck was then escorted to a special site where the search began to find the "small piece of paper hidden in a mountain of waste".

Finally after a two-day search, the winning ticket was reportedly found by a waste worker on Tuesday morning, with the workers cheering as if they had won the prize themselves.

"It was in a hole-ridden bag along with other damaged tickets: this was one of the few intact ones," Toscano told Ansa.

The cost of the recovery operation is set to be charged to the winner, who had previously signed a declaration promising to cover the search costs.

Toscano told BBC News that he was not authorised to reveal any details on the identity of the winner.

But the luck rubbed off - when Toscano and his colleagues bought a scratch card as a joke, they won €50 (£43).

Uganda team manager has 'no idea' why boxers have disappeared

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 12:23:38 GMT

The team manager for the Ugandan Commonwealth Games team has told BBC Scotland News he has no idea why four boxers with the team have vanished.

Two men and two women who competed for Uganda at the Games failed to turn up for their scheduled flights home and have since turned off their mobile phones.

Media reports in Uganda suggested the four may be looking to seek asylum, but Uganda's chef de mission Godwin Kayangwe said he hoped the athletes would return home before their visas expire in October.

Police say inquiries are ongoing into a number of Commonwealth athletes who have failed to turn up for homeward flights, but it is understood little can be done until the existing visas expire.

The four boxers - Ibrahim Kemis, 20, Nuhu Batte, 22, Emily Nakalema, 32 and Angel Katushabe, 21 - were due to fly back to Uganda on Tuesday.

Kayangwe said he has no idea why they have disappeared but suspects they are "probably still in Glasgow or somewhere in Europe."

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"Their visas are still valid until October so hopefully, probably, they will come back to their country."

Asked why the athletes might be looking to seek asylum, the team manager said he didn't know.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that] - I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

Sports media site NBS Sports said it had spoken to one of the four missing boxers, who claimed the athletes intended to seek asylum and continue their boxing careers in a country they believed offered better training facilities and opportunities than their homeland.

The boxer was also said to have appealed to Ugandans for understanding and asked not to be judged for the decision.

Kayangwe said the matter was now with the Ugandan high commission who will liaise with the authorities in Scotland.

He added that he had a simple message to the missing athletes.

"My message is pretty clear, observe the law and make sure the visa does not expire while you are still here. Come back to Uganda and and they can probably come back to Europe whenever they want."

He added he hoped the boxers would make the "right decision" and return to Uganda.

Pakistan Today also reported that the boxer Qudrat Ullah had not joined the rest of his team-mates in flying home to Pakistan, and that he was not found in his room when officials went to search for him.

From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 11:39:16 GMT

Flip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching weather - and now they've had a revamp.

The most stylish way to wear them this summer is with a kitten heel, according to fashion expert and trend forecaster Angela Baidoo.

"It's not a high heel and it's really kind of easy to just slip in and slip out of," she says.

However, heel or not, the flip-flop has earned itself a bad rap for lack of support and damaging our feet. Is that fair?

"In terms of arch support and joint support, it's not the best style, but people are investing a bit more, getting their flip-flops customised, because it's something that is just so easy to wear," Baidoo says.

Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite, who is also chief clinical adviser at the Royal College of Podiatry, says it's "not accurate" to say flip-flops are bad.

The problem comes if you go straight from wearing a very structured shoe to wearing flip-flops a lot, she explains. It means your foot is under more strain than normal, which makes you more prone to injury.

"The foot does start to change shape and tends to splay a little bit over time," says Branthwaite.

"A good analogy is if you were to wear a corset all the time and then took the corset off, everything would sort of all hang out, so to speak."

So what are the stylish and comfortable alternatives?

Baidoo suggests a more supportive flip-flop, such as a FitFlop, which is sturdier and contoured - a world away from the flat and thin flip-flops that have been cut from a big sheet of foam.

Sliders are out and Crocs are in for Gen Z, she says. They might be "anti-fashion shoes" but they're "really comfy" and designed "orthopaedically" with footbed sandals like Birkenstocks offering the same advantages.

The wooden clog is also making a comeback. It's worn by doctors and chefs on their feet all day. Scholl slider mules are the original orthopaedic shoe, Baidoo says - and admits she once had a pair in pink suede.

Wedges are another option in the heat. "When I speak to some of my friends and some of my clients who work in the plus-size category, the wedge actually provides a form of comfortable footwear. And it provides a nice kind of silhouette for the ankle. You've got the support all the way through the shoe."

You could always opt for the fisherman-style sandal, which looks like something a history teacher might have worn in the 1970s. With socks.

"Men can wear it as an alternative to a loafer. It's not as casual as a flip-flop, which might not be suitable for certain environments. It's a really cool kind of style to adopt for women too," Baidoo says.

So what about the trend for wearing minimalist barefoot shoes? It's all about easing into them, says Branthwaite. In other words, don't buy a pair and then decide to go on a 5-mile hike.

What can scientists learn from a stray SpaceX rocket hitting the Moon?

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 11:19:24 GMT

A stray SpaceX rocket is believed to have crashed into the Moon, forming a crater near a famous lunar landmark and giving scientists a unique research opportunity that could help future missions.

The empty upper stage of a Falcon 9 rocket was due to strike the Moon near the Einstein crater at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h) on Wednesday.

The short, dramatic flash it created would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories in the Americas are analysing the information.

It could be days or even weeks before the full picture of what happened and what we can learn from it is known - but for planetary geologists, this accidental collision is a scientific gift.

Space X's Falcon 9 rocket is a reusable model and has been sent into space on several missions. Its design allows part of the rocket to return to Earth, but other sections are shed in space.

The rocket blasted off from Florida in January last year, carrying two lunar landers into space.

Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon - mission accomplished.

The spent stage - which is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs at least 4,000kg - was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again.

Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with even light from the Sun, gave a faint push.

Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon and was picking up speed every day.

The impact at around 07:35 BST (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope.

Amateur astronomers observing in darkness would also have had little realistic chance of seeing the flash, given that it would have lasted a fraction of a second and occured on a part of the Moon bathed in daylight. And so it may also have been hard for them to see a plume of dust stretching as far as 100km (62 miles) that lasted for several minutes.

Even spacecraft orbiting the Moon were not in the right place at the right time to watch the impact happen live. South Korea's Danuri orbiter had the best chance, having passed near the crash site shortly beforehand. Its team has told Korean media that any footage will only be released once researchers have completed their analysis.

Over the next few days, Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will be in position to photograph the site, allowing images before and after the crash to be compared.

The science and probably the first images might come from powerful telescopes in the Americas where the sky was still dark. Even then, turning the detection of a 14m object hitting a daylight part of the lunar surface i385,000km away won't be easy but not impossible.

Image processing to clean up the picture can take hours, days or even weeks, as scientists check and process the data.

But the sight of the new crater from the orbiting spacecraft will be eagerly anticipated. Because researchers already know the rocket's exact size, speed and point of impact, this collision turns from being a random accident into a rare, controlled experiment.

It is a dream moment for planetary scientists because it lets them test their models of how impacts dig out craters, throw debris across the surface, and send tremors through the Moon's interior.

That has real practical value.

Understanding how much rock and dust an impact throws up will help engineers design safer landers and future Moon bases, working out how far flying debris can travel and how hard the ground might shake nearby.

Material thrown up from beneath the surface offers fresh clues about the Moon's geology, adding to what scientists already know about how the Earth-Moon system formed some 4.5 billion years ago.

This is not the first time a human-made object has struck the Moon. Since 1959, dozens of spacecraft have crashed into it, some by accident and many deliberately for science.

The Soviet probe Luna 2 was the first, followed over the decades by Nasa's Ranger probes in the 1960s, several Apollo-era rocket stages, and more recently the LCROSS mission in 2009, which was deliberately crashed to search for water ice.

The last confirmed accidental impact, in 2022, was thought to be the leftover booster from a Chinese lunar mission launched back in 2014 - a reminder that this sort of space debris has been quietly piling up above our heads for well over half a century.

Key questions as Infantino faces Fifa executives

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 10:08:49 GMT

Gianni Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016

Fifa president Gianni Infantino will meet with senior leaders of football's world governing body on Wednesday as criticism of his now scrapped plan to sell off Fifa's commercial and event operations intensifies.

After secretary general Mattias Grafstrom sent a highly critical internal memo to Fifa staff, Infantino summoned members of the Fifa management board to Morocco.

Tuesday also saw chief of global football development Arsene Wenger insist he was "not involved" in Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, adding that aborting it was "absolutely necessary and beyond question".

Prince Ali, president of the Jordanian Football Association, then accused Fifa of creating a situation which "amounts to blackmail" over unpaid prize money and support for Infantino's re-election.

These claims have not been verified by the BBC, and Fifa made no comment when approached. But Prince Ali's statement is indicative of the strength of feeling among the member associations that oppose Infantino.

At the weekend, Uefa said it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership. Several member associations - including Wales, with England set to follow suit - have withdrawn support for his re-election.

Now Infantino will meet with Fifa's hierarchy to try to secure his position.

This video can not be played

Arrivals for the emergency Fifa meeting in Morocco

BBC Sport understands the meeting will take place at Fifa's Africa office in Rabat.

It will include Grafstrom and members of the Fifa management board.

Among those in attendance will be finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.

It is unclear the intention of the meeting, but it is expected that Infantino will attempt to build bridges in an attempt to create a path to remaining as president.

However, this may not be straightforward.

In his letter to Fifa staff, Grafstrom said the events of the past week had been "a sad and reproachable series of events" which were "difficult to comprehend and accept".

On Friday, Kevin Lamour, Fifa's chief operating officer, said the private investment plan was "the project of one person". He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived".

Infantino will have to show contrition and perhaps offer a route to reform if he is to win back the support of his inner circle.

Gianni Infantino was first elected as Fifa president in 2016

Carlos Cordeiro, Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance, quit on Friday over the plan.

Cordeiro said the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Member associations had been given a deadline of 19 September to approve the plan or miss out on the extra funding that came as part of the deal.

In his resignation announcement, Cordeiro offered a series of questions which Infantino will likely face at Wednesday's meeting.

"Most troubling of all," Mr Cordeiro said, "is the absence of answers to fundamental questions.

"Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?

"These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet member associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind.

"That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game.

"This proposal has become a defining question for Fifa's future."

On top of this, Infantino may also have to map out - or could offer - a route for reform.

This may involve putting additional checks and balances in place that would make it impossible for such a plan to be devised and presented in this way again.

Perhaps he could shelve his plans for a 64-team World Cup? Or offer to open up Fifa's cash reserves?

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Infantino calls executive meeting as criticism mounts

Infantino opponents threaten 'non co-operation' with Fifa

It seems unlikely that Infantino will leave his position as Fifa president by the end of Wednesday.

Infantino has, so far, shown no indication he is considering relinquishing his position. Indeed, he has been trying to rally his core supporter base around the globe.

On Tuesday we saw African countries Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and DR Congo all issue statements in support of Infantino.

Infantino will, however, have to answer serious questions about a hugely controversial and damaging week for Fifa.

There may be those in the room who will query his ability to turn this around, especially with such fierce criticism from European countries.

Could that criticism be strong enough for Infantino to tender his resignation?

More likely, perhaps, Infantino could see this as the start of the fightback.

We may see a statement that will include an apology and a promise of change.

If Infantino does vow to fight on, Uefa and countries from other confederations must look to find other ways to oust him.

What other avenues are open?

The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.

Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.

However, BBC Sport understands there are doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved.

Another step could be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".

So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it wishes.

That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.

In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence.

Infantino would have time to win back votes from those who had been angered by the investment plan.

Uefa can only really go down this route if it is confident of getting over the line.

Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election at the Fifa Congress in March.

Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.

Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is seen as the most likely unity candidate to stand against Infantino.

But there should be no expectation of success. Even at the height of the Fifa scandal in 2015, Sepp Blatter was re-elected as president eight days before he eventually resigned.

If Infantino is still in position later on Wednesday, this story could yet have a long way to run.

Inside Fifa, the expectation is that Infantino has called the meeting in Rabat in an attempt to clear the air, have a show of unity and try to achieve some alignment with his senior staff.

But while that may be the beleaguered president's intention, what remains uncertain is what kind of response he will receive from those present, especially given the highly critical statements issued in recent days by chief of global football development Wenger, secretary general Grafstrom and chief operating officer Lamour.

Some staff are asking if that could have emboldened others at the top of the organisation to speak out against him or to even insist he steps down.

It is no surprise Infantino has chosen Morocco, where he has been based over the past week.

Morocco is friendly territory for him. Not only is the country hosting the next World Cup, its national football association has come out in support of him. And it is where he still hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term at next year's Congress.

The Uefa-led rebellion against him will be hoping that it does not get that far, and that he has been forced to quit long before then.

Afghan boxer appears in court in connection with death of Scottish woman

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 09:22:52 GMT

The man suspected of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece has appeared in court in Athens.

The body of Elisabeth Ross was found in a suitcase at an abandoned building on 18 July, days after she had been reported missing.

Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from Afghanistan, was told during the private court hearing that he faces charges of homicide with intent, robbery and weapons offences.

He made no comment and the case was deferred until Thursday, when it is expected that Ahmadzai will be formally charged.

Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.

Ahmadzai was driven to court in a grey Hyundai i30 with blacked out windows for the hearing.

He was escorted from the court more than an hour later by police officers with their faces covered. He kept his head down as he walked from the building back to the car.

Police said Ross - who is from Edinburgh and is known to family and friends as Lisa - had been volunteering with a refugee support group based in Athens.

She arrived in Greece on 26 June and stayed in the Keratsini area of Piraeus until 10 July.

Her body was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July.

Police said the coroner's initial report failed to determine a cause of death, but more detailed examinations concluded it was an "obvious criminal act, likely asphyxiation".

The BBC understands Ahmadzai, who left Afghanistan after being orphaned aged 15, lives in Greece with his American wife and their child.

After leaving his home country, he travelled to Greece via Iran and Turkey, according to a video telling his story which was published by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

He then settled in a refugee camp on the island of Lesbos, where he met his wife and converted to Christianity.

The couple then set up the charity Love Every Nation Athens to help other refugees.

He won a Greek super lightweight boxing title earlier this year.

The president of the Union of Police Officers of Southeast Attica, George Kalliakmanis, said it was "possible" Ross and Ahmadzai had crossed paths through charity work.

He said they were investigating whether Ahmadzai had a key to the apartment Ross was staying in.

The union said it had verified footage appearing to show Ahmadzai carrying a suitcase which is believed to have contained the body.

It added that a location sharing app, used by Ahmadzai's wife, showed that the suspect had been at the property in Rethymnou Street where Ross is thought to have died.

Kalliakmanis said Ahmadzai had admitted moving the body but denied murder, claiming he had found Ross dead in the bathroom.

The officer said police believed the suspect took the victim's bank card and phone, and "made sure" to send text messages to her family and friends to "make it seem like she was still alive".

He said the police also believed the suspect used the victim's bank card to make withdrawals totalling "around €10,000".

Kalliakmanis added that Ahmadzai's wife had no involvement or prior knowledge of the alleged crime.

A local shopkeeper, Anni Ntinta, told BBC News the area had been "shaken up" by the incident.

She said: "The whole neighbourhood is in major distress. Even the young children. My own daughter, who is 10 years old, is terrified and consumed by fear."

Additional reporting by Daphne Toli in Athens

Apology after carer fed dog food to elderly woman by mistake

BBC News Wed, 05 Aug 2026 05:07:43 GMT

A home carer unintentionally fed an elderly woman microwaved dog food, an investigation has found.

The Radis Community Care worker logged the meal, from the client's freezer, as a "lamb dinner", before a second carer saw the packaging and realised the mistake, the report said.

The food was just one instance of poor care over three months with some "abysmal failures", the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman concluded.

Portsmouth City Council said it no longer commissioned services from Radis. Both organisations have apologised.

The woman ate three mouthfuls of the food in June 2024, a month before she died from frailty of old age, the ombudsman's report said.

The meal came from a pack which was labelled "fresh take on dog food" and "for adult dogs and puppies", it added.

Previously, in April 2024, the council opened a safeguarding inquiry following complaints from the woman's family.

It eventually found concerns that Radis staff had logged visits that did not happen, fed the woman stale and inedible food and left her wet or in darkness overnight.

The woman's Do Not Attempt Resuscitation document was also found scrunched up in a cupboard, the report added.

The inquiry took six months to complete, when it should have taken no more than 28 days.

The council relied on Radis' internal investigation and did not exercise proper scrutiny, even though the company was already subject to a separate wider inquiry into its performance, the report said.

It warned: "Councils cannot outsource their safeguarding duty."

Ombudsman Amerdeep Clarke said: "This is a truly shocking case.

"A vulnerable woman's care deteriorated over many months while a statutory inquiry drifted without proper oversight."

Portsmouth City Council said it had refunded the care fees and paid the family an extra £1,000.

It said it had ended the Radis contract early and had improved its monitoring of care providers together with its response to concerns.

However, Radis Community Care said it "voluntarily withdrew" from providing services in Portsmouth at the end of 2025.

It said it had improved its services and procedures and was no longer employing the care worker involved.

In a statement, it added: "The fact that dog food was mistakenly provided was wholly unacceptable."
