The cost of being single – and how friends are teaming up to beat it

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 23:21:08 GMT

When Leanne split up with her partner in her late 20s she thought she'd have to put her dream of a buying a home in the area where she grew up on hold.

She was earning a good salary but the properties she was hoping for - with a garden and parking space - were too expensive on her own. While she'd just started seeing someone new, it was very early days - far too early to discuss living together.

Her friend since school, Sarah, was single and renting a room in a shared house in Brighton. She also wanted to move back home to Kent, but was worried about how she'd get on the housing ladder on her cabin crew salary.

When Sarah suggested they buy together, Leanne admits she "totally baulked". But after chatting with a mortgage adviser they went ahead - and say it's helped them avoid the so-called singles tax.

Not being partnered up can mean extra costs. It's tricky to quantify and varies by location - estimates suggest it could be anything from hundreds of pounds to £10,000 on average extra a year.

The cost of rent or a mortgage, household bills and subscriptions can't be shared. And a single person pays 25% less council tax than a couple - not half.

Many discounts involve pairing up - 2-for-1 cinema tickets, Two-Together railcards, couples gym memberships - plus solo travellers often pay a single person supplement.

This affects a lot of people. Some 18.5m people had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2024 – 36.8% of the population aged 16 and over, official figures show.

And overall 8.6m people were estimated to be living alone in the UK last year - that's nearly a third of all households.

Ahead of their house purchase, Sarah and Leanne agreed a minimum amount of time they'd live together for - two years, which they then extended to four - and discussed what would happen if one person wanted to leave.

Their mortgage payments were split proportionally to take into account their differing salaries, and the arrangements detailed in a declaration of trust so they would be protected when they came to sell.

They were able to split the household bills - with these coming out of a joint account and self-professed "bill keeper" Sarah keeping track of what they needed to transfer each month - but also cut costs by sharing some meals and the cooking as they had similar eating habits.

"We called it our happy home, not our forever home," says Leanne.

"And it was a very happy home," agrees Sarah.

Benefits to buying a home with friends include a bigger deposit and budget, and split costs, according to the Homeowner's Alliance. But it says people should consider potential pitfalls seriously and plan ahead by being upfront about their finances, seeking separate legal advice and drawing up a formal agreement.

Sarah and Leanne sold their house for a profit four years after moving in, and they put the equity they'd built up toward their next, separate purchases.

"Neither of us would have been able to do what we've done without having the property that we had together," says Sarah. "It's brought us a lot of freedom."

Leanne thinks she would have been able to afford what she wanted in time, but the financial benefits from buying with Sarah made this possible much sooner.

"The hidden singles tax is that everything has to take so much longer for you to be able to be in a position of affordability to do what you want to do," she adds.

Their success inspired their friend Philly to set up Cucoon - an online platform matching up singles to potentially buy together.

She says her aim is to "level the playing field", adding the singles tax is particularly high when it comes to housing.

Julia Pearson, from Hampshire, set up the Just4One website about nine years ago when she wanted to go on holiday and discovered many places would charge her extra if she went alone.

Alongside practical support for solo life, the platform lists travel providers which do not include the single supplement.

Being single feels like a "constant review of your costs all the time", she says.

In a list of a money-saving tips for drivers, the RAC suggests adding a named driver onto your car insurance.

It's something Julia has tried - and says it's saved her 8%.

The RAC says this can bring your premium down, but warns it can also do the opposite.

Julia also shares items with friends – she has borrowed tools to renovate her home and given people plant cuttings from her garden.

"I think as a society, we are becoming more social in terms of our sharing and thinking.

"Rather than thinking, 'I've got to go out and buy that', think about how else can you play that, what else can you do aside from having to buy something?

"And it's good for the social side as well, two benefits in one."

Three factors in midlife can delay the onset of dementia by 13 years

New Scientist August 05, 2026

People who steer clear of smoking in their mid-50s, while also maintaining healthy habits that stave off diabetes and high blood pressure, can expect to gain an additional 13 dementia-free years compared with those who live less healthily during midlife.

We already knew that smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure damage blood vessels and stir up inflammation in the brain, both of which can damage neurons involved in memory and learning, raising the risk of dementia.

But few studies have looked at how avoiding these risks in the 50s affects how long you live dementia-free later in life, says Josef Coresh at New York University. “We thought focusing on time gained may help get across the benefits of averting dementia risks.”

Advertisement

Symptoms of early dementia reversed by bespoke treatment plans

Coresh and his colleagues analysed data from a cohort of more than 12,000 adults living in the US, who were tracked for 26 years, on average. When the adults were 56 years old, on average, and free from dementia, they reported whether they smoked, had diabetes or had high blood pressure.

About a quarter of the participants later went on to develop dementia. The researchers found that the risk of this happening was highest for those who, during midlife, had reported that they had diabetes and high blood pressure, and also smoked. These participants were 2.7 times more likely to develop dementia than those who avoided all three risks during midlife.

Free newsletter

Crucially, participants who avoided those risk factors gained 12.6 dementia-free years, on average, compared with those who experienced all three. “By avoiding a few risks in midlife [when brain changes linked to dementia begin], you get more than a decade free of both dementia and death,” says Coresh.

Avoiding just one or two of the risks was also beneficial. Coresh says participants who did so gained roughly four and eight dementia-free years, respectively, compared with those who experienced all three risks.

Regular exercise and avoiding too many sugary foods are good ways to cut your likelihood of getting diabetes or high blood pressure, he says.

The researchers controlled for other factors known to influence dementia risk, including sex, level of education, physical activity level, body mass index and which variant of a gene called APOE people had – which is the main genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease, the most common form of dementia.

We now have a greater understanding of how exercise slows cancer

But they didn’t account for all of the additional factors that are known to affect dementia risk, says Richard Siow at King’s College London. These include hearing loss and how socially isolated people are. Because of this, the benefits of avoiding the three midlife risks the study focused on may be greater or smaller than the results suggest, he says.

Another limitation is that the study focuses on the population level, rather than individuals, and included only people living in the US. Individuals in other countries may gain a different number of dementia-free years by adopting a healthy lifestyle in their 50s, due to differences in their genetics or exposure to environmental factors known to influence dementia, such as air pollution, says Coresh.

Neurology Open Access DOI: 10.1212/WN9.0000000000000152

Swallowing faecal capsules reduces peanut allergy in six adults

New Scientist August 05, 2026

Six adults with peanut allergy have become more tolerant of peanuts after swallowing capsules containing the faeces of someone with no food allergies. The finding from the small clinical trial adds to growing evidence that food allergy is related to the mix of microbes in a person’s gut, and may be relieved by altering this mix.

“This study provides the proof of concept that microbial therapy is an intervention that should be further evaluated for treatment of food allergy,” says Rima Rachid at Boston Children’s Hospital, who led the research.

The trial involved 15 adults with an average age of 21 who experienced allergic reactions, like hives or lip swelling, if they ate even small traces of peanut. Over the course of a day, they were asked to swallow 36 capsules that contained the faeces of a healthy donor with no food allergies. The idea was to try to colonise their guts with the gut microbes of the donor.

Advertisement

The allergy culprit histamine also boosts our memory

When the participants were tested four months later, six were able to consume greater amounts of peanut without allergic reactions. Most could safely ingest peanut flour at a dose equivalent to one whole peanut, and one participant was fine with all the doses that were tested – including the equivalent of four whole peanuts. “These responses represent a marked improvement,” says Rachid.

Other participants dropped out of the study or didn’t become more tolerant of peanuts, possibly because the microbes from the donor faeces failed to colonise their guts, she says.

Some of the volunteers reported side-effects from the capsules, like diarrhoea or abdominal pain, but they were mild and short-lived.

John Ziegler at the University of New South Wales in Australia says it’s too early to judge the treatment’s efficacy because it was a “small open-label uncontrolled study”. In other words, all the participants knew they were receiving the treatment, so any positive responses might have been due to the placebo effect.

Your microbiome may determine your risk of a severe allergic reaction

Rachid and her colleagues are now running a larger trial in children aged 12 to 17 with peanut allergy who have been randomised to take capsules containing concentrated faecal microbes from a healthy donor or a placebo. This will provide a clearer picture of whether the treatment works, she says.

At the moment, peanut allergy is mostly managed by avoiding peanuts and carrying an EpiPen to inject in the event of accidental exposure. It is sometimes treated with oral immunotherapy, which involves daily ingestion of gradually increasing doses of peanut powder to desensitise the immune system. But some people find this regime too burdensome, and its protective effect wears off after discontinuation.

This is why it is promising that a single day of treatment with the faecal capsules reduced peanut allergy four months later in some participants, says Rachid. For now though, these participants still have to avoid peanuts and carry an EpiPen because “we do not know how long the protective effect will last,” she says.

Free newsletter

An interesting finding of the study was that when the faeces of participants who responded to the treatment was transplanted into the guts of mice, it resulted in a thousand-fold increase in gut bacteria called Bacteroidales. This backs up other research suggesting that Bacteroidales bacteria are protective against food allergy. For example, a study of 1400 Canadian children found that peanut allergy was associated with low Bacteroidales levels in their guts.

In a previous study, Rachid and her colleagues also showed that treatment with Bacteroidales bacteria prevented food allergies in allergy-prone mice. The reasons for this protection are still being figured out, she says.

Faeces capsules have also been successfully used to treat ulcerative colitis and auto-brewery syndrome. They are more convenient than traditional faecal microbiome transplants, which involve infusing donor faeces through a tube into recipients’ guts.

Science Translational Medicine DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed. aee3263

At what point does my family tree stop doubling and start decreasing?

New Scientist August 05, 2026

My family tree doubles at every past ancestor generation, branching back into the past. At what point does it decrease to reflect the size of the smaller historical population?

Hillary ShawNewport, Shropshire, UK

Global population was around 2 billion in 1930, 1 billion in 1820, 0.5 billion in 1640 and 0.25 billion in 900. Meanwhile, if your parents were born in 1950, and 10 doublings equal 1000 ancestors, theoretically you would have 2000 ancestors from 1700 (assume average maternal age 25), 2 million from 1450 and 2 billion from 1200. So, these two series cross around the year 1300.

Advertisement

However, your family tree numbers stabilise much later and smaller than that because, before railways, many people lived in isolated communities and married distant relatives.

As an extreme example, the Scottish archipelago of St Kilda had around 100 people for several centuries before mass emigration kicked in around 1800 – about the minimum number to avoid excessive inbreeding and genetic problems.

In the 1700s, chances are that most of your ancestors came from a village of a few 100. Before that, it’s almost all inbreeding

On the British mainland, before railways, there were travelling merchants, justices, preachers, soldiers and beggars, but people would marry in a similar social class, religion, et cetera.

In the cities, especially port cities, you might marry an outsider, but pre-railway villages were almost as isolated as St Kilda and of similar population size.

Around 1650, it took seven days to travel between York and London, due to atrocious roads, which would have been quagmires in winter, dust bowls in summer.

In 1700, just 15 per cent of the British population lived in urban areas, which were small. London then had 650,000 inhabitants, but other cities were much smaller: Bristol had 20,000, Manchester 10,000 and Liverpool 5000 people. So, chances are that most of your ancestors came from a village of a few hundred in the 1700s. Before that, it’s almost all inbreeding.

Simon McLeishLechlade, Gloucestershire, UK

It is actually more to do with the availability of unrelated partners than the wider population size. The availability of the bicycle has been cited as one factor that made it easier to find less closely related prospective partners. Parish records in Dorset, UK, show that, between 1887 and 1916, the proportion of marriages between people in the same village dropped from 77 to 41 per cent.

The royal families of Europe often married close relations for centuries to preserve the purity of the royal blood. The Habsburgs were the best known example, with the “Habsburg lip” a physical trait seen in many portraits of those related to the dynasty.

Robin MaguireHobart, Tasmania, Australia

The answer will vary when factors such as geography or social practices limit potential marriage partners to a particular segment of the population.

For an extreme example, consider the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egyptian rulers. After the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC, the Macedonian general Ptolemy I Soter appropriated the throne of Egypt and his descendants kept power in the family through the practice of intermarriage.

The final ruler in the Ptolemaic line was Queen Cleopatra VII (born in 69 BC), the paramour of Julius Caesar and subsequently of Mark Antony. Going back through her family tree, she had about the usual number of direct forebears in the late 100s BC, but all of these were exclusively descended from the irreducible minimum of just two ancestors in the late 200s, King Ptolemy V Epiphanes and his consort, Queen Cleopatra I. There were six incestuous liaisons along the way. This unusual background did not seem to do the final Cleopatra any harm: she was almost as famous for her learning as for her vivacity.

John DaviesHaverbreaks, Lancaster, UK

Your family tree’s size just stops doubling when it reaches the size of the earlier population, and you discover that two of your great- to-the-X-grandparents are the same individual!

Anthony WoodwardPortland, Oregon, US

It never does. Tracing your ancestors backward in time for 8 million years, approximately 32,000 hominin generations, they will become the last common ancestors of chimpanzees and hominins.

How does my energy use differ if I walk, jog or run for 1 kilometre?

New Scientist August 05, 2026

How does energy use by the body differ when I walk, jog or run for 1 kilometre?

Eric KvaalenLes Essarts-le-Roi, France

An article in Nature gives a graph showing oxygen consumption as a function of speed for walking and running (“Endurance running and the evolution of Homo”, 2004).

Advertisement

For walking, the curve is U-shaped, with a minimum of about 165 millilitre O2 per kilogram body weight per kilometre at around 1.3 metres per second. Running (which includes jogging) is a straight line that decreases from around 210 ml O2/kg/km at 2 m/s to around 200 at 6 m/s.

This means that if you want to go a certain distance in a given, fairly long amount of time while consuming the lowest possible amount of oxygen, then you should walk.

However, when the allotted time is less than a certain value, corresponding to a slightly fast walk, then you should alternate between running as fast as you can and walking at that slightly fast walking speed.

My theory is that, because dogs don’t climb and have no aerial predators, they tend to not have much concept of ‘up’

Note, however, that this is talking about total oxygen consumption, not extra oxygen consumption over normal basal rate. To minimise extra oxygen consumption, the optimum is a slower walk than that for total consumption.

The mathematics of balloon animals

New Scientist August 05, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

This edition of Feedback is an exercise in time travel – in that every item is something from absolutely ages ago that we somehow missed. We would feel guilty, but it is the summer holidays (in the northern hemisphere, anyway) and many readers will have half an eye on their errant children, so we thought we could get away with it.

So, cast your minds back to 2008. This, obviously, was the year of the 20th Canadian Conference on Computational Geometry, held in Montreal. A large amount of research was presented at this conference, but reporter Matthew Sparkes recently stumbled across a theoretical study by Erik Demaine, Martin Demaine and Vi Hart. It presents “a general mathematical and algorithmic theory for balloon-twisting structures”.

Advertisement

If you didn’t grasp that, allow us to clarify: it’s about the geometry of balloon animals. The authors develop a mathematical framework that allows them to calculate how many balloons you need to generate a particular shape, whether it is a dog (one) or some complicated polyhedron like a dodecahedron (10). These, naturally, are referred to as “Platonic balloons”.

Throughout the paper, the authors use the term “bloon” to refer to a mathematical entity equivalent to a balloon. Feedback wasn’t clear why this neologism was necessary, until we realised that they were therefore able to refer to a balloon of twice the usual length as a “doubloon”.

Curious to know what the authors had been up to since, Feedback went a-searching. Hart became a science populariser on YouTube, then a senior manager at Microsoft. Meanwhile, Martin and Erik are father-and-son researchers and artists, both fascinated by the mathematics of folding.

Erik, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has been in New Scientist a lot. Recent papers include “Overlapping unfoldings of cones and convex polyhedra” and “Tetris is hard with just one piece type“. More from Erik, please.

Continuing on the topic of being very late to things, reader Derek Long flagged a paper from 2018, “Parachute use to prevent death and major trauma when jumping from aircraft: randomized controlled trial”. It reports on a study called “PArticipation in RAndomized trials Compromised by widely Held beliefs aboUt lack of Treatment Equipoise (PARACHUTE)”.

(Side note: that is a truly excellent scientific acronym. We haven’t had any of those in a while.)

The problem posed is one of evidence. “Parachutes are routinely used to prevent death or major traumatic injury among individuals jumping from aircraft. However, evidence supporting the efficacy of parachutes is weak and guideline recommendations for their use are principally based on biological plausibility and expert opinion.” If readers haven’t yet twigged: the paper is satirical, poking fun at the idea that even the most common-sense interventions should be tested in a full randomised controlled trial.

As the authors write: “In seminal work published in the BMJ in 2003, a systematic search by Smith and Pell for randomized clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of parachutes during gravitational challenge yielded no published studies.”

Feedback actually ran across that review back in 2004. The authors noted they were “unable to identify any randomised controlled trials of parachute intervention” and suggested that “everyone might benefit if the most radical protagonists of evidence based medicine organised and participated in a double blind, randomised, placebo controlled, crossover trial of the parachute”. Oof.

Fifteen years later, they did do a trial. This showed that “parachute use did not significantly reduce death or major injury”, with the slight caveat that “the trial was only able to enroll participants on small stationary aircraft on the ground”. This was helpfully illustrated by a photo of one of the participants jumping, parachute-less, out of a grounded plane. As the authors say: “Our findings should give momentary pause to experts who advocate for routine use of parachutes for jumps from aircraft in recreational or military settings.”

Some concepts can’t be traced back to their origins. One such is the spherical cow joke, which illustrates the difficulties of working with highly simplified and abstract models of complicated, real-world situations. It involves a physicist who figures out how to improve productivity on a dairy farm, but their solution only works for spherical cows in a vacuum. Nobody seems to know who came up with this: the oldest references place it in the 1960s, but the origin stories are all vague and one reference replaces the cows with chickens.

However, another sphere-based physicist joke seems to be older. Feedback has just learned, many decades after the fact, about an insult deployed by Fritz Zwicky, who, in the 1930s, produced some of the first evidence for dark matter. A noted curmudgeon, Zwicky was fond of referring to people he disliked as “spherical bastards”. Such a person is a bastard no matter which way you look at them.

Feedback will be using that from now on. But we also want to know the etymology (if that is quite the term) of spherical bastards, chickens and cows. Any insights welcome.

We must adapt to climate change while also tackling the root cause

New Scientist August 05, 2026

When your house is on fire, should you call a firefighter, an architect or a politician? OK, that’s an easy one – but what about when the world is on fire? That is a question many of us will be wrestling with as dangerous blazes spring up across much of the world.

Calling a firefighter fixes your immediate problem, which is that your house is burning down. What it doesn’t address is why your house is burning, or the steps you could have taken to reduce the risk of disaster.

Why is climate action stalling, not ramping up as Earth gets hotter?

As we report this week, the question of how to prevent wildfires in Europe is now at the top of many minds on the continent. This means changing the way that land is used in order to build in resilience, much as an architect might design a home with fire doors or other safety features.

Advertisement

Learning to live with wildfires in this way is a form of climate adaptation. It is essential that we redesign our way of life to ease the burden of the warmer world we have created, but that doesn’t mean we should ignore the underlying cause: burning fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions.

As long as our society is dependent on fossil fuels, Earth’s climate will continue to warm

And yet, in responding to Europe’s extraordinary summer, some people seem to want to do just that. “We’ve lost the war against global warming – so we should ditch net zero and learn to handle hot weather” was the view of one columnist in The Telegraph, a UK newspaper known for publishing climate-sceptic views.

This is entirely wrong, and it is where our politicians must step in. If society is organised in such a way that your house keeps getting set on fire, there is only so much an architect can do – eventually, it will burn down. Similarly, as long as our society is organised around burning fossil fuels, Earth’s climate will continue to warm and the wildfires will continue to get worse. Achieving net zero, meaning we no longer emit a meaningful amount of greenhouse gases, is the only way to do that. Politicians who say otherwise might as well hand out matches.

Why don’t dogs look up when a low-flying plane or helicopter passes overhead? I’ve never seen one do this. (continued)

Dyane SilvesterArnside, Cumbria, UK

As a former dog owner, and now regular dog-sitter, my theory is that, because dogs don’t climb and, as a species, have no aerial predators, they tend not to have much concept of “up” (except where it’s upward- sloping ground).

Advertisement

If you drop something from a height, most dogs will look for it on the floor rather than realise that there was a table between the object and the floor.

I did, however, have one Alsatian who, if I appeared at an upstairs window when she was in the garden, could immediately locate and arrive at the room I was in, despite having never been able to see out of any upstairs windows in our house. She also noticed and watched birds and low-flying aircraft.

I did manage to stump her once: by climbing out of the skylight and appearing on the roof. She never worked that one out!

David LewisLondon, UK

Although unusual, a friend’s late spaniel would look at aircraft flying above her in the park. She would then bark and chase them. Fortunately, she never caught one!

C. H. JohnsonColyton, Devon, UK

Because they know planes and helicopters don’t bring their food or any doggy treats.

Mayor Wayne Brown makes light of billboard gaff revealing opening date for Auckland City Rail Link

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown has made light of an embarrassing gaff this morning in which a billboard blunder accidentally revealed the City Rail Link (CRL) opening date.

“[They] finally did something ahead of time.”

The country’s largest infrastructure project will be open to the public on September 13, according to electronic billboards appearing around the city centre early this morning.

Brown and Transport Minister Chris Bishop intended to reveal the long-awaited date outside the new Karanga-a-Hape station at a press conference this morning, alongside officials from the CRL, Auckland Transport (AT) and KiwiRail.

They have just confirmed the date to waiting media, with Bishop saying: ”This is one of the most significant transport investments in New Zealand’s history, and in just a few weeks Aucklanders will finally be able to use it."

Brown added: “People have been asking me for years when the CRL was going to open. Now we can give them an answer.”

The Herald asked Bishop’s office and AT if the timing of the billboards was an accident.

“It’s a bit ironic because City Rail Link is late and the announcement of its opening is early. I did find that odd,” Bishop replied.

Adding to today’s blunders, Bishop mistakenly said the project would be opened on Friday, September 13, not Sunday.

The billboards have since been swapped out with ads saying the CRL is “arriving soon”.

Bishop said the CRL was “a story bigger than the numbers that will grab the headlines”, saying the project was ultimately about the people who would use it every day rather than the infrastructure itself.

He described the CRL as “not simply another piece of infrastructure”, adding its real value lay beyond the tunnels.

“It’s about what’s outside them.”

Bishop called the project “a symbol of ambition for Auckland” and acknowledged it had come at a cost, with years of construction disrupting residents, commuters and businesses.

“That does come with trade-offs along the way,” he said.

While conceding mistakes had been made during the project’s delivery, Bishop said the end result justified the challenges.

“It’s been worth it. Have there been mistakes along the way? Absolutely. Are there lessons we must learn for the future? Of course, and we will.”

He said once Aucklanders began relying on the rail link, they would not be thinking about “the consenting challenges, the funding agreements, the arguments that have been had along the way”.

“That’s the point. Good infrastructure sits quietly, making our lives a little bit better than they otherwise would have been.”

Bishop noted the idea for the rail link stretched back more than a century, saying the project had first been discussed in the 1920s under the name the Morningside Deviation.

“Here we are 100 years later, finally delivering the City Rail Link project for Auckland.”

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten called this morning’s mistake a “bummer”.

“Yeah, it’s really disappointing.

“I mean, we wanted the opportunity to share that with our stakeholders and our people.”

She said they had been in contact with the billboard company and it was a “content loading issue”, and confirmed the date had only been decided this week.

Bishop said he hoped the error would lead to a discount on advertising in the future.

Brown also referenced this morning’s error, saying they “finally did something ahead of time”.

He said the CRL would fundamentally change the way Aucklanders travelled, describing it as “a significant step to a more connected and productive city”.

He said the focus now shifted to ensuring the network was well used, with Auckland Council working to increase housing around rail stations through Plan Change 120.

“We want people to use the City Rail Link. That’s our next step. That’s our next challenge,” Brown said.

Encouraging developers to build multi-storey homes near stations would place more people within easy reach of public transport.

“If we upset a couple of people in leafy roads, we’ve got to get people onto it to make it pay for itself.”

Brown said he was committed to doing things “better, faster and cheaper”, arguing trains offered Aucklanders a better and faster way to travel, while the $50 weekly fare cap made public transport more affordable.

He said businesses that had endured years of disruption during construction were already beginning to see the benefits.

“For business owners who’ve struggled while the CRL was under construction, they can reap the rewards of being so close to it with the increased foot traffic.”

Pointing to nearby hospitality businesses, Brown said one café owner had just recorded his best trading day in a decade.

“There’s more coming.”

While acknowledging the project “cost too much and took too long”, Brown said it would be appreciated for generations.

He said the rail link would provide quicker trips across Auckland, greater travel choice, increased rail capacity and easier access to work and school while helping reduce road congestion.

“We’ve got to sell that message. Get on the train. Get on the train,” he said.

Brown admitted he had long held strong views about the project’s cost but said there was “no doubt” it would help Auckland keep moving and support its growth for decades.

Thanking everyone involved in delivering the project, Brown said the CRL had “produced every form of human emotion” before adding: “I’m now delighted to say I’ve lived long enough to see it open.”

AT earlier announced the day would be on a Sunday, to help cope with the expected demand.

AT has also announced a new Journey Planner tool, which shows what public transport trips will look like when CRL opens.

The Journey Planner preview launch is set to coincide with the release of the initial CRL opening timetable that will take effect when services begin.

The date of September 13 had been suggested to the Herald this week.

Starting this weekend, AT is running three Saturday sessions to show the project to the public.

Those with free tickets can visit the stations.

The city’s mayor says the council’s 50/50 share of the project is why Super City rates have been hiked by 7.9%.

In May, former CRL CEO Sean Sweeney told the Herald there were missed opportunities earlier in the project, where money could have been saved.

The Government has said there will be a full review of the project, including cost and time blowouts.

Once the link is running, trains will run every five minutes through the city centre and, on average, about 10 minutes elsewhere on the network during peak times.

What New Zealand can learn from Andy Burnham’s UK plan – Eric Crampton

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

Andy Burnham at Labour's Special Conference, where he was confirmed as the Labour Party's new leader and the country's next Prime Minister. Photo / AFP

Election 2023 brought us a new Government committed to localist approaches. National had campaigned on greater localism as an alternative to the prior Labour Government’s more centralising tendencies across water services, polytechnics, housing and farming regulation.

In his Waitangi speech in 2024, the Prime Minister said that, “We, like you, believe in localism and devolution, not centralisation and control. No one understands your iwi like your iwi does.”

Since then, reforms to water services have kept them more local than had otherwise been planned. Housing incentive payments to councils will make it easier for them to say yes when developers want to build. There has been some progress in undoing the amalgamation of the polytechnics.

Local councils have been commanded to come up with ways of delivering integrated regional spatial plans that suit the proposed new resource management framework. But there is still space for more decentralised approaches within those amalgamated bodies around other functions. Probably safest to call that one “less than localist” overall.

But it seems at best unlikely that election 2026 will have either National or Labour campaigning on localism. And it is a bit of a shame. The change in leadership of the UK’s Labour Party has brought a thoroughgoing proposal for decentralisation. Parts of it would be well worth the attention of parties here forming up their own election platforms.

Last week, Andy Burnham’s Labour Government published a Cabinet Statement on “Rewiring the State”. It proposes radical decentralisation and outlines a model that it would like to apply in England, with the devolved governments in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland encouraged to follow a similar approach.

Burnham had been Mayor of Greater Manchester – ground zero for England’s experiments with devolution – for almost a decade before becoming Labour leader and Prime Minister.

Core to the proposal is letting local governments keep more of the tax revenue generated in their jurisdiction.

Currently, British regional governments receive grants from central government to provide services. From 2028, those grants will be replaced by a share of the income tax collected by His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs in the area.

The Cabinet Statement argues that it will “enable greater investment to fund interventions that will deliver a return”. In short, if a region invests in projects that increase local income, it will see the benefits directly in its accounts.

Mayors will also have more authority over outcomes that had previously been under centralised control. They will take up control of vocational training budgets for 16- to 19-year-olds and build training pathways suited to their regions. Employment support will devolve to mayors as well, with greater devolved responsibility for social housing. Funding lines would follow devolved authority.

Other funding currently controlled by bodies covering England as a whole, like sports and cultural funding, could also flow down to mayors.

At the same time, Burnham’s Government proposes strengthening local accountability to accompany mayors’ greater funding authority. The Local Audit Office will be strengthened. Chief executives of mayoral strategic authorities will become Local Accounting Officers, personally accountable for the use of public money.

UK Labour suggests a “smaller and more strategic Civil Service”, with functions devolved down to the local level rather than delegated down from central government. There is a considerable difference between delegation and devolution. Under delegation, central government tells local councils to perform a duty, and takes responsibility back if it does not like the outcomes. Devolution means local communities own the issue.

Central government will focus on the things that are best suited to central government; other functions devolve. And Cabinet agreed that devolution will be the default: Secretaries of State will have to justify maintaining central government control when policies or services are being designed or altered.

It would be a radical transformation.

The UK and New Zealand are among the world’s most centralised governments. Central governments and central government officials strongly resist arguments for devolution. It is easy to wind up in self-reinforcing spirals where underperformance by local government leads to greater centralisation, and greater centralisation means local governments lose the capability to perform well.

It will be challenging for Burnham to achieve the change he seeks. Just as it would be challenging here.

But consider the opportunity.

New Zealand will soon have amalgamated councils. I believe none of the stories arguing that amalgamation will provide administrative cost savings. However, they will mean that the larger councils will have more in-house capacity and resource. They will be more capable.

Those larger authorities would be well advised to maintain space for localism within their jurisdictions. It would be absurd for decisions about the location of a crossing in Masterton to go to a body that spans from Miramar up to the Kāpiti Coast.

But they could also pitch for greater devolved responsibilities and associated funding lines. A proposal from a small district council to take up responsibility for aspects of social service delivery might be laughed at by central government officials. One coming from strong regional mayors could be taken more seriously.

New Zealand’s Labour Party has not yet released much of its election platform. I hope Labour, and others, look at the UK’s proposal before finalising their plans.

Central Hawke’s Bay District Council decides to push for Burnside Bridge repair

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

Burnside Bridge near Takapau, Central Hawke's Bay, was left damaged after Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023.

Central Hawke’s Bay District Council has decided to spend $100,000 to test whether repairing Burnside Bridge near Takapau is feasible and affordable.

The decision was voted on at a council meeting on Wednesday, with six councillors in favour and three against.

The Takapau community has pushed hard for alternative repair or replacement options to be explored after being told during consultation that a replacement bridge was economically unviable.

The one-lane bridge over Makaretu River was smashed by floodwaters and debris during Cyclone Gabrielle and closed due to structural damage to the piers and two adjoining bridge spans.

Locals were told a two-lane replacement would cost up to $16 million, with the estimate for a one-lane bridge at $9m.

Previous funding applications to NZTA for a replacement bridge and lower-cost ford crossing were unsuccessful due to what NZTA said were the high cost, low traffic volumes of the bridge and the availability of an alternative route.

An agenda for the council meeting on Wednesday notes a targeted repair of the 100m bridge, built in 1921, could be done for an estimated $1.6m.

The agenda said the repair would be to 25% of the existing structure. It was expected to provide a 20-40-year service life with routine bridge maintenance, subject to investigation, design, consents, procurement and funding approval.

Wednesday’s decision authorises the council’s chief executive to progress technical investigations, economic assessment, and engagement with NZTA. The decision does not commit the council to repairing the bridge.

Councillors Brent Muggeridge, Kirsty Lawrence and Pip Burne voted against it.

Muggeridge said he didn’t accept it was a good use of money.

“We are not here to make decisions on sentiment; we are here to make them on the best outcome for the ratepayer of CHB, not just one community, and I just can’t see this $100,000 being a good spend.”

Councillor Todd Chote said he was in favour of the option, but felt consideration should be given to asking the community affected by the bridge to pay more of the $100,000.

He asked whether a targeted rate for Takapau and the surrounding area could help fund the bridge repairs.

“I love their heart and their passion they have got into this; are they willing to back that up?”

The council’s chief financial officer, Brent Chamberlain, told the meeting it was possible, but it would require community consultation and backing.

Councillor Gerard Minehan said the council owed it to the community to explore further.

“They have worked tirelessly to explore every possible solution, and I believe we owe it to them to ensure every reasonable option is properly investigated before making a final decision.

“For me it isn’t just about the financial cost; councillors have previously recognised the importance of investing in projects that have strong community support.”

Deputy mayor Jerry Greer echoed the sentiment and said no stone should be left unturned.

In July, a petition of over 350 signatures led by Takapau local Shelley Burne-Field was presented to the council alongside letters of support.

The petition requested that all options and funding be explored by local and central governing bodies to rebuild, repair or replace the Burnside Bridge to a standard and cost acceptable to the community.

Earlier, Central Hawke’s Bay farmer Dave Ellison sought his own estimate to rebuild the bridge from North Island bridge construction company Bridge It NZ after being told it was unviable.

The council agenda noted this estimate had since been withdrawn by Bridge It NZ’s company director due to it being inaccurate.

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Decades in the making: How Auckland finally got an underground City Rail Link

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

On his first day as the Mayor of Auckland’s new Super City, Len Brown had one goal in mind.

“I’m elected, I’ve got a big mandate and that mandate is to deliver on critical projects and, in particular, the City Rail Link,” Brown tells the Herald, standing outside the revamped Waitematā (formerly Britomart) Station.

The inspiration was of course Sir Dove Meyer Robinson, who advocated for a rapid transit plan for Auckland in the 1960s.

“Every second person at my transport meetings were telling me we should’ve just followed him. And if we’d followed him, we would’ve had [a] metro in Auckland already.”

It’s become a bit of a historical lore, the dream of “Robbie”, as he was known.

That wish – abandoned after it failed to get support around the council table and from the then Government – was for trains running every three minutes from an underground terminal in the city centre.

It would then connect to above-ground tracks leading to Howick, the airport and through a tunnel to the North Shore.

“I met him briefly once, in my very young days, and he was something of a legend around Auckland,” Brown says.

While Robinson’s dream was never achieved, Brown’s has now come true.

Brown says it wouldn’t have happened without the (then controversial) Super City being formed in 2010.

“The people had one plan, one vision, one budget and one leader. My expectation was that as soon as we announced these sorts of projects, the Government would come on board and be supportive.

“That of course, is not what happened. It was a much longer discussion, compromised by some extent because it was about significant funding from the Government.”

Then in February 2011, the Christchurch earthquakes hit.

The Government’s attention and finances were all focused on the Christchurch recovery.

“In the meantime, we spent a lot of time basically putting the right parts of the jigsaw puzzle in place,” Brown says.

“We introduced the Hop card, which was an extraordinary feat in itself. We completely aligned the public transport network in Auckland, so buses would go to trains.

“And then the Government supported us in putting in place new electric trains.

“There’s never only just one silver bullet. The public started to respond; they really started to flock onto public transport. That really proved the case for John [Sir John Key] and his Government.”

The business community had a vision too.

Precinct Property was looking to redevelop the old Downtown Shopping Centre and turn it into what is now Commercial Bay.

Others could see the potential around the Britomart Station for urban development.

But if that area of town was going to be dug up, surely underground tunnels for a rail network should be done at the same time?

“Commercial Bay was going to basically tap into the City Rail Link and into Britomart station, and it was critical for them that we were totally committed to this project and to the benefit of their development,” Brown says.

“I gave Scott Pritchard [Precinct Property CEO] my assurance that our council was committed. I said, we’re putting money in, which was also something a little unusual.”

Eventually, Brown talked the Government into it and in 2016, a deal was signed between Auckland Council and the National-led Government for a 50/50 split of the promised $2.4 billion bill.

The expected completion date was 2024.

It was the country’s largest-ever infrastructure project and the first time such an agreement had been reached.

There was, at the time, derision in Parliament from MPs who opposed the project, labelling the City Rail Link (CRL) “Len’s Loop” or “Len’s Train Set”.

“I just made an art form of ignoring the noise, and there was a bit of noise in Parliament about this whole thing. You’ve just got to really keep focused and stay the course,” Brown says.

Simon Bridges was the Transport Minister who convinced his colleagues Steven Joyce and Sir Bill English – who had the taxpayers’ wallet firmly closed – of the benefits of the project.

“There was a lot of resistance, and fair enough, at a level, it was very expensive,” Bridges, now Auckland Business Chamber CEO, said.

“And there were other transport projects that also needed funding, but Auckland was very committed to it, had an absolute cheerleader-in-chief in Len Brown.

“He persuaded me and I think my key role was then persuading John Key.”

Bridges is now revealing a “gulp” moment.

The night before politicians gathered at what is now Te Komititanga Square to tell media and the public that the deal for what was then the City Rail Loop had been struck, Bridges had a call from transport officials.

“Twenty-four hours before we signed the documents and we were heading down to press the dynamite button, transport officials came to me and said the cost had gone up $400 million, from $2.4 to $2.5 billion.

“I’m like, how does this happen? I ring Len Brown and this is news to him as well. The costs were going up and by then it was too late.”

Away from the politics, construction was beginning, with early works around Britomart and Albert St.

Heavy construction work was underway by 2019 and then in 2020, the required twin tunnel-boring machine landed in New Zealand and was named Dame Whina Cooper.

International tunnelling experts arrived with it and excavated two 1.6km-long tunnels from Mt Eden to central Auckland.

They worked 24/7, operated by a crew of 12 underground and a team of 12 above ground.

At its peak, 2000 construction workers were on sites across Auckland.

And then the pandemic hit.

Construction, and business, stalled. And those businesses facing severe disruption became increasingly upset, angry and disenchanted.

Around Albert St and Victoria St, many of the businesses that were there pre-2019 have failed.

Roma Blooms was one of the most outspoken.

Owner Shobhana Ranchhodji is still brought to tears when asked about what the past 11 years have been like and how they survived.

“We all did what we had to do to survive and that was to go without,” she told the Herald last week.

“That’s a sad one, I can’t talk about it. It was draining, mentally and physically.”

Businesses owners fought for compensation and recognition of the pain they were suffering.

“We were told to shut up and sit down, that we did not know anything. The thing that we heard over and over again, there’s no budget. And then we heard how many times they went back for more money,” Ranchhodji says.

Eventually the then Labour Government provided a small package to some business owners.

Bridges and Brown now say the business disruption was their biggest regret.

“I think our response to their concerns lacked the empathy that needed to be there,” Brown says.

“I really needed to be leading that off from the outset. Mea culpa on that front, we could have done a lot better.”

Bridges says in the scheme of the overall cost, a package of $30m or so for small business owners facing immense disruption would have been an easy win.

The Government says there will be a full review of the project.

“The human toll was real,” Bridges says.

“Were we to do something like this again, and actually a harbour crossing may have some of this, we need to make sure businesses and people around it are dealt with better.”

Also included in the review will be those cost and time blowouts.

Some of it was understandable. The pandemic hit, material costs skyrocketed and construction slowed through the lockdowns.

But former CRL CEO Sean Sweeney – who held the top job for six years – told the Herald in May he thinks more could’ve been done earlier to deal with those creeping cost overruns.

“I think we could have delivered this for half the cost, but it would have looked different. The stations would have looked quite industrial, and they would have been smaller, they wouldn’t have had anywhere near the extra facilities in them.”

Sweeney suggested the project would be “more Toyota Corolla, less Rolls-Royce”.

Many disagree with Sweeney, including Bridges, Brown and former Auckland Mayor Phil Goff.

“One of the great learnings for Auckland is don’t do half-baked stuff,” Brown says.

“The harbour crossing was a half-baked project.”

Goff took over the mayoral chains from Brown and was the one who approved those scope changes – the big one being larger platforms to accommodate six-to-nine-car trains rather than three-car.

“If we had not future-proofed this, we would barely have opened the City Rail Link and it would have to have closed for a year to expand the platforms,” Goff told the Herald outside Waitematā Station, where he’s stopped to have a chat with Brown.

“I’m a little bit surprised when the then CEO that told us we had to future-proof it when we made that decision is now saying we might have done it a different way. Frankly, he’s wrong. Did the stations need to be as beautiful as they are? Not so much.

“One thing New Zealand has done really badly is not plan for the future. We weren’t going to allow that to happen. What we did was the right thing and I stand behind that decision.”

Current Mayor Wayne Brown – who is a reluctant supporter of the CRL – says we have a habit of building expensive projects in New Zealand.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop says it’s one of the issues that will be looked at in that promised review.

The cost has now doubled to close to $5.5b. Governments of both stripes have signed off on that cost.

New stations have been built, just off Karangahape Rd and Te Waihorotiu on Victoria St, which is expected to be the busiest.

The Roma Blooms owner hopes the decade of pain is now over.

“I am crossing my fingers that it is everything they said it was going to be,” Ranchhodji says.

The politicians who staked their legacies on it say it will.

“I think those critics will be remarkably silent in the future when we see how used the City Rail Link is and, over time, how it becomes critical to the transport infrastructure across Auckland,” Goff says.

Now it’s time for Kiwis to witness that transformation.

“This feels like a real world-class city, a Sydney or a London, and when people go down, they’re going to see that. I think they’ll be excited,” Bridges says.

For Brown, it’s been 16 years in the making.

“What’s 16 years when you’re talking about waiting 100 years?” he says.

“It’s long overdue, but it is here. It shows that we as Aucklanders we’ve got our mojo, we can do this large infrastructure. We just need to be very clear with our vision, our plan, our budgeting and our funding and being a really good, reliable partner to the private sector community.

“I’m excited. Did I tell you I’m excited?” Brown says.

And yes, he got the train into the Waitematā Station for the interview.

Katie Bradford is a Senior Correspondent at the Herald. She has been a broadcast journalist for over 20 years and was based in the press gallery for 10 years. She specialises in politics, business and Auckland issues.

Tauranga junior netball bans courtside spectators over sideline abuse

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

A ban on courtside spectators at Tauranga junior netball games has left parents frustrated, disappointed and asking how the decision was made.

Tauranga Netball Centre has decided to restrict spectators from the court enclosure during games for the next two Saturdays, the final two rounds of the junior season, citing incidents and complaints about sideline behaviour.

One parent said the decision has come as a “surprise” and the general reaction is one of “dissatisfaction” and “disappointment”.

But Tauranga Netball Centre said the decision was not made lightly and its message has been misunderstood.

The centre emailed its database on Monday, advising parents, caregivers, whānau, friends and supporters of Year 6, 7 and 8 teams that spectators would be required to watch games from outside the court enclosure.

That would apply for the remaining two weeks of competition at Mount Maunganui’s Blake Park on August 8 and August 15.

Coaches and managers would be permitted inside the court enclosure.

This decision followed a “significant number” of incidents and complaints about sideline behaviour at junior games.

The email said umpires had been subjected to abuse, intimidation and criticism from spectators, and there were reports of adults directly targeting players from the sideline.

“Adult agendas, egos and frustrations have no place on the sideline,” the email read.

It said restricting spectator access was the most effective way to curb the behaviour, ensuring a safe environment for players, officials and volunteers for the remainder of the season.

A second email on Tuesday acknowledged feedback about the decision.

“To be clear, this decision is not the result of one isolated incident, nor is it simply about coaches requesting additional support for umpires,” the email read.

“The concerns are much broader and have been building throughout the season.”

The centre said players, umpires, staff and volunteers had faced increasing pressure throughout the season, with volunteers “exhausted” after spending months responding to complaints and providing support to umpires.

“This decision was not made lightly. It is a necessary statement about the standards of behaviour expected within our netball community, and it will not be reversed.”

The centre provided the Bay of Plenty Times with copies of both emails.

A parent who received the emails and wished to remain anonymous said they had no idea the decision was being considered or that there had been concerns of this nature.

“The decision came as a surprise.”

They said they had not personally witnessed the abuse, intimidation, or behaviour described in the email.

“I have heard parents provide feedback from the sideline when they felt young umpires had missed what they considered to be crucial calls.”

They said this had “generally” been in the context of frustration with decisions rather than abusive or intimidating behaviour described in the original email.

“Parents are disappointed that everyone is being treated the same way when the concerns appear to relate to the behaviour of a small number of individuals.”

They said if specific individuals were behaving inappropriately, they should be held accountable rather than imposing restrictions on every spectator.

“The majority of families are there to encourage their children and support them positively.”

The parent said there should have been more communication and an opportunity for feedback before a “significant” decision was made.

“I do not support a blanket restriction on all spectators for both remaining weeks.”

They said the general reaction from parents was one of “dissatisfaction” and “disappointment”.

“Parents are being asked to accept the decision, yet many feel they haven’t been given an opportunity to contribute to the discussion.”

In response to the concerns, Tauranga Netball Centre manager Tracy Walters told the Bay of Plenty Times the message conveyed in the emails had been misunderstood.

“It is probably seen to some people as an inconvenience, but we’re trying to combat and have some consequence around the sideline behaviours that are impacting these kids.

“We’ve made a decision; people just need to accept it.”

Walters said it was often difficult to identify who was responsible because many complaints were only reported “after the fact”.

“Then you have a he-said-she-said scenario, and I tell you we have many of those, so it’s just human beings, one thinks one way, one thinks the other.”

She said it was “not so easy” as identifying individual “culprits” and imposing consequences on them.

“We’re not doing it for our own gain, there’s definite thinking behind it, and we’re trying to look after these young umpires, ... the players, that’s the intention.”

She said the restriction was imposed to “minimise risk” and get through the rest of the season on a higher note as the league was “tracking downwards”.

“We want it to track back upwards in terms of the enjoyment that these kids get out of the rest of their season.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

Tokoroa under-14 rugby team disqualified after alleged headbutt

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

Battlefield or playing field? Photo / Kelly Hodel, Waikato Times

A team of Tokoroa high schoolers have been disqualified from their rugby competition after a match that allegedly involved a headbutt and men “barking” behind the goal post.

After the Tokoroa under-14 team lost a home game on Saturday, the situation was said to be “within an inch” of turning into a full-on brawl and the atmosphere was intimidating enough for St Peter’s of Cambridge spectators to leave “as a pack”.

This follows a string of incidents and complaints against the team throughout the season, with referees and teams alike refusing to travel to Tokoroa because of abuse.

On Saturday, a Tokoroa player ran over after the final whistle and headbutted one of the St Peter’s players, under-14 coach Simms Davison said. The Tokoroa player took a swing at the boy, then punched another player on the side of the face.

Waikato Secondary Schools disqualified the South Waikato team but could not be reached for comment. A spokesperson for Tokoroa High School said the school could not comment.

The ban is backed by council-funded Sport Waikato and their chief executive Matthew Cooper who “supported organisations making tough calls”.

A St Peter’s-linked witness said one of their players had overheard a Tokoroa player saying “I’m going to come and get you” before the final whistle.

“Sure enough, the final whistle’s blown this boy’s just come up for no reason [and] just headbutted him. It was something that we had been expecting.”

Middle-aged men were barking behind the goalpost – specifically to the St Peter’s goalkicker, according to Davison.

“It was in plain sight for everyone to see that behaviour. It’s only an inch away from escalating into something bad and we’ve seen plenty of stabbings, people getting punched in the side of the head and getting KO’d,” Davison said.

The witness said spectators left “as a pack” because of the intimidating atmosphere, with Tokoroa spectators “staring them down” and calling out threats.

Both the witness and Davison agreed the issue was with a small number of Tokoroa players and supporters. Davison said the captain and multiple players approached him to apologise once tensions eased.

“It’s a real shame especially with a lot of those players [who] are just coming to play footy.”

However, the witness said if the team wasn’t disqualified, many other schools had been ready to boycott the competition with semi-finals around the corner.

Referees had also been copping flak in Tokoroa, according to Davison, who played over 50 games for the Chiefs.

They’d raised concerns about manning the whistle in the town before the season started, he said. During the season, refs “wouldn’t go there anymore” because of the severity of abuse, leading to Tokoroa playing an abnormal number of away fixtures.

“That’s someone that’s meant to be completely neutral, that doesn’t have any other family there ... as far as I’m concerned, that was enough to get a team thrown out.”

Morrinsville College’s side had even forfeited their away game against Tokoroa after not getting a venue change to a neutral ground.

The Tokoroa team’s disqualification follows incidents involving other teams in the Waikato.

Allegations of another under-14 rugby fracas between St John’s College and Fraser High School occurred in May, while Waikato Junior Rugby League cancelled all matches for a weekend to curb violence and abuse.

Cooper, who has previously been vocal about delivering consequences to stamp out poor behaviour, said tough decisions have to be made to ensure the correct messaging gets across.

“It’s not the All Blacks, it’s not the Silver Ferns, it’s not the Warriors. This is community school sport and that should be all about the experience has to be a good one and an enjoyable one.”

Tickets are sold out for Robbie Williams’ Christchurch show – although eager fans may still have a chance to see the veteran pop icon live.

The Let Me Entertain You artist announced in March he was bringing his Britpop World Tour to New Zealand with two shows this year.

Williams will be the first international artist to play at the new One New Zealand Stadium in Christchurch on November 28.

The Christchurch show is now sold out – but lucky fans can still catch Williams live in Auckland.

Williams most recently performed a rendition of the official Fifa anthem Desire at the 2026 World Cup Closing Ceremony ahead of the final match between Spain and Argentina.

The singer said he has “always had a very special place” in his heart for Aotearoa.

“Ever since my first solo tours, you have welcomed me with open arms and made me feel at home.”

Williams last performed on our shores in 2023, playing two shows at Mission Estate Winery in Napier.

The hitmaker holds the record for the most No 1 albums by a solo artist in Britain, with 16, including this year’s critically acclaimed release, Britpop.

Williams described the album’s sound as a return to his 1990s pop roots.

“I set out to create the album that I wanted to write and release after I left Take That in 1995,” he said, calling the era a “golden age for British Music”.

He previously revealed he had a “complicated relationship” with touring and performing live because of anxiety.

“People say, ‘Oh, you going on tour? You must be really, really excited.’ Not really. I’m terrified,” he told the I’m ADHD! No You’re Not podcast in October.

“I will look full of bravado and look pompous and look smug and do these grand gestures ... But actually what’s happening is I feel like the opposite of that all the time, most of the time.”

However, he said he has been able to better manage his condition with age.

“I would say it’s gotten better from 45 onwards. This particular tour that I’m now in, I’m very pleased to say, for me, is that I’m dead excited to do my show.”

Williams said he was looking forward to his return Downunder.

“I’m immensely proud of this as a body of work and I’m excited for fans to hear this album.”

His last top 10 album in New Zealand was 2019’s The Christmas Present.

It’s early days, but 3% of roadside drug tests in Hawke’s Bay have been positive

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

Eastern road policing manager Angela Hallett said 3.1% of drivers stopped so far in Hawke's Bay under new roadside drug testing laws had tested positive.

Police in Hawke’s Bay say roughly 3% of drivers they’ve pulled over for roadside drug tests have tested positive for illicit drugs.

Eastern road policing manager Angela Hallett said roadside drug tests started rolling out in June, with road policing team members in the Eastern District trained to administer them.

Hallett said drivers impaired by illicit drugs featured prominently in serious injury and fatal crashes in the Eastern Police District, which included Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti.

“The aim of this is obviously to deter people from driving after having drugs.

“We don’t want more people on our roads to suffer from drivers who are under the influence of drugs.”

Each test detects recent use of cannabis or THC, methamphetamine, MDMA or ecstasy and cocaine.

An officer can stop any driver and require them to complete a drug screening test, usually after alcohol testing.

Drivers wipe the test device pads down the front of their tongue, then wait seven to 10 minutes for the result.

Hallett said the wait could inconvenience sober drivers, but the tests helped keep everyone on the road safe.

“It is what it is to help keep our road safe.”

If the test was negative, no drugs had been detected at or above the limit, and the driver was free to go once police procedures were complete.

Police do not collect DNA from saliva samples, nor will drivers test positive from passive or historical exposure to drugs.

Since testing began in Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti on July 1, 352 drivers had undertaken screening tests, with 11 tests returning a positive result and 10 infringement notices, Hallett said.

Hallett said the 3.1% positivity rate among tested drivers, was about the expected positivity rate nationwide.

“But those are purely infringement based, they’re not matters which a person goes to court for unless perhaps they defend the infringement.

“The whole idea is to deter, general deterrence and deter people from driving under the influence of any kind of drug.”

Hallett said the penalties for being caught driving drugged were “pretty up there” with fines and demerit points and she had some advice for anyone thinking of driving after taking illicit drugs.

“Don’t do it. You’ll end up not being able to drive and you’re creating a huge risk to other members of the public.”

If the police’s drug screening test is positive, the driver has to provide a saliva sample, which is sent for laboratory testing of 25 drugs and medicines.

Drivers can elect to provide a separate saliva sample for laboratory analysis at their own cost.

The driver will then complete a second drug screening test, like the first, to determine whether they could drive.

If the second test is also positive, the driver won’t be allowed to drive for 12 hours.

If it’s negative, the driver is free to go after police procedures are complete, with the sample sent for laboratory analysis.

An infringement notice would be issued if the lab test confirmed one or more of the 25 qualifying drugs were present or above the limit.

If a driver failed or refused to comply with roadside drug testing procedures, they would receive an infringement notice and be forbidden to drive for 12 hours.

Jack Riddell is a multimedia journalist with Hawke’s Bay Today and has worked in radio and media in the UK, Germany, and New Zealand.

Pātea River Bar tragedy: Coroner releases findings into deaths of boy and stepmother

New Zealand Herald August 05, 2026

Patricia Wiltshire and Zane Te-Arepa Milham-Maraki died when the boat they were on capsized on the Pātea River Bar. Photo / Bevan Conley

A family fishing trip off the Taranaki coast turned to tragedy in seconds when a boat stood almost upright on a sudden wave and flipped, trapping a young boy and his stepmother underneath.

Shane Milham managed to free himself when the Miss Molly capsized on the Pātea River Bar, but moments later he could hear his partner, Patricia Wiltshire, calling for help from beneath the overturned vessel.

His 6-year-old son, Zane Te-Arepa Milham-Maraki, was also trapped.

Milham reached back into the boat, grabbing what he believed was Wiltshire’s lifejacket, but he could not pull her free. He could not find Zane.

A rescue effort involving Coastguard volunteers, nearby boaties and emergency services followed, but neither survived.

More than a year on, coroner’s findings released today reveal how the tragedy on one of New Zealand’s most notorious river bar crossings unfolded and whether anything could have prevented it.

Zane was described by his mother, Carolynn Maraki, in the findings as affectionate, “easily entertained and impressed”, and a child who was “always talking to people”. He was the youngest of 11 children and loved going fishing with his dad.

The findings noted that Wiltshire, also known as Patricia Tolley, was very close to her mother and also enjoyed fishing with Milham.

The family had set out aboard the Miss Molly, a small fibreglass fishing boat, on the morning of June 15 last year after Wiltshire, 50, stopped at her mother’s to collect bait from the freezer.

According to the findings, Milham assessed conditions before attempting the crossing and waited for about seven minutes for a set of waves to pass.

CCTV footage showed the boat waiting near the bar while a jetski successfully crossed ahead of it.

Other boaties later described conditions as relatively calm with light winds. Maritime New Zealand said forecasts were for moderate seas with swells of up to 2m, and several other vessels had crossed safely that morning.

But shortly after 10.15am, as the Miss Molly attempted to leave the river mouth and over the bar, a large wave appeared.

“The boat’s momentum appears to take the boat into the wave, with the boat becoming vertical and landing on its stern,” the findings said.

“Miss Molly then capsized, with Zane and Ms Wiltshire becoming trapped underneath.”

The South Taranaki Coastguard first received a faint radio call referencing “Miss Molly” and “over the bar”. It was later advised by radio that a member of the public had seen the boat overturn.

Emergency services were dispatched while nearby boats rushed to assist.

Wiltshire was later seen surfacing from beneath the boat about 50m from the jetty. She was pulled from the water but had died.

Zane was found beneath the vessel by a rescue diver after the boat had been brought closer to shore.

Coroner Rachael Schmidt-McCleave found that both died from drowning, with inhalation of toluene, a compound found in petrol, contributing to their deaths.

The coroner heard that the Pātea River Bar was regarded as one of the country’s most dangerous crossings.

Scott Williams, vice-president of Coast Guard South Taranaki, said it was viewed as New Zealand’s second most notorious bar crossing after Greymouth. He said one of the dangers was that large waves could appear with little warning.

Investigators considered whether the condition of Milham’s boat, its engine size, weight distribution or, in Zane’s case, his lifejacket, played a role in the deaths.

A marine accident inspector described the Miss Molly as being in poor overall condition, but said it maintained structural integrity, propulsive power and steerage at the time of the capsize.

The inspector noted it carried a 115-horsepower engine, despite guidance suggesting boats of a similar size would typically have an engine between 40hp and 70hp.

He found the capsize was caused by a combination of factors, including weight distribution at the stern, the engine’s weight, the nature of the waves, and how the boat was being operated. However, he did not conclude the vessel’s condition contributed to the capsize.

Zane’s lifejacket also came under scrutiny.

Maritime New Zealand found it was the wrong size and had not been properly fitted.

Contact the Open Justice team

Although it complied with an approved Australian standard, it was designed for a person weighing between 40kg and 60kg, making it unsuitable for a 6-year-old.

Investigators found the lifejacket would have reduced Zane’s ability to float and keep his head above water but could not determine whether it directly contributed to his death.

The coroner heard that Milham was an experienced boatie who had crossed the bar many times.

Maritime New Zealand found he had broadly followed the agency’s code of practice for bar crossings by assessing conditions, notifying Coastguard of his intentions and waiting for another vessel to clear the crossing before proceeding.

Police investigated the incident but did not lay charges. Maritime New Zealand also did not pursue enforcement action.

While Coroner Schmidt-McCleave identified several potential areas of risk, including the boat’s condition, engine size, weight distribution and Zane’s ill-fitting lifejacket, she found there was insufficient evidence to conclude any directly contributed to the deaths.

She made no formal recommendations, instead drawing attention to Maritime New Zealand guidance on lifejacket use and river bar crossings.

In her closing remarks, the coroner extended condolences to both families and described Zane as a “much loved and loveable little boy” whose death had caused deep grief.

Pātea Area School principal James Davidson previously told the Herald that Zane’s death had “deeply affected” the school and community.

“Everyone who met Zane instantly fell in love with his cheeky grin and zest for life. We already miss him immensely,” he said.

Tara Shaskey is an assistant editor and reporter for the Open Justice team. She joined NZME in 2022 and has worked as a journalist since 2014.

After 30 years of ‘magic’ with Tina Fey, Tracy Morgan says this will be their greatest trick

Sydney Morning Herald August 06, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Tracy Morgan is experiencing déjà vu. Twenty years ago, he was playing Tracy Jordan – an erratic, child-at-heart celebrity who causes chaos on Tina Fey’s hit sitcom 30 Rock. Now he’s acting in another eccentric comedy backed by the same creative heavyweight. Only this time, the spotlight is squarely on him.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, a new mockumentary sitcom, reunites Morgan with 30 Rock writers Robert Carlock and Sam Means as showrunners, and Fey as executive producer. The comedian plays the titular star, a disgraced former pro footballer who hires a washed-up documentary director (Daniel Radcliffe) to film his life in a bid to redeem his reputation. Replete with absurdist one-liners and mad-cap pop culture references, it’s like watching an updated version of 30 Rock.

But what about the man behind these characters? As culture writer Nell Geraets learnt in this conversation, he’s just as eccentric. Despite 30 Rock being regarded as one of the greatest sitcoms of all time, he now has his sights set even higher.

NG: The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins has reconnected you with many of the creators and writers of 30 Rock – Sam Means, Robert Carlock and Tina Fey (the latter two who you also worked with a decade prior on Saturday Night Live). What was it like creating comedy with them again?

TM: We’ve always made beautiful music together. That’s my family, and we get each other’s voices. They get my voice, and they know exactly how to put me in a position to win. I love the things they have me saying. All of them are pure masterminds … It’s a labour of love. We’ve been proven to do great work together.
