The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins season 1 trailer

Loved 30 Rock? This cracker new comedy is the 2026 equivalent.

This show does feel like a blast from the past. It has been 13 years since the 30 Rock finale aired. There used to be waves of network sitcoms, but they’re much rarer these days. Did it feel like you were filling a gap in the market by making Reggie Dinkins?

I felt that immediately. When we first started this project, I just wanted to do good old-fashioned TV, and have everyone put something out there that everyone in the household can just watch together – put the phones down, let’s just watch some good old-fashioned TV like we used to.

But the industry’s obviously changed a lot since 30 Rock aired. Did you notice any differences between making a sitcom today versus making one in the 2000s?

I didn’t look at it like that. I didn’t see any difference. I said, ‘Let’s do the same formula, but let’s just update it’. And look what we’ve done. Nothing’s changed. You still like this? You like Reggie Dinkins just like you like 30 Rock? [Reporter nods, and Morgan relaxes into his seat, satisfied] There you go … It’s humanity. Nothing’s changed.

So many people know you as the hilariously out-of-touch Tracy Jordan from 30 Rock. What impact would you say that role has had on your career?

Tracy Jordan took me to the moon. Reggie Dinkins is going to take me to Mars. People used to refer to me as Tracy Jordan, now they’re referring to me as Reggie Dinkins. He’s a pretty funny guy. The thing that’s good about that is it’s the same sense of humour.

So, you feel like Tracy Jordan sent you on a trajectory that inevitably led you to Reggie?

Yes, you only get one sense of humour. You only laugh at one thing, you only laugh at one kind of funny. You don’t laugh at a million funnies. Everything ain’t funny to you, but this happens to be funny to you … Reggie Dinkins, Tracy Jordan: same one sense of humour.

It feels like everything Tina Fey touches turns to gold. What is it about her comedy that has managed to remain so relevant over time?

She’s a very smart lady. When it comes to showbusiness, she has the Midas touch. Everybody doesn’t have the Midas touch. She has found her Nirvana. You have to find your Nirvana. Do you understand what I’m saying?

Like find your peace?

Imagine. I can’t stand when somebody with no abracadabra is trying to tell me what to do with my magic. You ain’t got no abracadabra, and you’re trying to tell me what to do with my magic? I ain’t never seen you pull a bunny out no hat. [Tina’s] constantly pulling bunnies out of a hat. Magic. It’s all magic.

You’re obviously no stranger to sitcoms, having been part of 30 Rock, The Last O. G. and so on. What drew you to the mockumentary style this time around?

I just love looking down the barrel [of the camera]. I think that’s hilarious, when we’re directly in your home. And all of us know when to do it and how to do it. It makes it funnier because you [the audience] become a part of the show.

One of the greatest parts of Reggie Dinkins is the dynamic between you and Daniel Radcliffe. Your characters are so different, yet they have such great chemistry.

That comes from Robert [Carlock] and Tina [Fey], along their travels meeting people, and going, “hmm, how could we put this guy from the UK with this street guy from Brooklyn and make that funny?” And they did.

What was it like building that dynamic with Radcliffe?

Chemistry, it’s all chemistry. We’re not a team; we are family. The day before we started shooting, we had dinner at my house, so everybody could hit the ground running, and everybody could be comfortable with each other. And that’s how it turned out. By the time they turned the cameras on, we were already comfortable with each other. We were already having fun.

What’s your favourite thing about him?

Everything. He’s the sweetest person. He’s very generous, he’s kind, he’s helpful, and he’s always right there. We can’t wait to get back to work [together] now. This season is going to be hilarious for you … The thing about Reggie Dinkins is it gets funnier and funnier.

I can see how much you love this show and everyone in it.

It was like that with 30 Rock. We learnt so much from Tina Fey. Everybody did their job. We’re a family.

Season two has been green-lit. What are your hopes for the next season?

Keep doing what we’ve been doing. Keep being funny. That’s it. No expectations. That’s what I tell my whole cast: keep doing what you’re doing.

Can you offer any hints around what we can expect?

I wouldn’t do that. No way. I want you to be pleasantly surprised … I’m going to have this conversation with you again next year, and the only thing I will say is: “I told you”. We did seven seasons on 30 Rock. We’re going to do eight on Reggie Dinkins. Eight or nine or 10.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins airs 11.30pm Wednesdays on Seven and 7plus.

TV’s best spy drama is completely flying under the radar

Sydney Morning Herald August 06, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No one in the world loves spy dramas more than my father-in-law, a man who will only commit hours of his life to a show if someone is getting double-crossed, preferably while travelling on a fake passport to a far-flung corner of the globe.

He doesn’t discriminate. Any series will do. Homeland, Slow Horses, The Americans, The Night Manager, Day of the Jackal – you name it, he’s seen it. So imagine my surprise when I asked for his thoughts on The Agency – perhaps the best spy drama on TV, which is now in its second season – and was met with nothing but a confused look.

I peppered him with prompts: “The Agency? Michael Fassbender? A CIA agent in London? The spy show that gently forces us to consider America’s waning global influence while hinting we might be on the brink of a new world order?” He assured me he had not seen the show but would add it to the list.

Sadly, this was not an isolated incident. The Agency is so successfully undercover that very few people are across it (either that, or no one pays for Paramount+). But I refuse to live in a world where The Agency flies under the radar. So, like any self-respecting CIA agent, my mission is to recruit as many assets as possible. First it was my father-in-law, and now it’s your turn.

2:12

The Agency season 2 trailer

The Agency is TV's best spy thriller. Why is it totally flying under the radar?

At its core, the series operates inside the paranoid, fluorescent-lit pressure cooker of London Station, the CIA’s primary European hub. Fassbender plays Brandon Colby, codename “Martian”, a senior covert operative abruptly recalled to London after six years living a double life in Ethiopia, leaving behind his married lover, Sudanese anthropologist Samia Zahir (Jodie Turner-Smith).

Promoted to deputy director of operations, Martian must navigate the psychological bends of re-entering civilian life, reconnecting with his estranged daughter and shedding his cover identity. This delicate balance unravels spectacularly when Samia, Martian’s only weak spot, turns up in London. Before long, the usually protocol-obsessed CIA agent is breaking the rules to keep the relationship alive.

Beyond Martian’s personal tailspin, the walls of London Station house a network of operatives whose entire existences are defined by transactional relationships. Richard Gere brings significant heft to station chief Bosko, the man responsible for keeping the White House happy, which usually involves making sure no one dies and the mission comes in under budget (yes, even the CIA is cost-cutting). Meanwhile, Henry Ogletree (Jeffrey Wright) serves as the counter-intelligence chief and Martian’s direct boss. A lifelong agent, Ogletree is understandably suspicious of everyone and everything, all of the time. But The Agency comes into its own when dealing with the junior agents, like Danny (Saura Lightfoot-Leon), an academic recruited by Martian.

In many ways, Danny is an audience surrogate, curious about the CIA but naive to its inner workings. Together, the pair present as a classic case of before and after. Danny is the wide-eyed recruit convinced she can change the world, and Martian knows from brutal experience that the work only ever changes the person doing it. And rarely for the better.

“People are fascinated by the kind of people that go into this line of work and what kind of people come out of it at the end,” Fassbender recently told the BBC. “Martian was once idealistic and full of hope, then his moral compass gets eroded by the things he has to do and the sacrifices that go into it.”

Sorry Ethan Hunt, James Bond and all the other male spies with similar-sounding names: The Agency is not a world of Aston Martins, vodka martinis and high-speed chases. Instead, the series frames contemporary espionage as a chess match fought across multiple fronts simultaneously, from African resource diplomacy to Eastern European proxy networks.

Written by brothers Jez and John Butterworth (who also penned the criminally underrated 2010 political drama Fair Game), The Agency is unafraid of borrowing plot lines from the current news cycle.

In season one, a CIA asset goes missing in Russian-occupied Ukraine, requiring high-level negotiations to spare his life. In season two, Danny goes undercover in Tehran to target Iranian nuclear facilities because the US government is obsessively monitoring uranium enrichment operations tied to the Fordow plant. Sound familiar?

And much like the modern geopolitical landscape, the minute one crisis is averted, another appears in its place. Much of the action takes place in situation rooms and intelligence briefings, which admittedly sounds low-energy but really isn’t.

Take it from me: watching Fassbender’s Martian unpack the importance of diplomatic plausible deniability is just as exciting as Daniel Craig emerging from the sea in Speedos.

If you’ve ever watched Antiques Roadshow, you’ll know that the most valuable cultural artefacts often have a French provenance, and so it is with The Agency.

The American series is a remake of Eric Rochant’s Le Bureau des Légendes (The Bureau) – available on SBS On Demand and well worth the watch – often cited as the gold standard of the genre. And when I say remake, I mean remake in the truest sense: the first season of The Agency is almost beat-for-beat the same as The Bureau. This would usually be a cause for concern, but given The Bureau boasts a 96 per cent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” approach makes sense.

Rather than coming across as a cheap Hollywood knock-off, The Agency has pulled off a rare balancing act, maintaining the original’s French sensibilities while ramping up the production values. Alex Berger, a producer of The Bureau, says the US series “respected what we did originally” while upping “the scope, the scale and the ambition”. “We did the first season for €15 million ($24.6 million) in 2013, and the first season of The Agency is over 10 times that,” he told Variety. Money well spent, I reckon.

The even better news is that The Bureau ran for five seasons, and with The Agency having only just released season two, there’s plenty of time for everyone (you, my father-in-law) to join the bandwagon. Consider this your super secret tip-off.

The Agency is now streaming on Paramount+.

Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial records

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 21:12:07 GMT

President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm

Donald Trump’s legal team is making an 11th-hour attempt to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster.

Trump claims that the BBC’s 2024 documentary on the January 6 attacks have damaged the president’s business interests. In July, a Miami-based judge ruled that the president would have to start handing over detailed financial records to the BBC by 6 August. The records would reveal details into the hundreds of businesses owned by the US president’s family trust.

Trump’s attorneys asked the court on Wednesday to temporarily pause the enforcement of the court order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”.

Trump’s lawyers also asked the court to amend their initial lawsuit to instead focus on the “reputation harm” that was caused by the documentary, which would keep necessary disclosures “proportional to the needs of the case”, the lawyers said.

While it is unclear what Trump’s net worth is, recent financial disclosures showed that he had made more than $2.2bn during his first year back in office.

The lawsuit against the BBC is one of Trump’s several recent attempts to wage legal battles against media outlets that publish critical coverage of him. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys tried to argue that a $10bn defamation suit brought against the Wall Street Journal should go to a trial after it reported on a “bawdy” letter the president reportedly included in a birthday book for the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump’s justice department also issued and then recalled subpoenas to New York Times journalists after the paper reported on security concerns with the Air Force One presidential jet.

Trump’s initial lawsuit concerns a scene in the BBC documentary, entitled Trump, A Second Chance, that spliced lines from a speech the president made on 6 January 2021. The clip made it appear like Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol. The BBC has apologized for the edit but argued the defamation claims have no merit.

Trump recently claimed that the BBC “used AI” to insert words into his speech, which the network has categorically denied.

Gianni Infantino scrambling for future in Morocco, with Colombia his next stop

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 21:05:57 GMT

Fifa president sits at match with No 2 Mattias Grafström

Flying to South America on Thursday to shore up support

Gianni Infantino is continuing to fight for his future after holding crisis talks with senior officials in Rabat on Wednesday.

The under-pressure Fifa president has spent the last week in Morocco after attending Throne Day celebrations to mark the 27th anniversary of King Mohammed VI’s accession, and will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.

On Wednesday evening, Infantino appeared at a Women’s African Cup of Nations match at the Al Madina Stadium in Rabat, sitting alongside his No 2 at Fifa, the secretary general Mattias Grafström. Their appearance together came only a day after it emerged that Grafström had called the Fifa Forward Enterprise a “sad and reproachable series of events” in an email to the organisation’s staff.

Infantino decided to travel to Africa and South America in the wake of the storm over Fifa’s proposals to sell off 21% of the World Cup. Those confederations are his biggest supporters.

Neither the Confederation of African Football nor Conmebol have joined the Uefa-led rebellion against the Fifa Forward Enterprise sell-off, and remain steadfast in their support.

Infantino is hoping that Morocco in particular can play a crucial strategic role in galvanising backing for him in the Middle East, which is likely to become a vital battleground in determining the outcome of the vote for his re-election in March.

Unlike Caf and Conmebol, the Asian Football Confederation does not vote as a bloc, leaving Infantino to lobby individual countries for support if, as expected, Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf succeed in finding a candidate to stand against him in next year’s presidential election at Fifa’s congress, which will also take place in Rabat.

Few details have emerged about Wednesday’s meeting, which was attended by Fifa’s general secretary Mattias Grafström and chief legal officer Emilio García Silvero, other than Infantino’s determination to carry on.

Drone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior minister

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 20:56:06 GMT

Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt

The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe

Germany’s interior minister has warned that the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport marks “a new level of danger” for the country, as authorities examine whether the thwarted attack could have been planned by a foreign power.

The discovery of a small drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a leading shipping and military hub, set off alarm and caused flight diversions on Wednesday morning. German police deployed a bomb disposal robot to defuse and destroy the explosive device.

In public remarks on Wednesday evening, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs, and that investigators were treating it as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario”.

“We are dealing here with a competition that may also include foreign powers – this will be part of the investigations – who quite obviously want to contribute to considerable uncertainty in Germany,” Dobrindt said.

A DHL cargo plane that had been forced to abort its landing at the airport then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere.

Dobrindt and other German officials did not explicitly mention Russia as a potential suspect in their remarks. But the airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which has previously been accused of carrying out sabotage attacks in Europe.

Security experts said the incident could amount to a serious escalation in tensions with Russia if it was determined the Kremlin played a role.

Investigators said “a drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway” of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as “critical infrastructure”.

“A suspected second unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft after it had taken off again following the previous closure of the runway. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover,” the investigators said.

A Nato official said: “We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate.”

The drone, a quadcopter that was fitted with an explosive device, was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, according to media reports.

Some of the Ukrainian aircraft are emblazoned with patriotic slogans including “Be Brave Like Kherson” and “Be Brave Like Bucha”, the site of a civilian massacre early in the full-scale Russian invasion.

The tabloid Bild speculated that the explosive could have been fabricated ⁠from fertiliser and petrol, while a team from the public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche newspaper, said the device had contained pentaerythritol tetranitrate, or PETN – a primary ingredient in semtex that belongs to the same chemical family as nitroglycerin.

Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, blamed Moscow. “Who else could it be but Russia?” he told the commercial broadcaster Welt TV. Moscow has not commented so far.

Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called for an investigation to be conducted with the utmost urgency and also hinted at possible Russian involvement.

“Should it transpire that a state is behind this action, this would constitute not merely terrorism but state terrorism directed against the federal republic of Germany and its citizens,” he told Der Spiegel.

Marc Henrichmann, the CDU chair of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said the latest incident looked like “an attempt to target a company of importance for Ukraine”.

If the details are confirmed, it “would represent a new level of escalation in these sorts of attacks”, he told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

Several aircraft, including a passenger plane from Mallorca, were diverted because of the incident. Operations in the northern part of the airport resumed two hours later.

The southern runway, where the drone was found, remained closed. Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to examine the object.

Police and prosecutors said: “There is no danger to the lives or safety of passengers or airport staff. Passenger air traffic is unaffected.”

Germany and other European countries have had a series of suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies. They have accused Russian agents of being behind some of the flights, which Moscow has denied.

Germany is the biggest single national supplier of military aid to Ukraine and has accused Russia of orchestrating a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against it, which the Kremlin has denied.

Last year, a Chinese national was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing.

Separately, Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.

The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring. Thumann is said to be under police protection.

In 2024, US intelligence services reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, an apparent attempt at retaliation over the company’s role in providing a large amount of armaments for Ukraine.

The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced. Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

Cambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarism

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 20:08:47 GMT

Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career

Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: the claims surrounding a star Cambridge professor

Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career.

Arday, who had been dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials, issued a statement on Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.

In the statement, published on the Good Law Project website, he wrote: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.

“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”

However, after days of detailed scrutiny of his previous work and statements, which highlighted apparent discrepancies, Arday said he had “concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.

Simon & Schuster had been preparing to publish Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, later this month. His resignation may pause or even halt its publication and planned publicity tours.

Cambridge had initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions multiplied over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.

The Guardian published its own investigation uncovering discrepancies in Arday’s public accounts involving prodigious fundraising feats as well as claims he had been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders.

Arday first faced allegations that he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and other academic research late last year, and has rejected the claims. An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded his PhD in 2015, did not uphold the charges of plagiarism but said they were probably caused by “honest and reasonable error”.

Arday has denied all accusations of plagarism, telling the Guardian last week: “There have been multiple thorough investigations across several institutions as a result of the allegations, and immense scrutiny, including with an academic misconduct panel who concluded that there was no plagiarism or academic misconduct.”

On Wednesday evening, Cambridge announced it would launch an investigation after it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.

It said in a statement: “The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Prof Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.

“Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our misconduct in research policy. This is consistent with our previous statement on the matter.

“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.

“We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”

A spokesperson for Jesus College, Cambridge, said it was launching its own parallel “process”.

“Prof Arday’s college fellowship is linked to his university role and we will fully support the university.

“Prof Arday remains a fellow during this process. We recognise that this is a very difficult time for him and his family, and ask that they are treated with compassion and respect.”

The new investigations may have been triggered by Arday’s claims that he held a string of prestigious visiting fellowships and professorships at other universities, including statements in published biographies dating back to 2018 that he was a visiting fellow or visiting professor at Ohio State University in the US. Ohio State has denied that Arday was ever employed in any role.

Biographies linked to Arday have also claimed he had visiting professorships at Durham, Glasgow, Coventry and London Metropolitan universities as well as Nelson Mandela University in South Africa.

Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology at Cambridge, at the comparatively young age of 37, received wide publicity through Arday’s life story, which includes a diagnosis of autism at the age of three, being unable to speak until he was 11, or read or write until he was 18.

Despite those factors, Arday went on to university and swiftly climbed the academic ladder. After receiving his PhD in 2015 he held academic posts at Leeds Beckett, Roehampton and Durham universities, including a brief stint at Warwick University, before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Glasgow University in 2021. By early 2023 he had sought and won appointment to a professorship at Cambridge.

Arday also claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days as well as running 600 miles in six days, and raising £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions he revised some of those claims, and instead said he was part of a funding raising group that he cannot name for legal reasons.

Arday told the Guardian he had been the target of multiple threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.

Dear colleagues,

It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.

When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming Professor of Sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life. To become the youngest Black professor in the University’s history was something I could scarcely have imagined as a child growing up with a diagnosis of autism, unable to speak until I was eleven years old.

The response from so many people across the world was overwhelming. Thousands celebrated not simply my appointment, but what it represented: that talent, perseverance and hope can triumph over even the greatest adversity. It has been the privilege of my life to teach my students, to learn alongside them, and to witness their curiosity, kindness and ambition. They have given me far more than I could ever have given them.

Sadly, the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack. While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.

I have tried to continue because I believe deeply in the values of higher education, in rigorous scholarship, and in the transformative power of universities. I have tried because of my students, my colleagues and the countless people who have written to tell me that my journey gave them hope.

But there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great.

I have a family. I want to be present for them. I want to reclaim some peace, some privacy and some semblance of an ordinary life. I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement.

For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away.

This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge. Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me. It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.

To my students: thank you. Teaching you has been the greatest honour of my academic career. Your brilliance, compassion and determination give me enormous hope for the future.

To my colleagues and to the many thousands of people, from every corner of the world, who have supported me, defended me, written to me, and believed in me when it mattered most, I offer my deepest gratitude. Your kindness has carried me through some of the darkest moments of my life.

This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.

I need time to heal. I need time to simply be myself again.

And when that time comes, I will return.

I will return stronger, wiser and with the same determination that has always defined my journey. There is still so much work to do, and I look forward to doing it alongside so many of you in the years ahead.

For now, however, I ask only for understanding, for compassion, and for the space to begin again.

With gratitude, Professor Jason Arday

Social media users have criticized TikTok after the celebrity blogger Perez Hilton livestreamed himself self-harming on the platform, prompting many to question how long the broadcast remained live and others to share mental health resources and encourage those in need to seek help.

On Tuesday night, Hilton, 48, livestreamed himself engaging in self-harm as viewers pleaded for him to stop. Shortly after, local authorities responded to his home in Miami, Florida, where he was transported to a nearby hospital for medical treatment.

In the aftermath, social media users and influencers have criticized TikTok for hosting the live stream. Instagram user Gina Luciano said: “I find it disgusting and disturbing that TikTok allowed that livestream to go on for as long as it did. It just goes to show you that that app promotes bullying.”

Luciano continued: “Don’t watch that video, don’t watch any clippings of that live stream. It’s not content. It’s not entertainment. It’s a cry for help.”

Dana Bowling, another Instagram user said: “Can we file a class action suit against TikTok for exposing adults and teens to that trauma…? No one should be ok with this.”

Although several users claimed the live stream lasted more than 30 minutes, a TikTok US spokesperson disputed those reports, saying the broadcast was approximately half that length. The spokesperson said TikTok’s automated moderation systems flagged the live stream within minutes and referred it to the platform’s US moderation team for review.

Several subsequent live streams were removed within 90 seconds and Hilton’s account was ultimately banned, the spokesperson added.

The company said it also alerted local law enforcement officials and that the live stream violated its community guidelines, which prohibit content depicting or promoting suicide or self-harm.

Despite TikTok’s removal of the live stream, screen recordings of the footage have since widely circulated across other platforms including X and Instagram, in turn prompting users to advise others to turn off video autoplays and mute mentions of Hilton.

“Assume every Trending Topic link with his name on it will lead you to the video. Don’t click on the link. The video is everywhere right now. To be extra sure, turn video autoplay off (it’s in Settings) and mute the phrase ‘Perez Hilton,’” one person said on Bluesky.

Another person similarly said: “PLEASE mute ‘Perez Hilton’ (as a term) if images of self harm, a person in crisis… are bad for you. Please.”

Other users have encouraged those struggling with mental health issues to seek support. TV personality and influencer Tefi Pessoa wrote on her Instagram story: “If Perez Hilton’s live triggered you in any way, please call 988. There is help, I promise. I love you.”

The Guardian reached out to X for comment. Meta declined to comment.

Many users also commented directly on Hilton’s Instagram posts to express their concern, with one writing: “A lot of people care and are concerned for you. Please take care of yourself Perez. Please know that you are loved.”

Someone else said: “Perez I hope you are stabilized and doing alright now, that video has us all concerned. Please heal up.”

On Wednesday afternoon, Hilton’s team and family released a statement confirming that Hilton is receiving medical care.

“Many of you have reached out with concern for Perez, and we are incredibly grateful for the overwhelming outpouring of love, support, and prayers. We can confirm that Perez is receiving medical care, and our family’s focus right now is on his well-being. We kindly ask that you respect Perez’s privacy, as well as the privacy of his family, during this difficult time,” the statement said.

“If and when we are able to share any updates, we will do so with everyone as soon as we can. Thank you for your compassion, understanding, and continued support,” it added.

Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, rose to fame in the early 2000s when he started PerezHilton. com, a celebrity gossip blog with aggressive commentary that many, including celebrities, likened to online bullying.

Born in Miami to Cuban parents, Hilton graduated from New York University before working in a variety of roles, including a brief stint as an actor and later as a publicist, before finding success as a celebrity blogger under a moniker inspired by Paris Hilton.

By 2007, the New York Times reported that Hilton was spending 17 hours daily publishing an average of 30 blogposts every day. At the time, his website was charging $9,000 a week for a single advertisement, and as much as $45,000 for its most expensive ad package, the outlet added.

Speaking to the Guardian in 2014, Hilton described himself as being “sassy without being nasty”.

In his 2021 memoir, the father of three reflected on his earlier work, writing: “I have a ton of regrets, particularly because I now see that I never needed to be so mean or cruel.”

Earlier this year, Hilton revealed that he underwent “emergency surgery” for deep vein thrombosis after doctors discovered the condition following a three-week hospitalization due to sepsis.

Reflecting on the experience, Hilton said God “presented himself to me”, adding: “I’ve been crying but happy tears … because this is just …so crazy. I’ve been reading the Bible, and so much of what is said here I had already been thinking of. It’s just overwhelming in the best, most beautiful way.”

In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline. org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 20:00:28 GMT

The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.

Doctors and other medical professionals have warned of the impact that repeated heatwaves are having on the NHS in England, including advice from the Royal College of GPs to cancel surgeries in extreme weather. Radiotherapy machines and MRI scanners have failed in hot weather, wards have overheated and cooling units serving hospitals have broken down.

England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, with an estimated 2,877 people dying in the May and June heatwaves.

Summers are likely to become increasingly hot in the future, with temperatures topping 40C likely to become more frequent instead of being outliers as the climate crisis takes further hold.

Cooper told the Guardian that rising global temperatures were causing challenges for the NHS that it had not encountered before. “This is a new thing for the NHS to have to deal with. There is a remarkable determination of the NHS to respond, but we need much greater resilience.”

She said that in her new role as health secretary she had visited her local A&E in Yorkshire where staff described the overcrowding caused by heatwaves. “It would be normal during the winter weeks and months, but not in the summer, to have the very high attendances that they have had,” she said.

She said she had discussed a public health awareness campaign with the chief medical officer, Sir Chris Whitty, warning people to look out for elderly relatives and those with young babies to ensure they were coping in the heat.

Climate change meant “some immediate acute responses”, Cooper said, adding: “I’ve been clear we now need to prepare for summer pressures in the way that the NHS for a long time has prepared for winter pressures.

“We need a much clearer assessment now of what that means, what the pressures are going to be, what management needs to be in place to cope.”

The Climate Change Committee, the government’s statutory advisers on net zero, published a landmark report in May warning that the UK’s infrastructure was not built for such a climate, and calling for all hospitals and care homes to have air conditioning within the next decade, with all schools to follow by 2050. The CCC advised the government to plan for at least 2C of global heating by 2050, and potentially further rises.

Farmers this summer have also warned about how the extreme temperatures caused by the climate crisis were affecting the UK’s food security and ability to cope with drought.

No 10 said that improving the UK’s resilience to extreme heat was high on the agenda of the government – including building more reservoirs – saying the focus on tackling climate change must be on “practical resilience alongside cutting emissions”.

Cooper said that she and Whitty agreed there needed to be more public information about who was most at risk from extreme heat, because of the “distressing” number of heat deaths.

“There is a need for all of us to look out for our elderly neighbours and family members in the heat of summer, exactly as you would if it was freezing cold weather and you would be checking on elderly family members or relatives. We need to do the same thing now, in the summer, in the heatwaves and also for the very young.”

She said that cooling hospitals and other facilities would be a key part of the major investment in NHS infrastructure. “That is a new thing we are now having to address and to plan for. That obviously takes time as well to address that. But it is one of the things that’s being looked at now as part of the capital programme,” she said.

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, told a press conference in London on Wednesday that tackling the climate crisis should be higher on the agenda. “I think we need to sit with that reality: 3,000 people have died because of extreme heat,” he said.

“The scenes we have seen play out on our television screens are frankly apocalyptic. And yet the response from our government is to pretend none of this is happening. It’s an astonishing dereliction of duty from those whose first responsibility is to keep us safe.”

The Royal College of Physicians’ clinical vice-president, Dr Hilary Williams, has said the NHS currently had very little built-in resilience to cope with extreme heat. “The impact of heatwaves on staff cannot be overstated,” she said. “There is a sense of foreboding when we see the weather forecast, because we know what is to come, and there is very little staff can do.”

The government has also been urged by MPs to do more to allow people to cool their own homes. More than 50 MPs have written to the UK’s certification agencies to urge them to speed up a process to get air conditioning on to the boiler upgrade scheme, which offers grants for replacing gas boilers with greener alternatives like heat pumps.

Despite the government expanding the scheme to air-coolers last year, accreditation agencies have not yet given a stamp of approval.

“If people worried about a future of extreme temperatures know they can get a heat pump which will also act as air conditioning they will be more motivated to make the switch – that’s good news for energy bills and the planet,” said Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for Hitchin, who organised the letter. “The agencies accrediting this scheme just really need to get on with it now.”

July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England, with no significant rainfall expected in the area for some time.

The summer has already seen two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June, fuelling drought and wildfires. About 23 million people across England and Wales are under a hosepipe ban.

The National Farmers’ Union warned earlier this week that Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England. Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult.

This year’s El Niño, fuelled by global heating, is also supercharging temperatures: the World Meteorological Organisation confirmed this week that the weather system developing in the Pacific was likely to be unusually strong.

Andy Burnham has been criticised for failing to mention the climate crisis, net zero or the drought and heatwaves in his first weeks in No 10 – though he has promised the government will ramp up efforts to improve the state’s resilience.

A spokesperson for the prime minister said: “We recognise that climate change is already affecting communities across the country, through extreme heat, drought and pressure on food production. That’s why we’re focused on practical resilience alongside cutting emissions.”

He said the government would put “record investment in water infrastructure, including new reservoirs, while backing farmers to improve water security and strengthen the resilience of British food production.

“Planning reforms are also making it easier to deliver on-farm infrastructure, including reservoirs and other productivity improvements.”

Study finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 years

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 20:00:27 GMT

Research suggests addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health between the ages of 45 and 65 could help reduce risk of cognitive decline

Scientists claim to have identified three health measures in middle age that can ward off dementia for more than a decade.

Having normal blood pressure, no type 2 diabetes, and not smoking between the ages of 45 and 65 were associated with almost 13 additional years, on average, of dementia-free life, a study shows.

The research also suggested that, no matter how many risk factors people had, women lived longer without dementia than men, and that white people had more dementia-free years than black people.

The findings were published in the medical journal Neurology.

Researchers from NYU Langone Health analysed data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (Aric) study, which began in 1986 and followed Americans for decades into late life, measuring midlife vascular risk factors and dementia.

In the new analysis, researchers looked at 12,409 people with an average age of 56 who were free of dementia. Participants were assessed for three risk factors: high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and smoking. They were then followed for about three decades, with an average follow-up of 26 years.

During that time, 3,008 developed dementia and 5,238 died without developing the condition.

Those who had none of the three risk factors lived without developing dementia almost 13 years longer than those who had all three.

Those with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke at the start of the study had an average of 30.1 more years free of dementia, the study found.

Meanwhile, those with one risk factor had an extra 26.3 years, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years.

“Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,” said senior investigator Dr Josef Coresh, director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone.

“Hopefully, these results will encourage people to stop smoking and watch their vascular health closely from age 45 on.”

The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But experts believe almost half of dementia cases worldwide could be prevented or delayed.

Previous research has suggested that addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, could prevent or delay 45% of dementia cases, even as people live longer.

The NYU Langone study said the three factors it identified “often emerge in midlife” and “exert lasting effects on neurodegenerative pathology”, underscoring the critical importance of early identification and management.

Dr Jacqui Hanley, head of research funding at Alzheimer’s Research UK, who was not involved with the research, said: “Rather than focusing only on the chances of developing dementia, this study asks a question that matters to people: how long can we expect to live free from dementia?

“This approach gives a meaningful picture of how midlife health may shape the number of years we spend living free from dementia, while also recognising that high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking are linked to a higher likelihood of dementia as well as a greater risk of dying earlier from other conditions.

“These findings emphasise why it’s so important to look after your heart health as well as your brain health.”

Hanley said everyone should take practical steps, including staying physically active, not smoking, and managing conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes.

“While there is no guaranteed way to prevent dementia, research, including this study, suggests that addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health may also help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.”

Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 19:51:04 GMT

Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail

The chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

The Police Federation is contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison.

In August 2019, Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by a car as Cole, Bowers and their accomplice Henry Long fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

All three were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in prison and could be released early as part of the government’s drive to free up prison places.

Long, who was driving the car, was given a 16-year jail sentence and does not qualify for early release.

On Wednesday morning, Jason Hogg, who was on duty the night Harper died, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that he would “certainly” consider joining the Police Federation in court action if the government refused to reverse its position, pending legal advice.

“I was contacted by the Police Federation yesterday who informed me they are seeking legal advice, exploring opportunities for a judicial review against the government,” he told the Guardian on Wednesday afternoon.

“So I’m watching with interest and I will be speaking to the Police Federation again.

“But my hope is that we will never get there and that there is no need for the Police Federation to go down the line of a judicial review because the government will listen.”

Prison capacity in England and Wales is at critical levels. From October, the government plans to release about 5,000 prisoners who have served a third of their sentence.

Harper’s widow, Lissie, successfully campaigned for a change in the law after his death.

Legislation introduced four years ago – the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 – means those convicted of the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty now face mandatory life sentences. However, the law cannot be applied retrospectively.

Hogg said he wrote to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, 12 days ago to express concerns that Cole and Bowers might be included in the scheme, but had not received a reply.

He added that he planned to write again to Burnham, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to convey “the impact of the decision on the morale of my officers, but also on the 2,000 people who work in policing across the country”.

Hogg would not be drawn on whether all prisoners convicted of manslaughter should be exempt from the scheme.

The government has already said those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming will not be released early, after a campaign by victims.

“It isn’t my role to set government policy or set the law,” Hogg said.

“But I think if you ask most people in the streets, they would probably say people who take the life of another person in our country should remain behind bars as long as possible, and I don’t think that’s particularly controversial.”

However, he added that the fact Harper was an emergency services worker is a “significantly aggravating factor”.

Hogg said the criminal justice system also needed “greater investment around rehabilitation”. He said the National Police Chiefs’ Council estimated it would cost about £480m to manage the freed offenders in the community.

“I think there needs to be a balance between the risk caused [by] prisons being full, but also the risk of releasing people early who still pose a risk to the public,” he said.

“One of the challenges around the sentencing act [is that it] releases people on the basis of the crime committed, not on the basis of how reformed they are, have they been rehabilitated, and not on the basis of the risk they pose back in the community.

“So if you have somebody who still poses the risk … has felt no remorse, and they are back on the streets early, of course that risk has to be managed by the probation service and policing.”

‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakaway

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 19:19:47 GMT

Document shows Fifa staff were involved in project

Fifa was prepared to sideline member associations

Gianni Infantino held talks about rebranding the ill-fated European breakaway competition the “Fifa Super League”, with negotiations going as far as the term sheet for an agreement that would have changed the face of European football.

The term sheet, whose full contents can be revealed for the first time, is dated October 2020 and proposes renaming any new competition under Fifa’s branding. It outlines the extent to which Infantino’s administration were implicated in a scheme that caused widespread revulsion among fans and excluded clubs in April 2021. It also reveals that Fifa was prepared to sideline its member associations in pushing plans to cut back the number of international windows and outlines how global football’s governing body would have been given special governance and political rights with a “golden share”.

In a week when football is reeling from the fallout after Infantino scrapped his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, the document shows Fifa’s leadership was deeply involved in another attempt to put the sport’s major competitions under corporate control. It sets out a partnership of at least 12 years between Fifa and the Super League and proposes a joint venture that would have run its commercial operations.

The document also proposes that an iteration of Fifa’s expanded Club World Cup, referred to as the “global club competition”, would be held annually over an enshrined three-week period and tied directly to the Super League. That tournament would have been a straight knockout competition rather than the group-based version that relaunched in 2025. While the term sheet states that the new tournaments would have to be passed by Fifa’s annual congress and the Fifa council, federations around the world are understood to have been bypassed in the plan’s formation.

Infantino was among a number of Fifa staff involved in the project and is understood to have been fully aware of its progression. The term sheet says the founding clubs “want to agree the terms of a partnership” between the Super League and Fifa, leading to the creation of the two competitions. It follows an initial proposal to Fifa by the breakaway clubs, also seen by the Guardian, that sketches the framework for a potential agreement. While non-binding, a term sheet is generally the precursor to a definitive contract and suggests discussions between Fifa and the Super League’s creators were nearing a conclusion at the time.

It is unclear whether Infantino and Fifa progressed their role in the project beyond the term-sheet stage. After a version of the scheme was infamously launched without Fifa’s direct involvement in April 2021, ultimately scrapped following large-scale protests, Infantino addressed Uefa’s congress in Montreux saying his organisation could “only strongly disapprove the creation of the Super League”. Multiple sources have stated that an earlier conversation with the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, convened by a third party, hastened Fifa’s president distancing himself from the new venture. Infantino is understood to have told associates afterwards that he had no wish to work against football’s institutions.

Yet the evidence of Fifa’s outline agreement with the Super League, coupled with Infantino’s disastrous Football Forward Enterprise scheme, casts doubt on that assertion and suggests multiple attempts to reshape the game without consulting its most important stakeholders. The league would have contained 15 permanent members and five clubs qualifying from existing competitions. It also commits to creating a women’s equivalent, using the same clubs, by an unspecified date. The term sheet refers to Fifa under the name “WO1”, which is also the name used in the British army for a high-ranking officer.

In a section outlining the agreement’s key components, it says the Super League “is open to discuss naming the competition WO1 SL”. It also confirms Fifa would be “granted a preferred equity stake in the Super League”, which would give it decision-making capability on format changes, calendar alterations, distribution of solidarity money and the appointment of a chief executive for the competition.

Senior figures within European football are understood to have been shocked by the plan to drastically shrink the number of international windows, squeezing them into two fortnight-long spaces each year. Member associations, many of whom are being courted for support by Infantino as he battles to save his tenure this week, may have lost the commercial opportunities available from added visibility for their national teams and found themselves at the behest of a privately run club competition.

A separate point in the earlier proposal also notes “reduction of leagues” as a point for discussion. The term sheet states that “a new international match calendar” devised by Fifa, the Super League and “other relevant stakeholders” would be reviewed and implemented with Fifa’s agreement.

Clubs participating in the Super League would have been required to join the World Football Club Association (WFCA), which was a short-lived representative body launched by the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez, in 2019. Real were key drivers of the Super League scheme and only closed the door on the project when announcing an agreement with Uefa in February this year.

Fifa’s close proximity to the Super League proposal adds to the growing number of privately backed ventures brought to the table by Infantino during his 10-year reign. In 2018 he pressed the case for a $25bn offer from SoftBank, the Japanese institution, to create an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. Close allies within Fifa are understood to have cautioned him against the plan, which failed to gain support after opposition from Europe.

Fifa was approached for comment.

Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa?

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 19:00:26 GMT

Federation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World Cup

In recent decades the city of Salé, just across the river from Rabat on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, has undergone a remarkable transformation. At the start of this century it was a gritty working-class area, whose old town was still weathered enough to serve as a body double for the Somali capital Mogadishu in the film Black Hawk Down. But in recent decades, under the country’s autocratic government, the area has been transformed beyond measure, and largely beyond control.

The population has trebled in the space of 40 years. Slums have been cleared, often forcibly, to make way for grand megaprojects: a new tram system, luxury tourist spaces, a sparkling marina, a blue-chip business park called Technopolis, and – since last July – the African headquarters of Fifa. And in a way, this hub of disruption and avarice, unshakeable volition and rampant capitalism, feels like the perfect location from which a besieged warlord might choose to make his desperate last stand.

According to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been “holed up” in Salé this week as he tries to save his presidency. Apparently Infantino’s aides have been feverishly calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer Infantino their public support. On Wednesday one of them, Luís Figo, decided to break his silence. “Infantino must go,” he said, condemning his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup to private investors as “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed.” That’ll be a no, then.

Meanwhile, the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation are massing forces at the gates. A “governance boycott”, in which members refuse to attend meetings or ratify Fifa decisions, is one idea. A rival World Cup-style competition – which would in effect translate to secession – is the nuclear option. And yes, in the moment this feels good, stirring, cathartic, karmic. We should all take a certain satisfaction in seeing Infantino get his long-deserved kicking. For all this, a pertinent question should also pose itself. Why now? And why like this?

It is, after all, almost eight years since Fifa first proposed selling off a slice of its commercial legacy. In 2018 Infantino agreed in principle a deal with the Japanese firm SoftBank – whose main financial backer just so happened to be the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia – for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. The scheme eventually sputtered to a halt, but with virtually none of the screaming and apocalyptic threats seen over the past fortnight.

It is four years since the soiled, blood-soaked Qatar World Cup, and the “today I feel gay” speech that turned the sport’s most important administrator into a figure of ridicule. Two years since Saudi Arabia were handed the 2034 tournament in a bidding process no other country appeared to be prepared for. Three years since the Club World Cup was coerced into existence over a chorus of player welfare concerns. Two months since Omar Artan was summarily denied entry to a World Cup in which he was supposed to be refereeing. One month since Folarin Balogun had his suspension overturned in a supposedly independent process.

For the men and women who – as it turned out – held Infantino’s fate in their hands all along, none of this appeared to be a red line. For years the injustices, the indignities, the reputational and environmental damage, the ruptures to rules and structures, the stitch-ups and dead migrant workers, have been waved through by acclamation. And so it is worth wondering whether anything has materially changed here, beyond the fleeting opportunity for ambitious footballing executives to claim the keys to Infantino’s empire.

It is more than a decade since the late Lord Triesman, the former FA chair, described Fifa as a “mafia family”, and nothing about that description feels less true today. This is in many ways a supralegal body operating beyond the boundaries of conventional politics or economics, operating under its own rules and its own moral code, tied together not through popular consent but through a feudal system of tribute and protection, which changes not through legislation or overthrow but by occasional mob-style decapitation.

The moral objections to Infantino’s investment plan are manifest, but perhaps more striking still – for a president who has staked everything on his ability to drive revenue – is the economic illiteracy. One hand-picked buyer (Joshua Kushner), one made-up number ($20 billion) and an artificial countdown clock (19 September). Is this really how to fetch the best price for your asset? Or is it how you act when you want to secure a bigger piece of the largesse you have so selflessly created, but are statutorily bound to one more term in your current job?

And in hindsight, it seems clear that Infantino’s thirst for bending rules and breaking conventions was a kind of loyalty test, his Yakuza tattoo, a way of demonstrating to the billionaire investor class that he truly was one of them. No wonder his first instinct on finding himself cornered was reportedly to appeal to Donald Trump: his roof, his protection, his kindred spirit.

It is often said that Infantino is the symptom and Fifa is the disease. In fact Fifa too is the symptom; the disease is capitalistic fascism, a simple disdain for humanity, a belief that some are born to rule and others are bound to follow. And this is a cancer that will remain embedded in so many of our institutions long after Infantino has taken his last celebrity selfie, long after “45/47” has chowed down his last Oval Office Big Mac, long after the new Fifa regime has swept in through the door wearing the pageant sash of reform.

Football, the greatest mass pursuit ever invented, will of course endure. In a way its ingenuity, its ability to adapt and not be crushed by adaptation, is its beauty and its curse. Like the Salé skyline, it warps and shifts and grows and gentrifies and swells beyond recognition. This is still recognisably the same land, the same turf, upon which its ancestors once stood. But the old waterfront is gone for ever.

Mohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 18:00:25 GMT

In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a reality

The entrance to Al Mokawloon Al Arab’s youth sector feels imposing. At first it is confusing to pinpoint the reason. Is it the facade; a mesh of thick concrete slabs, a marble-like trim that alters in colour depending on the light, and the no-nonsense black steel gate? Perhaps it is the stately signage of white block letters in Arabic juxtaposed against the dark background, with satellite pieces of information and announcements signifying importance. But to stop and pay attention to buildings around Nasr City in eastern Cairo is to notice that the blend of functional and decorative elements of the entrance, down to even the font and array of notices, is not unique.

The building’s aura can be explained by the main image above its gates, and the knowledge that to walk through them is to follow the footsteps a history-maker took from the age of 14. Mohamed Salah’s face has pride of place above the gates; it is a reminder of where he’s been, but more pertinently, of why it is important to marry talent with discipline and determination. The truth is he has achieved the impossible.

Hamdi Nouh, Salah’s first coach at Al Mokawloon and who he has referred to as a “second father”, knows that is because “he was ready to sacrifice everything, he wanted to work hard, and liked to learn”. It sounds simple, until you start drilling at the heart of what it means for a boy from Nagrig to endure a nine-hour round trip five days a week simply to train in Cairo. Salah’s route has become so well known, you can read the tale of the minimum four buses he needed to take each way in Chinese, Spanish and every other major language. One from the T-junction at the edge of his village to reach Basyoun. The transfer from there to the capital of the Gharbia Governorate, Tanta. The great slog of around 100 kilometres to reach the rush of Ramses Square. A connection from Cairo’s chaotic central transport hub to Nasr City. And, on the luckier days, a ride close to the club’s gates to spare Salah having to run almost two kilometres up a steep hill, to be on time for his training session. After four hours at the centre, he would leave to do that all again in reverse.

The problem with summarising the journey in this way, as it has been done since 2017 when Salah started shifting the parameters for greatness in the Premier League, is that it omits the reality of what this daily grind truly entailed. When Nouh underlines sacrifice, part of it was Salah giving up his youth to sit shoulder slammed into shoulder, bodies filling up every available inch of the microbus and often even hanging off it, racing to the next stop and against the anxiety of missing a connection in a schedule that had no rhyme nor reason, with only enough cash for the exact journey. He was too respectful to ask his father for more, even though there was no margin for error. Salah weirdly enjoyed rather than endured the stressful odyssey. “I didn’t feel tired travelling when I was young,” he would reflect in 2022. “It’s because I was doing something I wanted, chasing a dream I had to reach. I wasn’t seeing my situation, I was seeing my goal. These are days I sit and think about, I’ll never forget them and I still smile now when I remember everything.”

It is not the same for Umm Mohamed (the Mother of Mohamed), who was averse to her eldest son spending only two hours at school, between seven and nine in the morning, and venturing so far away from his village, when lanes were seen as a mere suggestion and dangerous driving was the only type. Her memories were of worry and fear prompted by the high number of crashes involving microbuses. One major accident along her son’s route provoked sheer panic, which only increased as his phone rang unanswered. She tried calling over 20 times, and while Salah insists exhaustion didn’t grip him during his great trek, he didn’t pick up because he was fast asleep. She was also concerned if he had enough money, as was her husband, Salah Ghaly, who worked as a government administrator and traded in jasmine, Nagrig’s greatest export. He funded Salah’s football path, first to Ittihad in Basyoun, which was only a half-hour trip, then on to the Othmason club in Tanta, 90 minutes away, all before he became a teenager, followed by the almighty mission to Al Mokawloon.

Salah was eight when he started training there and rushed at opponents with the fearlessness of a microbus driver. “He was small, but his left foot and his shots were powerful,” Ghamri Abdel-Hameed el-Saadani, who was the juniors coach at the youth centre, says. “He was fast and could do things with the ball the other boys couldn’t.” Salah’s father knew it, and despite his own apprehensions about the big city and how it could swallow and spit out young hopefuls, he told Umm Mohamed they were doing the right thing.

Back to the entrance of Al Mokawloon’s youth sector, and just behind the black steel gates, lies a story that hasn’t travelled the world like the bus trip. One of Salah’s teammates had suggested they could stay at his uncle’s house in Greater Cairo for the week. It was located in the 10th of Ramadan City and it took plenty of convincing for his parents to green-light the sleepover. Salah’s father gave him 60 Egyptian pounds and he set off. When they arrived at the house, in the black of the night, his friend’s uncle was not there. They were stuck, with not enough money or knowledge to find other lodgings.

All Salah knew of Cairo were the roads through it to train at Al Mokawloon. His friend, whose name he doesn’t want to reveal to avoid the media frenzy that accompanies any detail about his life, suggested the house of someone else he knew not too far away. When they got there, Salah encountered a bigger problem. The dwelling was in a cemetery, a saddening – and scary – symptom of Cairo’s severe housing shortage and high population density. Salah was not going to stay in the necropolis. His friend had one final plan: he knew an on-site administrator at Al Mokawloon who could let them in. Right behind the steel gate, they laid out the sheets they had packed on the floor into two makeshift beds.

Salah used his shoes as a pillow and set his alarm for 6am so the pair could be up before anyone caught them and the administrator got in trouble. They packed up their bedding and headed off, returning to the complex at 9am as though they had just arrived. The sleeping arrangement stayed secret but needed to be amended; there was too much jeopardy being so close to the entrance. The next day, the duo slept on Field 2 of the four pitches, in the open under the cold night sky. In the morning, they would again go into covert mode and Salah enjoyed that he could be early for training.

Salah had already packed in a lifetime’s worth of sacrifice, effort and lessons by his 18th birthday. The moment he will never forget, however, was when he joined the first team group and moved into the Al Mokawloon’s residences. “Not everyone could stay there, so psychologically I felt like I became someone, like a star,” Salah would recall. “I used to see players finish training and go upstairs, while I would leave to take the journey back to Nagrig. I’d think, ‘One day I’ll go up there’.” He would go higher than any other Egyptian footballer in history.

This is an edited extract from Only Mo Salah: An intimate portrait of the Egyptian King by Melissa Reddy, which is published by Orion Publishing and available from 13 August.

More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:54:44 GMT

Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means

More than 1,100 people, including survivors of torture and trafficking, have been convicted of illegally arriving in the UK since 2022, according to freedom of information data.

The Home Office introduced the offence of illegal arrival in 2022 in a bid to deter those planning to come to the UK by small boat or by other irregular means such as lorries.

The decision was widely condemned at the time because the refugee convention states that those seeking sanctuary should not be criminalised for the way they travel, as they often do not have the option to move legally from an unsafe country to a safe one.

FoI data obtained from the Home Office by the criminologist Dr Victoria Taylor, a research fellow at the University of Manchester, reveals 1,109 people were prosecuted for illegal arrival between July 2022 and January 2026.

The data shows 628 arrived on a small boat, 296 of whom were captured on surveillance drone footage steering a dinghy. Others had previous immigration history in the UK.

Just 12 people have been convicted of the separate offence of facilitation, after steering the dinghies they arrived on. It is harder for the Home Office and Crown Prosecution Service to secure evidence that people on a dinghy were involved in organising a journey across the Channel than to prosecute them for illegal arrival.

People have been identified as having their “hand on the tiller” for many reasons, including having boating experience, steering in return for discounted passage, taking it in turns, or being under duress.

In one illegal arrival case, the Home Office settled a judicial review relating to a trafficking survivor from South Sudan who was forced at gunpoint to pilot a small boat. Officials have now agreed to ensure greater protection for trafficking victims in these cases.

Emily Soothill, partner at Deighton Pierce Glynn, who represented the man, said: “Unfortunately it is clear from our client’s case that potential victims of trafficking are regularly being convicted for illegal arrival and imprisoned for many months. The concessions made in our client’s case underline the need for a robust and consistent application of the UK’s modern slavery framework to prevent survivors of trafficking from being wrongly treated as criminals.”

Some of those convicted of the various offences were survivors of torture and trafficking, and there were at least 30 age disputed children among them, 19 of whom had spent time in adult prisons.

The organisation Captain Support UK has worked with hundreds of people imprisoned in illegal arrival cases, all of whom sought asylum in the UK in the hours before they were arrested.

A spokesperson said: “We see first-hand the negative impact these prosecutions have on people and their families. We urgently call on the government to stop imprisoning people on the move. No one should be put in prison for seeking safety and a better life.”

Taylor said: “The process of who is selected for prosecution is arbitrary and cruel.”

She added that the most of those imprisoned for illegal arrival since 2022 had claimed asylum in the hours before they were arrested. Many have been granted asylum since their release or have been recognised as victims of trafficking, or both.

“There are serious questions about the compatibility of these prosecutions with the refugee convention, which was drafted to prevent states from penalising refugees for how they seek safety. There is no evidence to support the government’s claims that these prosecutions will ‘deter’ people from attempting to cross the Channel,” Taylor said.

The Home Office has been approached for comment.
