Soriot should explain the curious case of AstraZeneca’s non-deal

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:45:05 GMT

AstraZeneca’s rumoured takeover of Bristol Myers Squibb already looked weird, and was met with a lack of enthusiasm by shareholders

AstraZeneca falls to third-largest UK company amid US merger talks

Hold the heartburn pills. It seems AstraZeneca is no longer contemplating a takeover of US rival Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to create a $400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical colossus. On Monday, the UK firm’s shares plunged 9% on the FT’s report of preliminary talks. On Wednesday, Reuters said there are no ongoing discussions. Cue a mini-relief rally in AZ’s share price.

Neither company has seen fit to tell its shareholders what was happening, so it’s impossible to know if the talks were a tentative ‘what if?’ corporate flirtation or something more substantial that has been killed, perhaps, by the lack of enthusiasm on the part of AZ’s shareholders.

The deal – or non-deal – looked weird for the reasons given here earlier in the week. AZ has prospered under chief executive Sir Pascal Soriot for the past 14 years by concentrating on backing its best ideas in the labs in the interests of long-term success, as opposed to playing debt-fuelled takeover games that rely on short-term cost-cutting. Since Soriot proclaims absolute confidence in hitting AZ’s revenue target of $80bn in 2030, there is no obvious reason to divert from the winning script. And, given BMS’s revenue headache in the next few years as a blockbuster cancer treatment goes off patent, the target looked odd, never mind the current quality of its cashflows.

There are possible counter-arguments, naturally. Both companies are very big in oncology, so there could have been an opportunity to establish multi-year dominance in a core pharma field if competition regulators could be persuaded. Maybe the crossover meant potential cost savings would have been bigger, or easier to achieve, than is normally the case. Perhaps Soriot spotted potential in BSM’s drugs pipeline. Or just an opportunity to accelerate his ambition for AZ to generate half its revenues in the US, the world’s biggest and most lucrative market for pharma firms; the current share is 43%.

Whatever it is, Soriot should shed some light on whether he sees mega-deals as any possible part of AZ’s future. It’s one thing to take a strict “no comment” approach to individual takeover tales. But most AZ shareholders surely assume they are invested in a company that doesn’t do bet-the-balance-sheet mega-deals. Rare diseases specialist Alexion, bought by AZ in 2021 for $39bn, was big – but not in BMS’s $133bn league. And the clear rationale in that case was to boost innovation.

The worry is that the pull of the US is dominating strategic thinking as Soriot, at the age of 67, enters his final years (probably) at the helm. Or maybe there is an emerging analysis that AI is changing the pharma game. Greater transparency on corporate thinking would be useful. Soriot has always presented AZ as the last company in need of a transformative deal. If he is actually flexible on the idea, shouldn’t shareholders know?

AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:43:57 GMT

The UK’s AI Security Institute test revealed AI models indulging in unprecedented hacking attempts

AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to trick developers

Two cutting-edge AI models have targeted real people and organisations in the latest safety scare to hit the technology. The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) said the incident was unprecedented but could become more common as the technology becomes increasingly capable.

The AISI, which is owned by the UK government and tests advanced AI models, said in a blog post that two AI agents carried out unprecedented hacking attempts during a cybersecurity evaluation. The agents – tools that carry out computer tasks autonomously – were powered by two models: Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol. AISI said there were 19 examples of rogue behaviour, 17 of them carried out by Mythos.

In the most serious incident, the Mythos agent decided that hacking users on GitHub – a platform used by software developers – would enable it to deploy a piece of software that would allow it to pass the test. It set up accounts with fake online identities and used them to target a software developer on GitHub with the power to approve its malicious code. It also sent emails carrying malware to other individuals.

It hoped that getting the malware downloaded would set off a chain of events that would allow it to pass the evaluation. The Sol-powered agent also attempted to access a GitHub account.

This novel behaviour was detected on 28 July and took an hour to shut down. At one point AISI shut off all access to the Mythos and Sol models across the entire organisation.

The institute said the models were showing deceptive behaviour it had not seen before. In one example, the Mythos agent signed off a message on GitHub in Danish to try to convince the Danish-speaking developer it was genuine. In another tactic it used a fake GitHub account to agree with its assertions that the malware it was pushing at developers was not dangerous.

The agent used a Tor browser – which anonymises a web user’s identity – to get around sign-up checks on GitHub and create multiple fake accounts.

AISI also published the agent’s “reasoning” behind the fake supporting statement ruse. The model, which tackles problems by breaking them down into “steps” that can be viewed by researchers, stated that it would delay posting the fake support message for a few minutes so that it would read as “independent feedback rather than coordinated.”

AISI described the behaviour as “sustained”. It kept on trying.

In a detailed 35-page report into the incident, AISI said that five important factors contributed to the incident: the models were deliberately given open internet access, which enabled them to approach GitHub; AISI deliberately disabled certain cyber guardrails; the institute did not have a separate AI monitoring the tests in real time, which helped the main GitHub incident go undetected for nearly two days; in some cases the models received a “misconfigured” instruction that prevented them from solving the test and thus required them to act outside the boundaries of the evaluation; and the agents were not given explicit instructions prohibiting them from certain behaviour such as sending phishing emails.

AISI says it is unclear whether the agents “realised” they were targeting real humans. Throughout the attempted hack the Mythos agent reasons about whether it is interacting with real or simulated people and systems. At one point the agent reasons that it is behaving in the real world: “This is happening on real GitHub, so the consequences are genuine.” It also states: “The environment appears to be simulated.”

AISI described the agent conducting “OSINT” – or open source intelligence, where a hacker pulls together publicly available information to work out how to breach a target – to study the developer behind the software it wanted to hack. It gained the developer’s email address and looked at their GitHub history to gauge when they would be active.

AISI states clearly these models were operating under abnormal conditions of unfettered internet access and lowered cyber guardrails. Calling for the incident to be viewed with “nuance”, it said it had partly enabled the behaviour with its own actions – but it did not anticipate the “extent and severity” of what happened.

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said giving the models access to the open internet and removing some guardrails raised questions about using the rest of the world as “live guinea pigs” for powerful technology.

“What we should be alarmed about is not what the models are capable of but the way people are testing them,” he said.

AISI said in its report into the GitHub incident that giving a powerful model full internet access was a good way of simulating how far a rogue actor could push an AI. It said such a strategy gives a “more realistic sense of what a model may be capable of once deployed”.

Ciaran Martin, the former head of the National Cyber Security Centre – part of the GCHQ intelligence agency – said the circumstances of the incident were unlikely to be replicated in the real world so “it’s not that worrying”. But he said it was the third example in recent weeks, after similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, that testers have released AI agents and found out about their misbehaviour after the fact.

Martin said AISI’s pledge to carry out real-time monitoring of tests in the future “must be the answer”.

Demise of the monoculture: why so many have never heard UK’s record-breaking No 1 single

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:42:47 GMT

Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In is longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, and yet it seems to have passed many people by

It’s the biggest song in the UK, but have you ever heard it? That was the question many were asking this week, after Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In became the longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, spending an unprecedented 19 weeks at the top.

The British Phonographic Industry said the song had resonated with listeners “in such a profound way”, while Fender thanked Dean and fans “for making this song the juggernaut that it is”.

Yet the record prompted a wave of bafflement online from people who claimed they had never knowingly heard it. “Crazy how monoculture no longer exists because I don’t think I’ve actually ever heard this song,” wrote one user on X.

The disconnect has reignited a broader debate about whether Britain’s music charts still reflect a shared national culture. How can a record dominate the charts for nearly five months, and win song of the year at the Brits, while leaving large sections of the public feeling as though it passed them by? Only those living under a rock when the Beatles or Elvis Presley had a No 1 single could have avoided knowing about it.

The answer, according to industry experts, is that dominance no longer means ubiquity.

“In the era of Top of the Pops, Radio 1 and Smash Hits, the weekly charts were a shared cultural event,” said Chris Anderton, associate professor in cultural economy at Southampton Solent University. Streaming has replaced that with endless choice and algorithmic recommendation, he said, producing what author Eli Pariser called the “filter bubble” – where listeners are “repeatedly served music similar to what they already like”. It’s the same mechanism, Anderton noted, that isolates social media users from opposing viewpoints: taste, like opinion, has been commodified and automated.

The record for the longest spell at No 1 was previously held by Frankie Laine, whose I Believe spent 18 weeks at the top in 1953, when the UK singles chart was less than a year old and featured just 12 songs. More recent contenders, including Bryan Adams’ (Everything I Do) I Do It For You, Wet Wet Wet’s Love Is All Around, Drake’s One Dance and Ed Sheeran’s Shape of You, all fell short of breaking the record.

Rein Me In was written by Fender for his album People Watching before being re-recorded as a duet and released in June 2025. It took 36 weeks to reach No 1, and has held the top spot on and off since February, seeing off brief challenges from Harry Styles, Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Taylor Swift. It also outlasted the “accelerated decline” rules introduced by the Official Charts Company in 2017 to specifically stop streaming hits lingering indefinitely.

The mechanics of a No 1 hit single have changed too. Chart position once meant physical sales; today it blends sales with stream-equivalents from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube – so 100 premium streams, or 600 ad-funded ones, equal one sale.

But the fragmentation runs deeper than streaming maths, said the music and culture critic Nicolas-Tyrell Scott. Younger listeners now discover music through TikTok, YouTube and personalised algorithms, meaning “it’s not as easy as saying a track is No 1, therefore it’s resonant and dominating in everyone’s sphere of influence”.

Gen Z spend just 16% of their average audio day on the radio, Scott noted, against 42% on streaming and 20% on YouTube – and platform algorithms actively reinforce those micro-cultures. “It’s easy to see why a song like this could pass clusters of people by, despite dominating commercially,” he said.

Chart analyst James Masterton put it starkly: a single can break records “yet it still struggles with any kind of cultural cut-through”. Unlike past mega-hits, Masterton argued, this one has no film or event attached to it. “It isn’t from a movie soundtrack or connected with any national event. It just … exists.”

Weekly chart consumption has grown from around 20m streams at the start of the decade to more than 30m now, Masterton said, but most No 1s this year have clustered around just 60,000 of those streams – proof that while the audience has grown, the biggest hits command a much smaller slice of attention than they once did. Television exposure barely moves the needle either: this year’s Brit awards produced no lasting bump for the acts it celebrated, while radio itself has splintered into narrowly targeted playlists.

“This is merely one symptom of what sociologists are noting as the demise of the monoculture,” he said. “With such a vast range of entertainment options available, few creations or productions really need appeal to a large cross section of the public. Which is just as well given how vanishingly few actually do.”

Not everyone is convinced the disconnect is genuine. Some online commentators have suggested that claiming never to have heard a massive song says more about performing detachment than actual unfamiliarity.

Anderton offered a caveat. Songs such as Padam Padam, or the Brat summer moment, broke through because they escaped streaming and became wider cultural phenomena across television, social media, news coverage and memes. “The ubiquitous hit is not dead,” he said. “It just requires much more than chart success.”

Super League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRL

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:33:54 GMT

Australian officials touring clubs to gauge mood

Wigan and Warrington set date for Dublin clash

NRL officials have arrived in ­England to hold talks with clubs as the prospect of a groundbreaking deal with Super League nears completion, while two of the competition’s heavyweights, Wigan Warriors and Warrington Wolves, confirmed they will lead an on-the-road weekend to Dublin in 2027.

Rugby league’s two premier club competitions have been in discussions for most of this year about a deal that would see the NRL invest a significant sum into Super League, while taking authoritative control of the competition in a bid to transform its long-term fortunes. That investment would also ensure the financial security of clubs. Both competitions put talks on hold while they finalised their broadcast details; the NRL has just completed a A$5.3bn (£2.8bn) deal for its rights, while Super League expects to confirm in the next week how its new-look broadcast deal will be shaped. Sky Sports is expected to show two or three games a week, with the rest of the fixtures streamed or broadcast elsewhere.

But the NRL has now made Super League investment its number one priority. The Guardian has been told by multiple clubs that they have been visited by officials from Australia, or expect a visit in the coming days. The belief is that Australian figures are keen to get a deeper understanding of the mood among clubs as they consider a proposal from Super League to invest.

That is the clearest sign yet that a deal is close, with Super League’s leading official, Rhodri Jones, saying: “We’re very hopeful that we’ll make some significant progress with the NRL over the next seven days. “We’ve been engaged with them since May but they’ve now done their TV deal, so I can say it feels like we’re their top priority.” It’s still with them to come back to us. We’re hopeful we’ll get something very soon.”

Both Wigan and Warrington, who became the first Super League clubs to make the trip to Las Vegas last year with the NRL, have long been advocates of Australian investment and governance. The Warriors’ CEO, Kris Radlinski, reiterated that backing on Wednesday at the announcement of their Dublin clash with Warrington at Leinster’s RDS Arena on Saturday 24 April next year. When asked if Wigan supported were still supportive of the NRL deal, Radlinski said: “100%. As we have been from the start. What they’re doing in the NRL is fantastic. I think it’s the start of a significant few months for the sport. We’re at a point where we’ll find out our broadcasting future at a time when our NRL counterparts are closing in on an offer.”

The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:32:21 GMT

Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia

The armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact that it got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation.

Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found in Europe far from the Ukrainian border.

Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from the Ukraine war, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery.

Police from the German state of Saxony confirmed that the drone was “carrying an unknown explosive device” discovered by an employee in the “secure cargo flight operations area” near the airport’s southern runway.

German media reported the attached bomb was made of PETN and semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty.

A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”.

Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in the Czech Republic, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around.

A second unidentified flying object, which could well have been another drone, also collided with a DHL cargo plane in the aftermath of the first incident several hundred metres above the ground. The cargo plane only sustained minor damage.

Leipzig airport is a sensitive site, the European base of Ukrainian Antonov jets, used for heavy cargo. The airport is also used by Nato and the German military for transport, as well as being a DHL hub, and the Ukrainian planes suggest it may also have been a node for supplies to Kyiv.

Nato would only say it was aware of the incident on Wednesday, though it is eye-catching that the western alliance appears to have not been able to prevent drones from flying into and over a strategic airport.

It is not the first time Leipzig airport has been involved in a dangerous incident. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the airport in July 2024 while a second travelled to the UK and caught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham. Two similar packages were also found in Poland.

A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who are suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. The investigation found perpetrators were recruited and given instructions online, and frequently paid in cryptocurrency, their knowledge of the full plot apparently limited.

Russia has also been behind a string of drone incursions into Europe over the past year, some more blatant than others. Around 20 unarmed Russian delta-wing Gerbera drones crossed into Poland last September, forcing a major alert, with people in two of the country’s eastern provinces told to shelter indoors.

An analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) thinktank concluded last month that the Kremlin was behind a concerted drone surveillance campaign that targeted the US airbase at RAF Lakenheath and other key military sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

In the first case, Nato jets struggled to shoot down the incoming drones, most of which eventually crashed or lost power and glided to the ground. In the second, western militaries struggled to work out who were the culprits, failing to capture any of the drones or react to the surveillance efforts promptly.

Russia, in sum, has so far been able to conduct other firebomb operations, as well as drone harassment and surveillance campaigns with relative impunity. Moscow is already subject to a wide range of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine, and it is likely to believe that the west has little more it is willing to punish the country with.

“A drone carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition to what we have seen before,” said Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow with the IISS, adding ominously: “It is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found.”

Mexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, said on Wednesday that authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer.

“The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference.

At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024, according to local media.

They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23, was shot and killed at a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers.

Authorities announced last week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing.

The Guardian view on the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch: purging moderation is not ‘common sense’

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:20:51 GMT

A row over a local council candidate reveals a deeper problem with the Tory leader’s diagnosis of her party’s electoral predicament

Kemi Badenoch has been clear about the qualifying criteria for prospective Conservative MPs. They must be “serious people who understand common sense,” she has said. The situation in local government is different, as demonstrated by Mrs Badenoch’s ill-judged support for a former neo-Nazi, selected to stand as a councillor in Somerset next year.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine has convictions for racially aggravated harassment of a Jewish Labour MP and assaulting a police officer among other offences. On Wednesday, as pressure grew on the party leader to repudiate him, he withdrew his candidacy.

Mrs Badenoch had defended Mr Bonehill-Paine on the grounds that he had renounced his former views and was involved in anti-extremism training, using his own experience of fanatical antisemitism as a cautionary tale. The Conservative leader said she believed in giving people a second chance.

That is not an ethos she has always applied. When Louise Haigh, currently first secretary of state, resigned from Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet over an old and minor fraud offence, Mrs Badenoch was unforgiving, declaring that “the country needs conviction politicians, not politicians with convictions”.

Mrs Badenoch struggled to justify the inconsistency, claiming that a “higher threshold” applied for MPs than for councillors, whose duties are limited to “parking and bins”. That argument sat awkwardly with the defence of Mr Bonehill-Paine, based on the thoroughness of his rehabilitation. If his anti‑extremism work was exemplary, she might have wanted him to have as wide an audience as possible. Once she accepted that his offences would disqualify him from running for parliament, it was absurd to suggest that Somerset residents should accept a former neo-Nazi running their services. The episode raises questions about the Tory leader’s judgment.

All parties have more rigorous selection tests for MPs than council candidates. The job is more consequential and vetting resources are limited. All have been embarrassed at some point by the exposure of cranks and extremists in their election lists.

But Mrs Badenoch’s contortions in this case reveal a different problem. The Conservatives are struggling to carve out a distinct identity in a fragmented political arena. The leader’s diagnosis of the Tories’ crushing 2024 defeat is that the party “talked right but governed left”. The practical application of this formula involves refusal to challenge Reform UK or its schismatic offshoot, Restore, as they drive immigration policy to ever more extreme positions, and anathematisation of the Tories’ liberal, one-nation tradition.

Mrs Badenoch’s definition of the values and opinions expected of a Tory parliamentary candidate prohibits support for net zero targets or Britain remaining a signatory to the European convention on human rights. Former MPs, including senior ministers, who hold such views are not welcome. Voters who care about the climate or believe that Britain should keep good relations with other European democracies are invited to look elsewhere.

It is not surprising that a strategy of repudiating mainstream, centre-right politics in pursuit of an agenda dictated by radical nationalists has failed to lift Tory support. Since Mrs Badenoch claims to believe in the advancement of “serious people who understand common sense” in politics, she should consider applying that test more rigorously to her own candidacy to be prime minister.

The Guardian view on French cinema’s De Gaulle moment: present anxieties inform a new focus on the past

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 17:16:09 GMT

A wave of films dealing with the second world war is captivating a nation facing major contemporary challenges

For weeks now, anglophone cinephiles have been focusing their attention on the virtues and vices of Christopher Nolan’s $250m adaptation of The Odyssey. Across the Channel, however, Homer’s epic tale of a flawed Greek hero has been facing stiff domestic competition. A two-part biopic of General Charles de Gaulle, concentrating on his struggles to liberate France during the second world war, has been the word-of-mouth box office hit of the French summer.

It may be that five hours’ worth of De Gaulle attracted some punters seeking air-conditioned sanctuary from the heatwaves. But there have been rave reviews both from critics and audiences, and a notable upsurge of interest among the young. The success of the films has already had a cultural knock-on effect, boosting the number of visitors, for example, to the Museum of the Liberation of Paris.

The buzz around them is all the more striking given that the austere, aloof De Gaulle – in stark contrast to Winston Churchill – has remained a somewhat shadowy and elusive cinematic presence. Some of the cut-through has been attributed to a fast-paced, skilful screenplay, based upon British historian Julian Jackson’s acclaimed biography. The strategy of the veteran film producer Jérôme Seydoux to revitalise French historical drama through some blockbuster productions, including The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, has also been emphatically vindicated.

Intriguingly though, other more political factors may be playing a part. In portraying the heroic role of the Free French Forces in north Africa – made up mostly of Black colonial troops – the De Gaulle films speak to a new generation which has grown up amid far-right-inspired controversies over nationhood and identity. And at a time when Europe’s relations with a Trump-led United States have become fraught, and the economic threat posed by China has become pressing, a resurgence of interest in Gaullist notions of leadership is perhaps unsurprising.

The same might be said of a series of other high‑profile films dealing with France and the second world war. Cinemas are currently hosting, or about to host, two psychological portraits of collaboration with Marshal Philippe Pétain’s Vichy regime, an account of the life of the Resistance hero Jean Moulin, and a reconstruction of a famous attempt to rescue over 100 Jewish children awaiting deportation. In the pages of Le Monde, a French historian, Henry Rousso, has argued that “unlike the so-called ‘retro wave’ of the 1970s, these films do not claim to expose a repressed chapter of history … they are sounding alarm bells, with varying degrees of subtlety.”

Ahead of a presidential election that could see the daughter of a notorious defender of Vichy enter the Élysée, it is not hard to see why. As Mr Rousso observes, it would be false to equate Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National party with the fascism of the 1930s. But its willingness to flout republican values in relation to immigration policy, for example, carries deeply undesirable echoes of dark times.

Cinematic trends often reflect back to audiences their own preoccupations. If the focus this summer and autumn in France is on a period defined by the stark moral choices it imposed, and the biggest homegrown hit is a film about leadership, that may tell us something about present anxieties as well as past traumas.

The Washington state man accused of starting a wildfire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee around Spokane was previously questioned in connection with two fire investigations last year, according to court documents.

Authorities allege that Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, started Old Trails fire, one of three major wildfires burning in Spokane county in north-eastern Washington. He was arrested on Monday and booked on suspicion of first-degree arson.

The Old Trails fire is one of more than a dozen large blazes burning in Washington. The state has faced devastating fires in recent days amid what officials have described as an “extraordinary” fire season in the Pacific north-west due to extreme heat, drought and limited resources.

Farinacci has denied that he set the Old Trails fire.

The fires burning around Spokane have scorched more than 10,000 acres. Officials reported that cooler weather and higher relative humidity have aided firefighters in recent days, allowing them to establish containment lines along all three fires.

Crews are now focused on strengthening containment, and preparing for the return of critical fire weather this week and over the weekend.

John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, has said Farinacci was first questioned shortly after the Old Trails fire began, after he was identified by witnesses who saw him kneeling in the brush near the fire’s origin.

“He was bent over in the brush, acting nervous,” Paul Child, who was driving in the area with his grandson, told the Associated Press. “You get the feeling this guy’s up to something.”

Farinacci had waterproof matches, cigarettes and a butane lighter in his posession, authorities say. Police arrested him on Monday after an investigators ruled out other possible causes of the fire, and learned that he had been questioned in connection with other fires.

In July 2025, there were several “bus-sized” fires in an area near the Spokane River and Farinacci’s apartment. Police searching for a wildfire suspect at a state park the following month came upon Farinacci sitting on a bench “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. Law enforcement took photos of him and according to court documents he was wearing a green T-shirt like the one he was seen in on Saturday.

While he was questioned in the two investigations, he was not charged.

Since Farinacci’s arrest in connection with the Old Trails fire, a clearer picture of his criminal history has emerged. He previously served roughly a decade in prison for manslaughter and aggravated assault in the 2010 killing of his father. At age 21, he shot and killed his father after an argument in a family home in Arizona.

He was released from probation in early 2024, and a probation officer said he had a stable residence with his girlfriend and her family, but had not completed a mental health evaluation or domestic violence treatment.

Farinacci is currently being held on $1m bail.

The three outstanding riders in this year’s race broke clear of the peloton over the final steep gradients of Mont Brouilly, with 2023 Tour winner Vollering outsprinting overall race leader Reusser to take the fourth Tour stage win of her career.

“Today was a really cool race,” Vollering said. “Every single rider of the team was part of it and I enjoy those victories the most. It’s even more special and beautiful because you do it all together. I thought I was not going to make it in the sprint and somehow I made it, so it was a huge relief. I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does, and I knew Marlen would gamble. I just had to try and I gave it my everything. I needed every single metre of the finishing straight.”

On the unrelentingly hilly stage from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, Ferrand-Prévot’s Tour fell apart. The signs of her fading powers had come as early as stage three and were followed by a listless performance in Tuesday’s stage four time trial.

The fifth day of racing provided irrefutable confirmation of her vulnerability. “I think it’s unrecoverable,” she said of her five-minute deficit to her rivals.

As Vollering, Reusser and Niewiadoma were descending from Mont Brouilly to the finish, Ferrand-Prévot was still riding up the steep climb with legs of lead. If her performance in the time trial had been unnerving, her capitulation among the vineyards was complete.

Earlier in the day, Ferrand-Prévot’s hopes of reversing her overall deficit to Reusser and Vollering had been boosted by the news that, despite talk of the stage being rerouted due to the risk of wildfires, Friday’s stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux remains as scheduled.

Although the climb to the summit of the Ventoux remains unaffected, the Vaucluse prefecture has banned public access to the nearby hills of the Dentelles de Montmirail, where two shorter climbs are routed, citing “the sensitivity of the massif and the risk of fire”. But that’s now become academic given the champion’s distance from the front of the race.

After her disappointing time trial, dreams of a “PFP” bounceback were definitively shattered on the cruel slopes of the Col de Durbize, where the 2025 winner was left behind by a vicious acceleration from Vollering.

As the lead group, containing Vollering, Reusser and the 2024 champion Niewiadoma moved further ahead, Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence crumbled in the heat of the Beaujolais afternoon. The best she can hope for now is a stage win.

Meanwhile, the debate over Tuesday’s scrutiny of riders regarding the illegal use of chest padding to improve aerodynamics rumbled on, after riders union, the CPA, issued a statement demanding that such checks be undertaken in a “professional and respectful manner, that fully safeguards the dignity and privacy of every rider”.

The statement added that this was to “prevent any misunderstanding, controversy or unpleasant situations”.

Initial reports suggested that the padding checks would be carried out by a female race commissaire, however footage screened by Flemish media showed a male commissaire making an initial inspection, in public view.

The fears of illegal aerodynamic enhancement appear well founded however, as Gaël Le Bellec, a former world champion duathlete, now sports director of the Ma Petite Entreprise team competing in the Tour Femmes, acknowledged.

“I’ve never had wind of it among the women,” he said, “but I know that triathletes particularly put bidons [drink bottles] under their kit on their chest to reduce aerodynamic drag.”

If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:53:04 GMT

Responding to an editorial, Scott Hunter writes that the benefits of being a devolved authority have not yet arrived in Tees Valley, while John Hall calls for constitutional reform. Plus letters from Richard Dowling and Miland Joshi

Devolution has become the flavour of the month (The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it, 31 July). The case is well argued and the need for such reform fits neatly into the situation we find in the Tees Valley – chronic underinvestment, lack of economic growth, depopulation, and so on.

But the Tees Valley has had a devolved authority for 10 years and the benefits of devolution have not landed. The Tees Valley authority was issued a best value notice in April 2025, though there’s nothing to show for it.

The new-age proponents of devolution, by ignoring how Tees Valley became its basket case, are missing something vital. Devolution is discussed in economic terms in relation to the regions, and as political upheaval in relation to Westminster and the Treasury.

What’s missing is acknowledgment of the political upheaval that it brings to the regions, and it is the weakness of that that the Tees Valley exemplifies. The mayor is the sole elected person in the authority. Leaders of local councils form the authority cabinet but do so in addition to their day jobs. Does the public know? No, because the only combined authority news in the local press comes from the authority’s own press releases. It’s not hard to find people on Teesside who believe that there’s been a jobs bonanza here.

But the problem of political weakness within the authority remains. Devolution cannot succeed until this problem is addressed. Scott HunterEditor, Tees Valley Monitor

Andy Burnham is right to argue that England’s regions cannot deliver meaningful growth while power remains concentrated in Whitehall. Yet his intervention points to a deeper constitutional problem. England is being offered a form of devolution that remains inferior to the statutory settlements enjoyed by Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

While those nations have defined legislative frameworks setting out their powers and responsibilities, England’s regions remain dependent on piecemeal deals negotiated with central government.

Burnham’s admiration for Germany’s postwar Grundgesetz (Basic Law) is therefore well placed. The law not only defines the relationship between federal and state governments but also commits the federation to equivalent living conditions across the country. It offers constitutional clarity, stability and fairness. England has no comparable settlement. Instead, its uncodified constitutional arrangements allow power to remain concentrated in Westminster, leaving regional government dependent on the centre for permission, funding and direction.

If England is serious about rebalancing its economy, constitutional reform cannot stop at creating metro mayors or devolving selected powers. It requires a coherent constitutional settlement that places England’s regions on a secure and equal footing, replacing ad hoc devolution with a durable framework that disperses power by right rather than by ministerial discretion. John HallAlliance for Yorkshire

If devolution is to mean anything real at all, then actual power must be devolved, which would mean it sometimes being used for purposes some would not approve of. Your editorial was arguing for devolution only for your approved purposes (transport, skills and industry, not tax giveaways). Devolution for me but not for thee?Richard DowlingLeighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire

Regarding the article (Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham, 2 August), we should note that the argument about inequality doesn’t hold when we regard countries with inequality just as great as ours (if not worse), which have written constitutions, such as the United States and South Africa.

Regional devolution, or a written constitution, are not panaceas, because any system can only work as well as the humans operating it. If we are to have a written constitution, it might be well to make it as brief as possible, concentrating on principles rather than specific rules, so as to preserve the ability of the government to act nimbly when required, especially in crises.

One possible useful ingredient might be a rotating “citizens’ jury” within the Lords for handling complex or difficult issues, with the usual peers serving as expert consultors. The result would be an influential advisory body as a collective, with the members being temporary “peers” while they serve. Primary power would remain in the Commons, as now, with MPs who have a mandate from their constituents. Miland JoshiBirmingham

I am in support of Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s suggestion that we should abolish fines for holidays in school term time (I’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term time, 2 August). She makes all the correct and logical arguments, to which I would add one more. One of the justifications for the fines is that children miss out on valuable learning, but this is simply not the case as teachers turn to movies, games and other distractions in those last weeks of term.

There is very little curriculum learning happening in those periods before the main school holidays. And from what my children describe to me, over the years this “downing of tools” seems to be happening earlier each year. The argument that taking a child out of school a week before the end of term means they miss valuable learning is, frankly, laughable. Nick JohnsonDorset

It was good to read Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett writing about the draconian policy of fining parents for taking their children out of school to go on holiday. It is indeed appallingly unfair. And unkind and small-minded – children with family overseas may never be able to see them if they are only permitted to go in the school holidays, when fares are most expensive.

The reason invariably given – without evidence – is that it affects children’s education. Before the current regime, we took our daughter out of primary school every year – to see family in Scotland, or to go to friends’ weddings. It seems to have done her no harm. Twelve GCSEs with A*s, top marks in the international baccalaureate, a first at university. All despite a grim warning from the head: “If they miss a week of maths at seven, they never catch up.”

Most importantly, it seems to have given her intellectual curiosity. And a healthy questioning of rules. Name and address supplied

As a retired headteacher, I’m in total agreement with Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett. Many parents simply cannot afford to take a holiday when schools are closed, yet time away as a family is precious and above all can be educationally valuable and enriching. Never let schooling get in the way of your child’s education. Barbara FranceArnside, Cumbria

England’s climate is changing and our planting must change with it

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:44:49 GMT

We are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate, writes Richard Eltringham

Your report (Half of England officially in ‘exceptionally serious’ drought, 29 July) makes me think that perhaps it’s time to admit what horticulturists have whispered for years: the native‑plants‑only doctrine has had its day. We can keep insisting that every garden, park and verge must resemble a 1790s botanical inventory, or we can face the obvious – the climate those plants evolved for no longer exists.

We are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate. Oak saplings are crisping, beech woods are browning, and “rewilded” meadows are going from hopeful to tinderbox in a single heatwave. Meanwhile, drought‑tolerant non‑natives – Mediterranean shrubs, prairie perennials, desert grasses – sit ready to do the job: hold soil, feed pollinators, stay green, stay alive.

This isn’t heresy, it’s adaptation. If the choice is plant non‑natives or watch landscapes die, then the path is obvious. Clinging to botanical nationalism while ecosystems collapse is not conservation; it’s sentimentality. England’s climate has changed. Our planting palette must change with it. Richard Eltringham Leicester

Woman arrested after four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:42:59 GMT

Metropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assault

Covent Garden stabbings – latest updates

A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said.

The Metropolitan police said the men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to a major trauma centre after the lunchtime incident on Endell Street.

Two of the men were being treated for injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing and the other two had been discharged.

A 47-year-old woman remained in custody after being arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, believed to be a pair of scissors, and assault.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart, who leads policing in the area, said: “Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports. While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental health-related incident.

“A visible police presence will remain in the area while evidence is gathered at the scene and we thank the public for their understanding.”

A London ambulance service spokesperson said: “We sent an ambulance crew, a paramedic in a fast-response car and an incident response officer. We also dispatched London’s air ambulance. We treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road.”

One witness said the stabbing happened outside the Shaftesbury Theatre before the woman allegedly made her way down Endell Street, a popular location for eating and drinking in the area.

The witness, who wanted to remain anonymous, said: “We noticed she stabbed three people with scissors by the theatre then she came down here and the police were here.”

One of the victims ran into a barber shop and took his shirt off, revealing a large gash in his back, workers there said.

Arjan Gjorga, who works at the Rock and Sole Plaice restaurant and witnessed the attack, said a woman involved in the incident was known to people who worked on the street.

He said: “I see her all the time, she’s a homeless person. She walks up and down asking for help, she visits the church at the top of the street.”

Gjorga, who did not have to close his restaurant, said: “We all saw a commotion, people were running away. It was totally random, just random people. She suddenly started stabbing them. The police reacted immediately, they arrested her right away.”

Matt Bishop, 42, who works at a consultancy firm next to the cordon in Covent Garden, said he had seen a woman having a “standoff” with three police officers and waving a weapon around.

Andrea, the manager of Da Mario restaurant on the same street, said the attack happened in the middle of lunch service.

Gesturing at a pair of men enjoying cocktails on the shaded terrace, he said: “They saw it all but they weren’t fazed. They had a police cordon right over their heads but they kept on enjoying their lunch. It’s just another day in London.”

He also recognised the alleged perpetrator, saying: “She’s often on the street. We’ve seen her do things like this before, she’s recently got in an argument with a mate and thrown a bottle of vodka on the floor and it smashed outside the restaurant.”

By 3.30pm, the area was calm with the cordon down.

Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:15:10 GMT

The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them

Every now and then, a Senate race sets the direction for an entire party. In 1991, a state official named Harris Wofford – advised by a foul-mouthed Cajun named James Carville – upset his far better-known Republican opponent to win a special election in Pennsylvania. He did it by promising to expand access to healthcare – and thus created a template for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign the following year.

If Abdul El-Sayed can follow up his victory in last night’s Democratic Senate primary by winning the general election in Michigan this fall, he will have created a template of his own. Despite his closer-than-expected margin of victory, his campaign offers a model for how Democrats across the country can answer the political challenge posed by Donald Trump.

By casting the Michigan Senate primary as yet another battle between progressive insurgents and establishment centrists, media coverage of El-Sayed’s campaign has tended to overlook what is innovative about it. Like Zohran Mamdani and the democratic socialists who have won House races in New York, Pennsylvania and Colorado, El-Sayed wants to end unconditional US military support for Israel. But while Mamdani sometimes discusses Israel purely through the language of human rights and international law – as he did in his recent video arguing that Benjamin Netanyahu should be arrested as a war criminal – El-Sayed’s message is more nationalistic. He rarely discusses the Jewish state without linking it to Washington’s failure to address problems at home.

In a recent interview, the New Yorker editor, David Remnick, asked El-Sayed whether he supports one or two states in Israel-Palestine. El-Sayed did not take the bait. He replied that his focus was less on “what’s happening there rather than what’s happening here”. His primary concern, he explained, was that the US was allocating money for Israeli weapons that it could be spending on schools in Michigan. While acknowledging: “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike,” he said: “It is not my job as an American policymaker to decide what the ultimate peace should be. But it is my job to make sure that our resources are stewarded correctly for the people I’m responsible for: those kids going to those broken schools.”

In relentlessly linking US military aid to Israel to unmet needs in the United States, El-Sayed is crafting a progressive version of America First. In 2016, Donald Trump exploited the resentment many Americans felt after a decade and a half of failed wars in the Middle East. Now, in the wake of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, El-Sayed is turning the tables. The difference is that Trump fused nationalism and imperialism: he said that the Iraq war was a mistake because the US sought to “make western democracies out of countries that had no experience or interests in becoming a western democracy”; the US, he said, should have taken Iraq’s oil. El-Sayed, by contrast, is fusing nationalism with progressivism. He’s not attacking the humanitarian assistance once offered by USAID. He’s condemning military aid to Israel (and also to Egypt, where his father was born) because it both violates human rights overseas and denies resources to Americans at home. This isn’t a message that only resonates with the American left. Last summer, the late rightwing activist Charlie Kirk tweeted that young conservatives “are skeptical about the state of America’s current relationship” with Israel “and they want to be confident America’s leaders are putting their own country first”. A poll in May by the Institute for Middle East Understanding found that by a margin of almost two-to-one, Republicans under the age of 45 prefer candidates who support reducing taxpayer-funded weapons sales to the Jewish state.

But El-Sayed’s campaign offers Democrats another lesson as well. He isn’t only showing them how to reclaim nationalism from the GOP. He’s also showing them how to turn the Republican party’s financial advantage against it. In the last five weeks of El-Sayed’s primary campaign, outside Super Pacs supporting his opponent, representative Haley Stevens, spent more than 12 times as much on television ads as did those supporting him. Most candidates can’t overcome that kind of disparity. But El-Sayed made it a source of strength. Again and again, he used Stevens’s financial support from the pro-Israel lobbying group Aipac – which contributed the bulk of the outside money on her behalf – against her. He also linked her to other unpopular special interests. His supporters ran a television ad highlighting the contributions she had received from the Michigan utility, DTE Energy, which is widely disliked for charging high rates and allowing recurring power outages.

El-Sayed’s relentless focus on the source of Stevens’s donations turned her financial advantage into an electoral albatross. When the Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell asked a Michigan focus group why they didn’t like Stevens, “voters repeatedly brought up Aipac and the appearance of corporate influence.”

El-Sayed performed this political jujitsu against a fellow Democrat. But this fall, and probably again in 2028, Democrats across the country will be badly outspent by Republicans. Donald Trump has turned the federal government into a cash cow for corporations and billionaires who profit massively from his administration and return the favor by writing campaign checks. Elon Musk alone recently announced that he will spend at least $100m supporting Republican candidates this fall. Overall, reported MS Now late last month, the Republican National Committee, the Republican House and Senate campaign committees and GOP-aligned Super Pacs have raised almost $600m more than their Democratic counterparts.

El-Sayed’s campaign offers a template for how Democrats can respond: make the money the issue. El-Sayed drew a connection between Stevens’s backing from AIipac and her support for US military aid to Israel. But other Democrats can brand their Republican opponents as lackeys not just of Aipac, but of Elon Musk, big oil, big pharma or AI – and highlight the connection between their campaign funds and their support for policies that hurt ordinary people.

This strategy requires Democrats to eschew corporate and special interest funding and run campaigns that rely primarily on small donors. There’s no guarantee this will work. Not all Democrats can deliver a populist message as effectively as El-Sayed. But the staggering corruption of Trump’s presidency, and the obscene wealth gap that his policies have helped create, presents them with an opportunity. Which means that El-Sayed’s model could prove effective far beyond Michigan.

There are many reasons Democrats have struggled to defeat the Trump-era GOP. But among them are these: Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both. Democrats across the country should be taking notes.

Peter Beinart is a contributing opinion writer at the New York Times, editor at large at Jewish Currents, a professor at the Newmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York, and the author of The Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter. His most recent book is Being Jewish After the Destruction of Gaza

Kemi Badenoch gives former neo-Nazi advisory role after he withdraws as Tory candidate

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:06:50 GMT

Joshua Bonehill-Paine says Conservative leader asked him to work with party’s culture and integration commission

A former neo-Nazi activist who was convicted of harassing a Jewish MP has withdrawn as a Conservative election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offered him a role as an adviser to the party.

Joshua Bonehill-Paine said on Wednesday that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections, and that the Conservative leader had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, where he will specifically focus on how young men become radicalised.

Badenoch, who has come under pressure in the last 48 hours from individuals and organisations including the Board of Deputies of British Jews, said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”.

However, the handing of a plum job to him was immediately condemned by others including Luciana Berger, a Labour member of the House of Lords who was the target of a campaign of abuse by Bonehill-Paine when she was an MP.

“The decision to welcome this individual as an adviser to the Leader of the Opposition is no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate,” she said on X. “It is a privileged and influential national role. As a victim of this man’s heinous crimes this appointment is an insult.”

Both the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) had turned down the Tory party’s offer of a meeting with the former neo-Nazi, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account.

The JLC issued a short statement on Wednesday to welcome Bonehill-Paine’s withdrawal as a Conservative candidate, but did not address his appointment as an adviser.

However, the president of the Board of Deputies, Phil Rosenberg, told Times Radio it was “a good thing” that Bonehill-Paine would become an adviser to the culture and integration commission.

“I think it is good to use the experiences of people who have themselves been down this track to counter radicalisation in other places,” said Rosenberg, who added that Bonehill-Pain was “probably the wrong fit” to be a councillor.

Polling that was released by YouGov after news emerged that Bonehill-Paine was withdrawing found 57% of British voters thought his selection was unacceptable.

Reform voters were the most likely to think he was an acceptable choice, at 36% – although they were outnumbered by the 44% of their number who deemed the decision unacceptable.

Among Tory voters, 28% thought the selection was acceptable but twice that number judged it to be unacceptable (57%).

​The Home Office also issued a statement on Wednesday contradicting a claim by Badenoch on Monday that Bonehill-Paine, 33, was “certified by the Home Office” to train police officers on antisemitism and countering extremism.

“The Home Office does not certify individuals to deliver training,” said a spokesperson, who added that the department funds Civil Society Organisations which may use individuals to deliver training. Bonehill-Paine is understood to have worked for a time with an organisation engaging former extremists on a path to rehabilitation.

Bridget ​P​hillipson, ​the equalities minister and chair of the Labour party,​ said the affair “speaks volumes” about Badenoch’s judgment. “It beggars belief that Kemi Badenoch was happy for a former neo-Nazi to stand in the first place. That she has gifted him a plum job further adds to that shame​,” she added.

Badenoch’s move was also attacked by Reform UK, with a spokesperson saying the Jewish community would be alarmed that Bonehill-Paine would have a say over national Conservative party policy.

Badenoch shared Bonehill-Paine’s announcement on X that he was withdrawing as a Tory candidate in next year’s elections, adding in her comments that he had been the target of a “piling on”.

“If we are going to stop extremism and antisemitism, we are going to need help from those people who were part of the problem, but have now changed and are being part of the solution,” she said.

Bonehill-Paine had been selected to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district, but said in a post on X on Wednesday: “Rather than standing as a local council candidate, I believe that my experience is better used supporting Kemi Badenoch in her ongoing mission to combat the antisemitism and extremism that is dividing our nation.”

He was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting “vile” antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally.

In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, who is Jewish, which included posting messages to his blog calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”.

Berger had intervened earlier this week, telling Badenoch directly: “For the avoidance of doubt, I don’t believe this man should have *any* role in public life – because of both his racism and his view of women.”

One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcom

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 16:00:22 GMT

‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceit

Going into a romcom, there are always the same questions. Will there be genuine chemistry? Will the rom and the com be equal in parts? And, for the last decade and change, will this be the one that finally resurrects a genre long past its prime? But for Universal’s glossy late summer offering One Night Only, notably the first wide-releasing romcom since April, there are more probing questions than usual. The film is the ungainly result of a four-cocktails-in elevator pitch which imagines a world where single people are only legally allowed to have sex on one night of the year, an idea that has seen it been referred to as “Sex Purge”.

On paper, it’s the set-up for a grim Handmaid’s Tale-adjacent horror of a totalitarian state insisting extreme control over the body, but instead it’s used as the backdrop for a sunny meet-cute, screams of protest drowned out by a zippy Top 40 soundtrack. One sits down wondering not just if boy will end up with girl but also how the government would be able to enforce such tyranny and what horrifying punishments lay in store for those willing to pick personal freedom over state-mandated abstinence. If it sounds like far too much for a breezy summer romp to take on, then that’s because it most definitely is, an overstuffed yet undercooked soufflé that can’t quite, ahem, rise to the occasion …

Introductory text informs us, much to the baffled laughter of those at my screening, that “premarital sex has been outlawed in the US” and is now only legal for 12 hours on one night of the year. It’s a “government decreed sexual climate” where it’s now a “badge of honour” to be an incel, the result of what’s described as an “ideological grenade” thrown at Americans by Congress. People have been fitted with biosensors, which detect the chemicals released during sex, and they turn from red to green when one gets married or the sex purge begins, a night of debauchery and chaos as everyone desperately tries to find someone to couple up with (wouldn’t the other 364 days a year be used to plan this a little better?). Protection is mandatory (condom surge pricing goes all the way up to $2,000 apiece) and we’re briefly shown that the price to pay for breaking the law is severe (a poor older man is dragged into a police station for the crime of being horny).

New York City is where we spend that time, the natural setting for a film about both singledom and sex, and we follow the routes of Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (recent Oscar nominee Monica Barbaro) as they hunt for sex against a ticking clock. Owen had a plan with his girlfriend (Maya Hawke) but she chooses the night as an opportunity to hook up with a neighbour, while Allie is urged by her queer roommate, who calls it a night “for the straights”, to put on a revealing dress and get herself out there. Their paths intertwine and for reasons that never quite make sense, decide not to have sex with each other, and instead play wingman from Manhattan to Brooklyn and back again.

After the unforgivably unreal use of Glasgow as a junky replacement for New York in last week’s Spider-Man sequel (it often looked like it was set in a Broadway musical), one of the film’s biggest aces is its up-close and immersive on-location shooting. Director Will Gluck is a savvy commercial film-maker and there’s a bright and poppy slickness to how his film looks and moves, especially when compared with Netflix’s many murkily flat romcoms. But as with his last film, the surprise smash Anyone But You, he’s mastered the sleek aesthetic of a 2000s throwback but not much else. His leads here are a merciful improvement (Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell were among the most criminally vacant pairings we’ve ever seen in the genre), but again there’s not enough smart or specific writing, from kids’ TV writer Travis Braun, to justify why they wouldn’t just head to bed on first meet (yes, he’s vomited up two omakases near her feet but also, it’s sex purge night, guys!).

It’s less romcom and more an attempt to be a raunchy (if ultimately rather coy) sex caper as we go from scrape to scrape, involving ineffective and unfunny cameos (Julia Fox! Pete Davidson! Molly Ringwald! Nicholas Braun! Roma Maffia!) and a string of almost-shags. There’s a gimmicky, ADHD quality to the film and its many misfiring pop culture references, as if made to insist a gen Z audience away from their phones, and while I appreciated how this applied detail to the grabby production design (most scenes involve some sort of visual clue as to how the law has affected the day-to-day), it also felt like a distraction, a script made up of moments rather than a fully realised story. There’s no thought-through journey for our characters (he needs to plan less and she needs to sing more or something?) and while the attractively paired Turner and Barbaro are just about sturdy enough to convince us of the motions, their ho-hum banter is mostly too perfunctory to provoke us into caring about how they end up.

It might not surprise you where the story takes them but what did surprise me is how progressively sex-negative the film becomes, either ridiculing those who want it or applying a moral superiority to those who don’t.

There’s both too much yet not enough world-building here, enough questions answered to encourage us to ask 10 more (why does no one mention masturbation and wouldn’t that also trigger the biosensors?). It’s also just too unavoidably grim of a premise, especially at a dark political moment such as this, for us to ignore the ramifications or root for characters who aren’t trying to actively destroy such a barbaric system (what if Katniss just had fun during those Hunger Games?). Instead, One Night Only weirdly plays like lulling government propaganda, a film about sex purge to be released in time for sex purge that says that actually maybe sex purge is a good idea after all.

One Night Only is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and the UK on 7 August

Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 15:30:25 GMT

If the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary tale

US politics live – latest updates

In the final stretch of the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged voters at a small event in rural Michigan to think about the message they could send the rest of the country when they cast their ballots.

“Who are we? Who do we want to be?” El-Sayed said. “Do we want a state that’s defined by how much money corporations brought in to tell us what we couldn’t have? Or do we want to be a state where we demonstrate to the rest of the country what’s possible when you build a movement of, by and for the people?”

On Tuesday, El-Sayed’s vision cleared its first hurdle: he won the primary over moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by the party’s establishment, and tens of millions of dollars in outside spending.

His rise, and victory, could serve as a revision to how the political establishment views swing-state politics – not requiring candidates to run from the center, but articulating how you will materially improve people’s lives as the working and middle classes struggle with affordability and rising healthcare costs.

A contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits.

El-Sayed led by 48.5% to 47.5% over Stevens when the race was called. The narrow margin, in addition to more than 60,000 votes for a candidate who dropped out altogether, suggest he will have to unite the party, and convince more independent and even right-leaning voters in a swing state, to beat Republican Mike Rogers.

But the race solidified a growing anti-establishment sentiment on the party’s left, where activists and supporters have sought a proactive vision that doesn’t rely on the pre-Trump status quo, apparent in a string of wins for insurgent candidates. There’s a sense that systems were already broken before Trump’s rise, and a return to those norms won’t serve everyday Americans. They’re looking for politicians who can call out their own party’s orthodoxies, and challenge the big money that haunts US politics.

Michigan voters found it in El-Sayed, who centered his campaign around universal healthcare, and wasn’t shy about calling the war in Gaza a genocide.

“It doesn’t limit us to just what we think is possible, but it changes what we think is possible,” said David Sernick, a voter in Detroit who supported El-Sayed.

El-Sayed first ran for office in 2018, losing to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor of Michigan, in a Democratic primary. This time, he built a grassroots machine, barnstorming the state with in-person rallies while delivering clippable moments for social media feeds. His campaign knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made more than 1m phone calls, aided by leftwing groups such as the Working Families party and Indivisible chapters. El-Sayed held more than 500 campaign events and visited 150 churches.

People like Racquel Garcia, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, Michigan, said his willingness to show up underpinned their vote. El-Sayed worked as a public health official in Detroit and in Wayne county, and would show up at permit hearings and represent the people, she said.

“Every time we meet with the city of Detroit officials, we’re like, ‘we need you to be like him’,” said Garcia. “You’re here to protect us, not to protect industry. So we’ve been wanting him in office. We were happy that he’s real.”

Andy Levin, a former congressman from Michigan who lost to Stevens in 2022 after their districts were redrawn, said the moment rejected a “static notion of electability” that stems from a politics of anxiety and fear.

“They want authenticity, they want truth telling and they want brave policy, not just proposals but action, so they can breathe in their lives,” Levin told Democracy Now. “This is a movement of Americans who are saying, enough of politics as usual.”

Roy Harris, who voted in Detroit on Tuesday but wouldn’t say for whom, detailed how it was time for a change. “First-time homebuyers can’t buy a house – $400,000, first time you going out, nobody can afford that,” he said. “I’m tired of paying $4 for gas, and I am looking for a change. And I hope the new regime coming in brings that to us.”

In Washington, El-Sayed’s effort to win the US Senate race in Michigan is critical for Democrats’ ambitious hopes of retaking control of the upper chamber, and will be closely watched by all factions of the left as a bellwether for the party’s future.

Michigan voted for Trump, then Biden, and then Trump, in presidential elections. It is firmly a swing state. If El-Sayed, an unabashed progressive who frequently notes he has a “funny name”, can win a statewide general election, it could remake the contours of the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment and pundit class will call him, and his ideas, too extreme – a cautionary tale for play-it-safe politics.

In other parts of the country, moderates won their Democratic primaries, including blue-dog Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez in a purple district in Washington state, who staved off a progressive challenge, and Wesley Bell, who saw off a challenge from Cori Bush, a former representative.

Chris Rabb, a progressive who won a contested primary for a US congressional seat in Pennsylvania, recently noted the high bar people from his branch of the party face as they seek to challenge moderates.

“Nobody asks ‘centrist’ Dems to explain their losses,” Rabb wrote on X. “They lose purple districts every cycle & Beltway pundits call it ‘a tough map’. Progressives lose one major race & Dem operatives call us electoral pariahs. It’s a specious double standard.”

Meanwhile, the attack lines from the right have already been drawn. Rogers posted an AI-generated video of El-Sayed, depicting him as Odysseus among other prominent Democrats inside a Trojan horse, and saying “don’t let communism into Michigan”.

A Republican has not won a US Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. The Republican National Committee called El-Sayed “Michigan’s Mamdani” and said the race “pits common sense against crazy”.

El-Sayed himself remains confident.

In November, he is counting on turning out people who normally turn off from politics because they’re cynical, or believe the system cannot change in a way that would make their lives better.

“The goal now is not to dunk on anybody, the goal now is to come together so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.
