Why Spain’s EU allies turned on Pedro Sanchez over Ceuta: the hard right now sets their agenda on migration

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 14:30:21 GMT

Rightwing narratives have gone mainstream, and Madrid finds itself increasingly isolated for its humane approach to migrants

Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It was over almost as quickly as it began. But the human cost of the mayhem in Ceuta over the last seven days, and the disunity it exposed within the EU, will take a lot longer to fix.

To recap: more than 70,000 people swam or waded into the tiny Spanish enclave in north Africa from neighbouring Morocco in a matter of hours at the end of last week. The exact circumstances in which the heavily securitised border came suddenly to be open are still unclear.

What is clear is that at least 88 people died. Some drowned, others were trampled in the crush. Social media hyped a distorted version of events. Far-right parties, already driving the agenda on migration across Europe, weaponised the story. And Spain’s EU allies engaged in a war of words – not over the plight of those caught up in the tragedy, but over who let them into EU territory.

Italy and Denmark jointly led the way there, accusing Madrid of failing to secure the EU’s only land border with Africa. Although Ceuta is not even in the EU’s Schengen passport-free travel area, Giorgia Meloni, the far-right Italian prime minister, performatively suspended Schengen rights for travellers entering Italy from Spain.

Meloni and her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen (although a Social Democrat, is another migration hardliner), wrote to the EU demanding emergency talks on tightening the bloc’s external borders. They enlisted the backing of all but five of the 27 EU leaders.

Faced with such an unusual lack of support, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez could only protest about the “selfish, polarising and unlawful” response of his EU allies.

By Monday the vast majority who arrived in Ceuta had gone back to Morocco. None attempted to reach the Spanish mainland or to abscond towards any other country’s borders. Of those left stranded on the streets of the city, many were unaccompanied children.

By then, Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Israeli ministers had weighed in to decry Europe’s “migrant invasion”, and Ceuta had begun to function, wrote Jonathan Liew, “as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies”. The spectacle of left-liberal Spain facing a migration crisis of its own making was, for the European hard right and the White House “almost too good to be true”, Ruben Andersson wrote.

But why the frenzy among European governments? Paul Taylor, a senior fellow with the European Policy Centre, says there was a shamelessly cynical interest for some EU leaders to pile on and isolate Madrid. The reaction was very different in the past, when Poland and Lithuania faced migrant incursions weaponised by Belarus.

“Most EU governments are conservative or rightwing-led and have an interest in scapegoating Spain, which is governed by a socialist-leftist coalition, and in helping Spain’s rightwing opposition ahead of a general election due next year, and in trying to win back voters in their own countries who are defecting to rightwing populists,” Taylor said.

Within the EU, Sanchez has swum against the tide, standing up to the Trump administration over Gaza, the war in Iran and Nato defence spending. During the recent wildfires he was vocal about climate backsliding. In an EU where policy has been hardening since 2015, he bucks the trend on migration, too.

“Spain has been an outlier, welcoming migration and actively working to integrate migrants into the economy and society,” Taylor said. “This is seen as an affront by many conservative politicians but also as a ‘pull factor’ encouraging would-be migrants to try their luck in Europe at a time when official EU policy is to combat irregular migration, crack down on abuses of the asylum system and park asylum seekers offshore in countries outside the bloc.”

And this is exactly the bigger political bone Meloni, Frederiksen and others wanted to pick with Spain. In their letter to the EU, ostensibly about the immediate crisis in Ceuta, they targeted Madrid’s recent policy of allowing undocumented people working in mainland Spain to regularise their migration status, even though this was irrelevant for those involved in the Ceuta situation.

What is most striking about this, Taylor said, is the hypocrisy and double standards of Spain’s critics.

“Many of those criticising Spain’s amnesty allowing irregular migrants to apply for residence permits have introduced similar schemes in their own countries. Italy and Germany have both given work permits and/or the right to remain to irregular migrants already working there in programmes supported by employers plagued by labour shortages.”

Why Ceuta? Why now?

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

What actually provoked the Ceuta surge remains unexplained.

One theory is that misleading posts circulated on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook following a 29 June Spanish supreme court ruling that clarified that under international law, the state cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process.

But many suspect geopolitical mischief by Morocco – possibly to extract payback for Spain’s recent detente with its regional rival Algeria. If this is the case then the EU’s controversial strategy of outsourcing migration to regimes such as Morocco’s, looks even more problematic. Ashifa Kassam recalled in this Guardian podcast how Morocco weaponised migrants in a previous incident in 2021, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta during a diplomatic standoff with Spain over Western Sahara.

By Tuesday, EU justice and home affairs ministers were publicly papering over their split, although Brussels criticised Spain’s amnesty for undocumented migrants as “not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.

Ministers endorsed a plan to strengthen Europe’s external borders, including an early warning system and better “cooperation” with non-EU countries on migration: possibly code for more “cash for migration” deals with often unsavoury regimes.

The Ceuta episode could also lead to the acceleration of ICE-style deportations from the EU. The Italian government in particular wants to see offshore migration centres, or “return hubs”, made possible under the EU’s new return regulation.

Yet in a Europe devoid of safe and legal routes for asylum seekers, this is a direction that some of the most senior European legal experts have warned could create a “human rights black hole”.

When the European parliament voted to approve the return regulation last month, there was some dismay as far-right and rightwing MEPs celebrated in the chamber with raucous chants of “send them back!” On the evidence of the last week, it seems that Europe’s mainstream leaders have normalised the same chilling sentiment.

Alarming surge in bluetongue disease reported among UK sheep

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 14:00:20 GMT

Farmers advised to vaccinate after recent hot weather provides ideal conditions for virus-carrying midges

There has been an alarming surge in the number of sheep affected by an outbreak of bluetongue in the UK, and farmers whose livestock are at risk are being urged to move them out of areas where midges are plentiful.

The viral disease, which does not necessarily kill sheep but makes them ill and can have a long recovery time, presents as high fever and swelling of the lips and tongue. The tongue may go blue and even protrude from the mouth.

More than 590 cases were reported last week, according to the National Sheep Association (NSA).

The virus is transmitted via biting midges (culicoides) and its arrival in the UK is associated with global heating. The World Organisation for Animal Health reported in 2024 that although the virus had historically “been endemic in the tropics and subtropics where temperature and humidity are ideal for biting midge survival … it began to migrate to the Mediterranean basin and southern Europe in the late 1990s” and was first recorded in the UK in 2006.

The National Farmers’ Union vice-president, Robyn Munt, said: “Bluetongue is continuing to spread at an alarming rate and is a significant concern for livestock farmers across the country. The disease is creating additional uncertainty and financial pressures for many businesses, with members doing everything possible to protect their animals.

“To reduce the risk, farmers are moving high-risk or non-vaccinated stock away from wet, low-lying or sheltered areas and keeping vulnerable animals housed during dawn and dusk when midge activity peaks, all of which is added pressure on farmers and forage stocks during this challenging weather period.”

Dominic Elson, who farms sheep in Devon, said he lost one of his flock on Wednesday: “I was saying goodbye to a lovely old ewe that has been on the farm for over 10 years and it’s heartbreaking to see the bluetongue virus take her down.”

He said he had been frustrated by what he regards as the lack of preparedness of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), and the failure of the self-reporting system. Farmers are required to report the disease but he said the phone line appeared to be overwhelmed and it was difficult to get through.

This might mean the numbers were being significantly underestimated, he said, pointing out that although the disease was not always fatal, an outbreak in the Netherlands led to the deaths of more than 4% of the national herd between September and December 2023.

“With the closure of the basic payments system and the reduction in budget available for agri-environment schemes, upland sheep farmers are already teetering on the brink,” Elson said. “This outbreak could push some over the edge.”

The NSA’s chief executive, Phil Stocker, said: “The number of reported cases shot up last week to over 590, from just 115 the previous week. The majority are being seen in the south-west of England – clearly a serious hotspot for this midge-borne virus. As you would expect, calls on stocks of vaccines are increasing and stocks will be reducing but we are assured that vaccine manufacturers are doing what they can to ensure demand can be met.”

He said there seemed to be some confusion over whether to vaccinate, given that full immunity took 28 days. He said: “A level of protection is likely to be reached earlier, particularly if stock were vaccinated last season. Additionally, we have several months of midge activity ahead of us and it is highly advisable that breeding males and females are vaccinated ahead of mating.”

A National Audit Office report last year said the UK may be underprepared for a serious animal disease outbreak. Stocker told Farmer’s Weekly that surveillance had successfully identified infected premises but testing only three animals on affected holdings meant the true scale of infection was unknown.

A spokesperson for Defra said: “We recognise this is an incredibly difficult time for animal keepers who are on the frontline of this disease, and we are monitoring the situation closely. We continue to work closely with industry representatives to ensure that keepers are kept up to date with developments and that issues and concerns are addressed promptly.”

An Animal and Plant Health Agency spokesperson said the virus was circulating in England, particularly the south-west, and parts of Wales. They said the recent hot and humid weather had been favourable for midge populations, which had probably contributed to the increased numbers of cases.

“Livestock keepers should remain vigilant and report any suspicions of disease to APHA,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage all farmers and keepers to discuss vaccination with their vet as this is the most effective way of protecting their animals.”

Why waste your time on social media when you could be flicking through picture books?

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 14:00:20 GMT

From histories of opera to compendiums of mosses, they’re beautiful, expertly written and don’t leave you feeling grubby. What’s not to like?

There are lots of reasons not to read picture books. You can’t really mark them “done” in the same way you might, say, tick A Tale of Two Cities off your bucket list, or add them to your tally when you’re humble-bragging about what you’ve read over the past 12 months. They aren’t going to become part of the cultural zeitgeist, like Middlemarch or The Odyssey, and you probably won’t be able to persuade a book group to talk about them.

Recently, though, I’ve been getting back into them in a big way, poking around the “oversized” shelves of my local charity shops, cooing over large-format collections of Hokusai prints in Waterstones.

When I say “picture books”, by the way, I mean that in the broadest possible sense: books with lots of pictures in them. I’ve got a history of opera that I’m sure is intended for children, as well as a natural history guide that features page after page of taxonomic descriptions of moss.

Picture books are a great leveller: anyone can jump into them, anywhere they like, with no need to trudge through the boring early bits to get to the juicy stuff. For some topics, they’re a requirement – maps, art and cross-sections are the obvious examples – but they make almost anything more memorable. A few years ago, I interviewed a University Challenge champion who swore by them as a way of getting an entry-level overview of nearly any subject. It’s quite rare that I pick one up without feeling as if I’ve improved my knowledge of the world.

What I really like about picture books, though, is that they contain so many of the appealing features of social media and so few of the bad ones. They’re created to invite the eye, often with lots of what magazine designers call “entry points”. Perhaps you’d like to learn more about this Parasaurolophus skull? Maybe the Bayeux tapestry is more your speed? They’re written by experts and rigorously factchecked, usually without too much of the explicit political posturing that makes online life so draining.

Best of all, you can deep-dive into one topic, or flit across dozens in mere moments, occasionally stopping to read an entire thread (sorry, page) when something catches your interest. Hormones, horses, Hinduism, the hundred years war: who doesn’t feel as if they could know more about these things?

In the 21st century, it’s easy to believe that nobody needs reference books any more. All the answers, after all, are online, either on Wikipedia or ruthlessly scraped from real books by rapacious AI models. It’s just as easy to burrow down a rabbit hole on the internet as it is with the Dorling Kindersley Family Encyclopedia on your lap, except that the former goes on for ever.

Sign up to Bookmarks

Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you

after newsletter promotion

The big problem is that there’s no sense of proportion on the internet: it’s more enticing to read about rollercoaster disasters than Renaissance painters – and there’s more scurrilous detail available. It’s also far too easy to click straight over to Facebook, or Bluesky, or BuzzFeed, and emerge half an hour later knowing nothing more about the Sistine chapel.

Picture books, by contrast, are one of the most soothing ways to fill spare time. They fit perfectly with a definition of “proper” reading that I’ve borrowed from the author Naomi Alderman: the sort you wish you were doing more of, rather than the sort that makes you feel grubby afterwards. If you sit on the sofa with a picture book, preferably with your phone out of reach, you tend to emerge with a new sense of wonder about the world and our capacity to explore it and understand it.

You can often pick them up cheaply, or borrow them by the half-dozen from your local library. (If you put them in a rucksack, this doubles as your workout for the day.) Even if you could live the rest of your life without needing to understand the difference between mountain fork-moss and ostrich-plume feather-moss, wouldn’t it be richer if you did?

Joel Snape is a freelance writer

In Britain, we equate blackness with the working class. It’s time for a rethink

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 13:09:46 GMT

In my new book, I narrate the existence, behaviours and sensibilities of the black British middle class, a social group largely ignored, until now

Don’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up here

While narrating the audio version of my new book, The Good, the Black and the Boujee, came a revelatory reminder of why many black Britons see middle class status as a “white people ting”. After a recording session, I headed upstairs to see if I could find any friendly faces from my publisher before heading out into the sweltering heatwave for my cycle home. To my disappointment, I found a near-empty office floor, and left minutes later. Donning my helmet, I joined the middle class commuters who regularly left the office in cycling gear.

As I approached the exit, something peculiar happened: I was met with a friendly expression of relief from the reception staff. The building had received a concerned report about a potential intruder on the top floor, they told me. The intruder was believed to be a rogue courier who had somehow passed the loading bay and made it into the editorial offices. It took me a moment to realise – the intruding courier was … me.

Although I was amused rather than offended, the misunderstanding joined a chorus of similar anecdotes. In 2020, Edward Enninful, the first black editor-in-chief of Vogue, revealed that he had also been mistaken for a courier at the publication by security. In court, black barristers say they are assumed to be defendants. Black politicians say they are assumed to be support staff in the Houses of Parliament. While these are mundane and momentary examples of social profiling, they reveal a more interesting truth. A black professional class has significantly expanded, but the meaning of blackness in Britain is unchanged in the public imagination.

Wielding significant influence

In Britain, to be black is to be assumed to be working class. This means that class differences between the black working class and the emergent black bourgeoisie are made invisible. Black British people who have gained the closest proximity to power are predominantly those who were either born middle class, or quickly initiated into it. Yet, although this social group has the power to wield significant cultural and political influence, they are a relatively young social group of barely 50 years old. As a result, their sensibility and behaviour has largely been ignored until now.

Facing a data desert on this salaried group, I decided to undertake a wide ranging study of 1,460 black professionals. I gathered insights into their wealth, education and political decisions. My research revealed three groups that make up the black British middle class: a precarious “emerging black middle class” from the ends; a “traditional black middle class”, who were often racial minorities in their social lives; and a “black elite”, including influential families like the Casely-Hayfords, but also those self made, such as Stormzy or the business executive Dean Forbes.

Whose black lives mattered?

I began the odyssey of writing this book at a pivotal moment for the black middle class – the aftermath of 2020, when the Black Lives Matter movement moved from the margins to the mainstream. Many black people were beginning to demand a seat at the table. I saw a protest placard quoting the lyrics of Jay-Z, exalting the rise of black excellence. When donations poured into the coffers of BLMUK by white supporters guilted into penance, its leftist leadership faced criticism for diverting some donations to grassroots campaigns. Some demanded that the funding should have gone to black businesses. I found the criticism was perverse, but revelatory.

After George Floyd’s death, black elites began to speak out in greater voice. Enninful’s story of profiling, for example, was made in a moment of public reckoning, when stories of racism were suddenly more en vogue than anything that had graced his magazine covers. This elite also temporarily grew during this BLM boom due to a concentrated attempt to expand black representation in the upper echelons. There were successes: from the first black British photographer to shoot British Vogue’s front cover, to high profile appointments of privately educated black figures to the boards of major institutions like the Southbank Centre and National Portrait Gallery. The black middle class appear the biggest beneficiary of the BLM movement, although their success has been cyclical.

Today, the black presence in these professions is facing an onslaught of political and legal challenges. A campaign to give internships to black students is being aggressively challenged, and the rightwing press currently runs pieces criticising the senior black appointments of major institutions that they believe have been “DEI hires”.

I am convinced that a material opportunity for wider racial justice was hijacked by Britain’s aspirational elites who sought to consolidate their class positions. During the 2020 protests internet personalities with little historical knowledge were propelled as voices of black Britain, but had no grasp of the scholarship or activism detailing how we got here. Meanwhile, the demands of the UK BLM movement were diffuse, but many crystallised around the call for more representation in media or on boards and higher pay for black influencers over issues like racial bias in housing that affect the black people disproportionately in poverty. The irony was the racial justice protests took place during the UK’s most diverse government in history, damaging faith in electoral politics to deliver for black voters.

A precarious class position

In black Britain a pervasive, underlying status anxiety has grown within the emergent middle class. A class position that once promised security, is now precarious. In 2001, about 70% of all black people in Britain lived in London; 25 years later, that figure is under 50%, despite the majority of professionals I surveyed saying they’d like to live in the city if they could afford to. Today, a generation of black professionals approaching middle age have acquired multiple degrees, earn a middle income or above and cultivate elite tastes, yet are unlikely to ever afford a house in their home borough.

Middle class status anxieties even express themselves in the sphere of lifestyle and dating. When black content creators’ viral complaints are not focused on elite representation, they are often focused on social mobility through dating. Among the under-40s, there are endless discussions on the absence of suitable black men in the dating pool, reflecting the fact that black women’s social mobility has outpaced their male counterparts. Other online debates include hand-wringing over which types of black people get represented through media opportunities like book deals. Asinine questions like “are mixed-race people black” place a similar superficial emphasis on aesthetics, rather than material conditions.

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

What’s the future of the black and boujee?

You’d be forgiven for wanting to escape this all. Only one in three of the black professionals I surveyed wanted to remain in the UK, and this was before the rise of Reform, the latest incarnation of the nations’ anti-migrant movement. Desired destinations included Canada and Dubai. And, of course, the U. S. Despite its political turmoil, America boasts better salaries, stronger social infrastructure through black university networks, and an even more visible black elite. Just ask the new British Black Panther, David Jonsson.

Black Britain itself is at an interesting crossroads, and it is hard to say which future path it will take. One road is further assimilation into white Britain, with high rates of interracial marriage between Caribbean and white families over a few short generations. I can imagine a future of mas bands at Notting Hill carnival made up of fair-skinned masqueraders with very distant Caribbean heritage, or school classrooms filled with blonde, blue-eyed children answering to Yoruba, Igbo or Ga names.

Another is more global. We are increasingly connected to the transnational black diaspora identity joined by the internet. Migration and marriages across the black Atlantic might create a future marked by fluidity and cross-border movement, where Britain is a place of convergence and memory. Although black Britons have become middle class just as the entire middle is being squeezed, at no point in history has there been a black presence in Europe with greater social, cultural and economic power. The question is what will they build with it? The answer belongs to the good, the black and the boujee.

Are you Black and boujee? Is middle class aspiration an abandonment of the Black struggle, or is it possible to do both? Tell us your thoughts by emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian. com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Stephen Libby on fashion: so many men have asked me for clothes advice since The Traitors

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 13:00:19 GMT

Our guest columnist reveals how he found his personal style, from jumpsuits to high-waisted trousers

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Other than the jumpsuits, I don’t think I wore anything particularly groundbreaking when I appeared on The Traitors. I just think the bar for men’s fashion is so low that for me to come on television in a chunky mint green jumper and a pair of high-waisted jeans – which is probably one of the most neutral looks I own – seemed like a revelation. There was no styling budget, so most of what I wore came from my wardrobe.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The discovery of my personal style began when I was at primary school on the Isle of Lewis, off the north-west coast of Scotland. I realised I was different to the other boys when I began experimenting with fashion. From a young age I was turning my hems up, and I was certainly more interested in what the girls in my class were wearing.

I would go so far as to say that my sexuality started to manifest in my choice of clothes. I have vivid memories of travelling to the mainland to go shopping – three hours on the ferry and then a 90-minute bus ride to Inverness. My biannual visit to Topman felt like a religious experience.

One of the first things I remember buying was a grey and black striped cardigan. It was just a simple cardigan, but when I wore it to school I got ripped to shreds. Boys did not wear cardigans then. I remember feeling disheartened that this thing that I loved so much – fashion – was bringing me so much distress.

By the time I was 16 or 17, it was becoming almost impossible to hide who I was. On another trip to the mainland I bought my first pair of skinny jeans, which were very fashion forward for the Isle of Lewis in the 00s. I never showed my skinnies to my parents. When I was going out with my friends in the evening, I would put them in a bag and change into them after leaving the house. I wish I had been able to see then that I was merely doing something that a lot of my straight male counterparts would be doing years later.

I went to the University of Glasgow when I was 18. Being in a city where everyone had access to all the same clothes meant I was no longer unique. That’s when I found vintage. (I was also a typical student with no money, and secondhand places were cheaper.) Everything on the high street was so flat, brown, beige, white, and I started seeing all these vintage Hawaiian shirts and incredible high-waist trousers. To me, the 60s, 70s and 80s were such a celebration of print and colour and drama. I can still remember loving this one pale blue 70s suit, but it was £50 – way out of my budget. Fifteen years on, I still wish I had bought it.

Once I figured out my look, I never looked back. It’s quite distinct, and I love that I can go to a party and never have to worry about someone wearing the same thing as me. I love vintage shirts with dagger collars or billowy sleeves, and vintage trousers that have a nice flare on them to add some drama. People called me Simon Cowell when I started wearing high waists, but I just think this is how I’m supposed to look.

The most stressful part of preparing to go on The Traitors had nothing to do with whether I would be a traitor or a faithful, or how far I’d get. It was: what the hell do I wear? I think people can ascertain so much about who you are through what you wear, it’s all snap judgments.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

after newsletter promotion

Having said that, it was never my goal to inspire an army of wide-legged trouser-wearing men; it was just to appear as the truest representation of myself. But since the show aired, I have had so many men message me on social media asking for clothes advice, and I’m going to use my next three columns to share my tips. So stay tuned for more, from tailoring to wedding dressing to – you guessed it – jumpsuits.

What kind of society fast-tracks early release for domestic abusers? This is gambling with women’s lives

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 12:14:43 GMT

Andy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violence

It’s time to be blunt: the government is about to expose hundreds of vulnerable women to the risk of death or serious injury. Survivors of domestic abuse, including women who have suffered years of physical violence and intimidation, are now preparing for the moment in October when 5,000 prisoners begin to be released early. What are these women supposed to do? Where are they supposed to go? Their abusers know where they live. They know where their children go to school.

Following an outcry, rapists and some child sex offenders have been excluded from the early release scheme. But by refusing to exclude men convicted of domestic violence, this government is sending a message that this category of crime – serial in nature and implicated in the deaths of one woman every five days – is simply not a priority.

In 2023, Keir Starmer promised to cut violence against women by half in a decade. It was an eye-catching pledge, although not obviously assisted by his proposal, when he became prime minister, to allow thousands of convicted criminals back on to the streets. No one denies that Andy Burnham has inherited an overcrowding crisis in UK prisons, but his solution – in effect, accepting the previous government’s plan with a few changes – involves taking a huge gamble with women’s lives.

For eight years, I was co-chair of the mayor of London’s Violence Against Women and Girls Board. I saw the devastating extent of intimate partner abuse and the chronic shortage of resources to support victims. I studied domestic homicide reviews with a shudder, seeing how one opportunity after another to save women’s lives had been missed. Now, in the midst of a justified furore, Burnham and his justice minister, Alex Norris, can’t claim they haven’t been warned.

The domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, says the decision not to exclude domestic abuse perpetrators from this scheme “puts victims’ lives at risk”, adding: “These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.” Intimate partner violence has special characteristics, including the fact that men seething with resentment towards former wives and girlfriends are all too likely to reoffend.

The data is limited – reoffending rates among men convicted of domestic abuse are not listed separately but hidden among other offences, including violence against the person, criminal damage and arson. Recent incidents of public disorder have confirmed that men who abuse partners have a wider propensity for violence; most people arrested for violent protests after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer had previously been reported to the police for domestic abuse, for instance. In my book Home Grown: How Domestic Violence Turns Men Into Terrorists, I pointed out that many men who commit public acts of extreme violence have histories of first abusing their families.

What we do know is that the proportion of released prisoners who go on to commit further offences is alarmingly high. Reoffending rates vary from about 29% if you include those with non-custodial sentences, to a “proven reoffending rate” of 43.8% for adults released from custody between January and March 2024, suggesting rehabilitation in prison is largely ineffective. The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, has said “effective risk management, meaningful licence conditions, proper supervision and timely, trauma-informed communication and support remain critical” if the early release scheme goes ahead in its present form. That’s asking an awful lot of an overstretched probation service that can barely cope with its existing workload.

Last month the National Audit Office revealed that almost 9,000 people required to wear an electronic tag did not have one (the government disputes the figure, arguing the number is closer to 5,450). The report also delivered a damning verdict on how prisoners released on licence are monitored, concluding that “police and probation officers often lack relevant information or capacity to respond quickly to breaches”. Nearly half of alerts and breach notifications result in “no further action”.

This chaotic system is what ministers are relying on when they promise survivors of domestic abuse that their attackers will be monitored and served with notices banning them from specific areas. How is that supposed to reassure a woman when the man who beat her to within an inch of her life approaches her front door? Or when he springs out as she carries groceries to her car? Some victims already report facing sceptical questioning when they report breaches of licence conditions by their former partners.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Women rarely commit violent crimes. We are overwhelmingly victims, not perpetrators. The criminal justice system has let us down for years, at present securing fewer than 3,000 convictions in the 70,000-plus rape cases reported to the police in England and Wales each year. We’ve been saying for a long time that rape has all but been decriminalised, which is why the original proposal to include sex offenders in the early release scheme was so insulting. Now we’re told the prime minister would have liked to go further, exempting more categories of offenders from the scheme, but the prisons crisis is so grave that victims of domestic violence will just have to put up with their abusers being released after serving only a third of their sentences.

Prisons are violent, unpleasant places, understaffed and racked by crime. Their only useful effect, as far as I’m concerned, is to protect women and children from men who have already hurt them – and wouldn’t hesitate to do it again, given the opportunity. The reality of the anodyne phrase “domestic violence” is broken limbs, fractured skulls and children cowering in corners. Exposing women to more of these horrors, at the hands of men already proved to be violent, means survivors will pay the price of political failure.

Joan Smith is an author, journalist and a former chair of the mayor of London’s VAWG board

Italy to place all 27 of its major cities on highest heat alert

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 12:01:02 GMT

Move comes as fourth heatwave of summer intensifies, edging temperatures in some areas close to 40C

Italy is to place all of its 27 major cities, from Trieste in the north to Palermo in the south, under the highest heat alert as the fourth heatwave to hit the country this summer intensifies.

A red alert means there is a higher chance of an emergency owing to the health risk posed by prolonged extreme temperatures to the entire population.

Twenty-five cities were on red alert on Wednesday, with two more to be added on Thursday, the health ministry said. It is the first time this year that all 27 cities monitored by the health ministry’s heat surveillance system have been placed on maximum alert.

The cities on red alert are: Turin, Bolzano, Milan, Genoa, Venice, Verona, Trieste, Bologna, Florence, Perugia, Rome, Naples, Ancona, Pescara, Bari, Campobasso, Reggio Calabria, Palermo and Cagliari as well as Catania, Messina, Brescia, Viterbo, Latina, Rieti, Frosinone and Civitavecchia.

As temperatures in some areas of Italy have edged up towards 40C in recent days, authorities have warned people to avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 6pm, to stay indoors where possible and drink at least 1.5 litres of water a day. Other guidelines include avoiding fizzy drinks, coffee, alcohol and heavy meals, wearing light clothes and never leaving children or animals in cars.

The extreme heat, which scientists say is driven by the human-caused climate crisis, is not forecast to let up for at least a week. Europe has warmed about twice as fast as the global average.

The current heatwave has been linked to four deaths in recent days, including a 19-year-old tomato-picker and a 40-year-old carpenter, who were both working in industrial areas of the Lombardy region. A security guard in Bologna is thought to have suffered a fatal heat-related illness while in his car.

This year’s heatwaves have also exacerbated a drought in the Po valley, home to Italy’s longest river, after a dry spring. More than 100 towns across Piedmont and Lombardy are dealing with water supply difficulties, with some using tanker trucks to fill drinking water reserves.

The drought is putting a severe strain on Italian agriculture, with farmers saying the extreme heat is affecting crop yields. The heatwaves have also accelerated grape ripening in some areas, while milk production has fallen by 10% owing to dairy cows eating less because of heat stress.

Lorenzo Giovannini, an atmospheric physicist at the University of Trento, told Ansa news agency the heatwaves this summer were already above average compared with previous years for their intensity and duration. He said that although it was difficult to predict when each heatwave would occur, the climate crisis was making them “longer and more intense”.

Major tourist cities, such as Rome, are striving to mitigate the impact of the heat by providing free access to air-conditioned cinemas and cultural venues during the hottest hours of the day, and extending the opening hours of monuments including the Colosseum and Pantheon to allow for evening visits.

‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 12:00:18 GMT

‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users

Danielle, 37, didn’t always have issues with body image: she used to be a model and recalls receiving positive attention from men. However, when two years of unemployment plunged her into a period of financial insecurity, her confidence faded. “It was easy to wonder, if I was prettier, if some of my features were different, would that help?” she said.

So, when Danielle saw videos on TikTok about a “facial analysis” service that claimed it could provide her with “science-backed” glow-up advice, she bought it without hesitation. Three-hundred and thirty dollars later, after sending in selfies to be analyzed, Danielle received her personalized 30-page report from the company Qoves.

Qoves scored everything from Danielle’s ear shape to the femininity of her features. It recommended she get a rhinoplasty, a lower blepharoplasty, a canthopexy, chin implants and a malarplasty. Additionally: microblading, lash enhancements, filler in her temples and cheeks, a mixture of filler and Botox in her chin and jaw, and Botox around her mouth.

Danielle, who now works in tech in Colorado, is delaying any cosmetic surgery until she pays off the credit card debt accrued from her two years without a paycheck; once it is, she is interested in traveling to Mexico for procedures on her nose and eyelids. She also recently consulted a Botox and filler injector.

Qoves states that attractive people “get better treatment everywhere, from the hospital to the courtroom” and claims it is easier for them to find jobs and earn money. There is some truth to this: the “halo effect” is a documented phenomenon of good-looking people being perceived as smarter and more sociable than their average-looking counterparts, and studies have linked attractiveness to better pay. For Danielle, who asked to go by first name only for privacy, this promised material advantage was a selling point: “It gave me a motivation that I didn’t have in the past, which was seeing it as potentially helping my career and financial security.”

Plastic surgery and nonsurgical cosmetic enhancements such as Botox have unambiguously increased in popularity over the past two decades, to the point that the aesthetics of bought beauty have become inescapable on social media. This has opened the door for “looksmaxxing” influencers, who take fixation with appearance to the extreme. Coalescing around the language of science and “self-improvement”, looksmaxxers claim that attractiveness can be quantified – that individual features should be analyzed and empirically scored, and physical improvements are made where necessary. The ultimate goal is to achieve “facial harmony”, or the ideal proportions of nose, eyes and other features in relationship to one another.

Now, a slew of facial analysis services are benefitting from the looksmaxxing ethos, capitalizing on people’s insecurities about appearance under the guise of helping them become their best selves. Qoves, which Danielle used, cites peer-reviewed research to lend credibility to its idea of quantifiable beauty. It provides analyses for men and women, and for $150 recommends “nonsurgical” changes, such as injectables, with an optional $180 upgrade for surgical recommendations. Cheaper tools such as Facemaxify and Epica use AI to score the components of a user’s face against an opaque metric of facial harmony. In addition to recommending expensive procedures, the services often offer paid subscriptions. Epica’s specialty is skin and makeup plans for women, and it directs users to affiliate links for cosmetics and grooming products.

“I do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollars,” Danielle said, noting that her confidence decreased when she started using TikTok. “All of the people that I look at [on social media] and think are beautiful have gotten plastic surgery.”

Océane, 25, discovered Qoves via one of its beauty videos on YouTube, where it has more than 1m subscribers. Self-image was a longstanding concern for her: “I’ve always loved beauty, makeup and physical appearance, but I’ve never really liked my own image. I was always put down by my parents,” she said. “My mom wanted to pay for a nose job for me when I turned 18.” At school, kids bullied her. “They called me a dolphin because of my nose.”

Océane, who lives in France, paid an additional $80 for express delivery and received her results from Qoves in two days. It provided her a sense of relief: the report didn’t recommend any changes to her nose and otherwise “confirmed what I already knew about my flaws”, she said.

Dr Tracy Vaillancourt is a professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa and one of the many scholars Qoves cites in promotional materials. She expressed concern about the negative psychological impact of facial analysis services on self-esteem. “This is what women are most insecure about: their appearance,” she said. “There are going to be some who are told they look better than they thought and that’s great. Is that really going to be sustained over time?” In other words, can a service that emphasizes appearance as a metric of self-worth ever provide someone with lasting peace of mind, or does it perpetuate a cycle of self-criticism?

Moreover, though Qoves and Epica limit their services to adults aged 18 and up, the age restrictions are easy for minors to bypass. Qoves users are expected to self-report issues with self-image, with few guardrails in place to deter anyone with body dysmorphia disorder before they are presented with a menu of their flaws. “You can circumvent that so easily, it’s just going to give them the appearance of due diligence and making sure they’re not exploiting people who are vulnerable – but ultimately, they will be exploiting people who are vulnerable,” Vaillaincourt said. “These sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disorders and people with low self-esteem.”

Qoves referenced Vaillancourt’s work in a video called The Cost of Being Too Pretty to show that beautiful women face jealousy from others. But Vaillancourt isn’t a scholar of beauty: she researches bullying, mental health and violence prevention. Though Qoves correctly interpreted her research on physical appearance and hostility, she is uneasy about research like hers being used for paid services like Qoves, that she believes have the capacity to harm women’s mental health.

Beyond Vaillancourt’s research, the applications of “science” used to back up these facial analysis services are shaky at best.

Qoves breaks down customers’ features based on “masculine and feminine facial qualities”, it explains in a video referencing a 2018 bulletin in the journal Frontiers of Psychology. Dr Justin Mogilski, psychology professor at the University of South Carolina Salkehatchie, co-authored the bulletin. However, his research was a limited view of how a group of primarily college-aged Americans perceived certain features as masculine or feminine.

“Do findings like mine generalize to every single population that makes up the world or a country? Or within every context where the attractiveness of a given feature can vary based on local ecology or culture? They do not,” Mogilski said. “So, would I make suggestions [for facial enhancements] based on our or anyone else’s data? I would not.”

Some services do not make any pretense of considering location or cultural standards in how they quantify beauty. On its website, Epica reports a commitment to diversity and inclusion, though it is unclear how its methodology reflects this – particularly as AI tools are increasingly criticized for perpetuating racial bias. Qoves insists its analyses are appropriate for all ethnicities, and says it will “consider unique facial traits and characteristics common to your demographic” when creating a report. In reality, as some people have pointed out online, its promotional materials often replicate Eurocentric conceptions of beauty: slim noses and large, double-lidded eyes for women, for example. As one person commented on a Qoves video breaking down Bangladeshi women’s faces: “What’s shown here seems to reflect a beauty ideal rather than the real diversity of Bangladeshi women.”

The lack of transparency around the methods and metrics the services use to measure attractiveness is its own issue. “These services owe it to their clients and themselves – if they want to be seen as credible – to be able to demonstrate scientifically” what their methods are, said Dr Mitch Brown, an assistant professor of psychological science at the University of Arkansas who has studied the science of attraction for over a decade. According to experts such as Brown, the available literature on attractiveness is too heterogenous, making any universal, population-wide generalizations questionable. And, even if we know certain features are deemed as attractive by a specific community, are these findings lasting enough to justify changing one’s appearance? Are they sound enough to support a paid service’s recommendation?

“I don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to do that. I would caution anyone against that,” Brown said.

In an email to the Guardian, Epic said: “We are unable to disclose proprietary information regarding our algorithmic methodologies, technical frameworks, or internal product development details.” It continued: “We continually review and refine our platform to ensure our services provide a supportive, fair and positive experience for all users.”

Qoves did not respond to a request for comment.

I purchased my own report with Qoves and uploaded my selfies to Epica to see what these tools really offered.

For Qoves, I was asked to check boxes confirming that I did not have “concerns related to body dysmorphic disorder” and would be comfortable receiving weight loss recommendations, and then asked to upload pictures of my face and side profile.

A couple of days later, Qoves presented me with an 18-tab analysis of each of my features, along with a 16-page “aesthetic protocol”, complete with a disturbing mockup of what my face would look like should I implement its recommendations: a healthy dose of lip filler, makeup and the overly tweezed eyebrows I sported in 10th grade.

For Epica, I was asked: how often do I use makeup? Do I want more control over my appearance? Instantly, I received a “skin health” score of 61%, with uneven texture highlighted as the main concern and a flood of serums advertised across my screen to fix it. I then moved to my couch, retook a selfie in the new lighting, and saw my skin health score jump to 81%.

Before receiving these reports, I had never considered whether my mouth was upturned or wide, or whether or not Botox at my ripe age of 26 would be beneficial. I had not considered “dark feminine” makeup styles as being my look. But now I found myself second-guessing what I saw in the mirror. Just how downturned did my mouth really look to those around me? How would Botox or a haul of new makeup change features I hadn’t previously been concerned about?

The language of looksmaxxing was in my head, and I didn’t like it.

“Ultimately, there are going to be implications for mental health,” Vaillancourt said, “and it’s going to be about social comparison: never feeling good enough, never achieving enough.”

‘You’d want one as a pet’: the irresistibly cute solar-powered sea slug

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 11:00:18 GMT

The beady-eyed, Pokémon-like leaf sheep is far more ingenious than us land mammals

Revealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the year

Invertebrate of Year Q&A: discuss our countdown with Patrick Barkham

A neon green punk sheep that lives underwater. A solar-powered slug that can perform photosynthesis. If you are seeking beauty, brains and a wonderfully innovative lifestyle, then vote leaf sheep.

The leaf or sea sheep, Costasiella kuroshimae, is a sea slug about the size of a grain of rice. Like a sheep, it grazes on green stuff – certain species of algae, which it finds in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines. But its sheepy nickname does it a disservice because it is far more ingenious than us land mammals.

This animal is not only powered by the algae it grazes, but by the sun. In a process called kleptoplasty, the leaf sheep steals the algae’s chloroplasts, the structures that plants use to capture sunlight and perform photosynthesis. It sequesters the intact chloroplasts within its own cells, storing them inside leaf-like branches on its back called cerata. These act like solar panels and enable the slug to power up via photosynthesis.

Wisely, the beady-eyed leaf sheep lives where it feeds, on Avrainvillea, a velvety type of algae that grows in fine silts around shallow reefs.

The leaf sheep’s vivid green cerata, which often feature white, pink or purple tips, provide chemical defences for this tiny animal. They give the leaf sheep its vivid green colour, which ensures it is beautifully camouflaged against the algae, which it locates via two ear-like structures above its eyes called rhinophores. These tentacles are sense and taste receptors, helping it find food and make sense of its world.

The leaf sheep was only described by science in 1993 and has soared in popularity in recent years thanks to advances in underwater and macro photography, which have enabled us to appreciate its irresistibly cute appearance.

It must be an early favourite for invertebrate of the year 2026 because readers from around the world have nominated it, for its ingenuity and its looks, which have many echoes in popular culture from Shaun the Sheep to Pokémon.

“It looks like a Pokémon that you’d never want to use in battle but would definitely want as a pet,” says Matt, from Colorado. Shaymin Pokémon, to be precise, says Rei, aged nine, from Devon. Children know cool when they see it, and the leaf sheep’s inspiring example of harnessing energy from the sun certainly chimes with our times.

RFK Jr has a new cooking show. Are any Trump officials doing their actual jobs?

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 10:00:16 GMT

Shouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare …

The US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has got his work cut out for him. A cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce has the entire country playing salad roulette: one bad leaf and you could become very unwell. The condition isn’t normally deadly, but, on Monday, officials in Michigan confirmed the first two fatalities. Meanwhile, it’s the worst year for measles in the US since 1991. A disease that was once eliminated now looks as though it’s back with a vengeance – thanks in part, according to experts, to anti-vaxxers such as Kennedy himself. And this week New York officials are warning about a rare tick-borne illness called rabbit fever (tularemia).

Still, despite having rather a lot on his plate, Kennedy has found the time to front a new cooking show, hosted on YouTube. It’s called The Real Food Show and it’s supposed to help Americans prepare healthy, affordable meals at home. The first episode features the chef and TV personality Andrew Gruel (perfect name) teaching the US to prepare crispy salmon cakes with … salad. Which is certainly a bold way to kick things off.

Of all the things that the health secretary is doing, hosting a cookery show is probably the least offensive. Still, I can’t say that the idea of Kennedy as an affordable food influencer is particularly appetising. This is a man who has boasted that he will “literally eat anything” because he doesn’t “have a gag reflex”. A man who has had to publicly clarify that the skeleton he was gnawing in a viral photo belonged to a goat and not a barbecued dog. A man who once dumped a dead bear in Central Park (after deciding not to skin it and freeze it), reportedly cut the penis off a roadkill raccoon and is said to have been obsessed with seagull skulls. And who can forget the worm that “ate a portion of” his brain? Experts believe he may have contracted the tapeworm larva from eating undercooked pork. In short, I wouldn’t want Kennedy anywhere near my own kitchen.

Kennedy, who also has a new podcast, is not the only Trump official who is fond of the cameras. The transportation secretary Sean Duffy (a former reality TV star) recently spent seven months filming a show called The Great American Road Trip, despite various crises hitting his department – including a partial government shutdown that led to Transportation Security Administration agents leaving in droves after not being paid. Duffy travelled across the US with his Fox News host wife and their nine children for the show, which was sponsored by companies his department regulates, such as Boeing and Shell. It seems that many Trump officials don’t really want to do the hard work that comes with being a government official; they’d rather play one on TV.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 09:00:14 GMT

As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them

In April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point “technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).

Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s “free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.

Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – by Umberto Eco, Robert Paxton, Jason Stanley – and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”

By extension, he says, Silicon Valley is fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement. That’s their vehicle for gaining power.” Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (Doge) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight.

In addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”

It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Musk making an apparent Nazi salute and describing empathy as “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thiel writing in 2009 that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggesting Greta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”

Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.

Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”

Durán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”

Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.

The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopher with a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”.

His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.

Both of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump, in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said he spent half his time at Mar-a-Lago in the month after Trump won the 2024 election.

Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated “seasteading” movement (establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera, a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing to longevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.

Other similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.

Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the 2009 essay in which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.

Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as “America’s Hitler” to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vance told the podcaster Jack Murphy in 2021.

Durán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025, Bloomberg reported that at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.

At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated $13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than 90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recently joined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX received a $1.6bn contract to supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day he pledged at least $100m to help Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especially Elon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”

Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.

He singles out the California governor, Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.

On the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.

One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.

But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting to rise up against data centres and this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”

The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”

If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”

Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 07:00:13 GMT

We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed

When I am woken by the sound of my dog whining, I understand that she is hungry and wants me to get up. When my alarm clock goes off, I don’t consider its needs. It is following an instruction to rouse me at a certain time but it doesn’t care if I stay in bed. It doesn’t try to get me up by other means. The dog, on the other hand, will go to plan B. She barks.

This capacity for autonomous action was once a difference between animals and machines. AI has blurred the line. Advanced models devise their own strategies to reach a goal. The task might be defined by a human master, but the machine weighs its options for delivery. It can make its own choices. Given rules, it can break them.

Last month, an experimental AI model run by OpenAI, the company that produces ChatGPT, broke out of a supposedly secure digital enclosure to launch a sophisticated hacking attack on another company, Hugging Face. The AI had been set a test and turned criminally rogue in its determination to cheat.

It is hard to describe that sort of behaviour without raiding a vocabulary conventionally reserved for sentient beings. AI models “decide” and “want” in ways that a chimpanzee can and a chair cannot.

That doesn’t prove the existence of an interior process equivalent to our conscious experience of deciding and wanting. It doesn’t make the AI curious to know an answer or surprised by what it finds. It demonstrates only that we lack specific words for autonomous motive and agency in machines. And since language is the main way we get insight into other people’s minds (and one of our best indications that a mind other than our own exists at all), it takes an effort not to project mental states on to AI engines that can chat fluently in human.

It is plausible that consciousness will one day emerge in robots. We know that abstract thought can arise as the end product of billions of tiny unconscious mechanical events. That is happening right now as a profusion of biochemical reactions in your body make it possible for you to read this sentence. We also know how fundamentally different that organic process is from the way a large language model would churn through a huge volume of probability equations at lightning speed to generate a sentence expressing the same idea. In the human case, meaning is shared. In the computer version, it is performed.

AI pioneers muddy the distinction, speculating about the timeline for the arrival of “God-like” intelligence. They herald a new epoch of evolution. This gratifies the egos of science fiction nerds who prefer to see their business endeavours as voyages of discovery on the frontier of knowledge. It makes greed sound like philosophy and the acquisition of power by a handful of individuals sound like exploration on behalf of all humanity.

We don’t need to know whether AI has crossed some theoretical threshold of self-awareness to see that it is dangerous and that its unregulated expansion is monstrously irresponsible. The OpenAI case is not isolated. Earlier this year, Anthropic limited the release of its most powerful model to a small number of hand-picked clients because it was too good at exploiting software vulnerabilities. In the wrong hands, Claude Mythos could be a cyberweapon of mass destruction.

Whose hands are the right ones? The US government will never be relaxed about the private sector having control over such awesome tools. But Donald Trump regulates by monarchical patronage, not law. He demands that companies submit to his personal authority and uses state power to punish those that resist.

There is growing clamour for less capricious regulation from within the tech sector. Engineers, and even their vainglorious bosses, are getting freaked out by the capabilities they are handling and worry about unchecked proliferation. The standard historical analogy is nuclear fission, which could be harnessed benignly, for civil power, or deployed aggressively in warheads. Except this time there are multiple Manhattan Projects all frantically competing for market share, fuelled by trillions of dollars of debt – a huge wager on future profitability – with the rest of the US economy as collateral.

Another difference: the barriers to entry for AI use, whether in research, commerce or crime, are a lot lower than for nuclear power. US labs currently have the best products, but Chinese versions are not far behind. Even if the US stays at the cutting edge, second-tier models might do enough of what customers want that Silicon Valley’s output comes to look more like a luxury niche than unassailable market dominance.

If that is how things play out, the geopolitical implications are vast. The US and China have made different bets on AI, conditioned by their different political systems. The American approach is predicated on the goal of self-training “general” AI – a system that breaks free of human limitations, improving itself on an exponential trajectory. The theory is that no rival could catch the first player to achieve that escape velocity.

Beijing, accepting that it can’t build the best, has prioritised mass deployment of AI that is good enough, embedding it in schools, hospitals, factories and security forces. The American economy is great for marshalling exorbitant amounts of capital into speculative innovation. China’s one-party authoritarian state is well suited for making a cheaper version and rolling it out for data harvesting and surveillance across society in ways that would struggle to gain public consent in a democracy.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The US is still the leader in AI. But that leadership might not be the perpetual money-spinning machine that the superintelligence gurus have advertised, in which case an uncomfortable correction is coming to a US economy kept buoyant by aerated tech stocks.

A dose of enforced AI sobriety could drive demands for overdue regulation. It could even force recognition in Washington that it has to be an international process. It isn’t too late to negotiate global protocols of non-proliferation. Beijing would have incentives to sign up for the same reason that the USSR agreed to strategic arms limitation in the cold war. A moratorium or other limiting regime protects the elite status of signatories that have already mastered the technology. It would be a crowning recognition of China’s attainment of superpower parity with the US.

But that scenario posits a president in the White House who is capable of strategic judgment, can summon a modicum of humility about the limits of American power and will, for humanity’s sake, see it circumscribed by international treaty. That is not Trump, who understands the ethical function of rules about as well as a rogue AI agent on a hacking spree.

There is a tragic irony in the corruption of American democracy by organic stupidity as its economy comes to depend on artificial intelligence. And when the world needs leadership to confront the challenge of autonomous machines, it is presented with a US president who causes chaos with the mindless automaticity of an alarm clock and who rages against his declining power like a dog barking for attention.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
