Murderous heat, an endangered food supply and no net zero: this is the life the radical right wants you to have

The Guardian Wed, 05 Aug 2026 05:00:10 GMT

As climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like it

Can’t you leftists understand? Mass death is good for you. Reject the woke love of life! Welcome civilisational collapse! Watch it all burn, then dance in the ashes! This, roughly speaking, is how the dismissal of climate action is now being justified: the argument has shifted from science denial to outright nihilism.

The new incendiary spirit is exemplified by that serial arsonist Allister Heath, editor of the Sunday Telegraph. In a column in the Daily Telegraph last week, originally titled “Britain can’t stop climate change. Scrap net zero and embrace Mediterranean life”, he argued that “climate change is real” but “the war against global warming has been lost”.

This is a classic progression among those who seek to prevent a shift away from fossil fuels: first deny the problem, as the Daily and Sunday Telegraph have done for many years, then accept the problem but claim it’s now too late to act. If it is too late, it’ll be in no small part because of the deniers. So, Heath continued, we in Britain should “ditch the despicable con that is net zero, and learn to cope with … a warmer, drier, more volatile Mediterranean climate, if that is indeed to be our fate”.

Seeking to cut our emissions, he argued, shows that we suffer from an “advanced case of suicidal empathy”. I’m not qualified to diagnose people, but as a general rule, a lack of empathy, alongside callousness and an absence of guilt, is a strong indicator of a psychopath. Yes, he continued, “there will be plenty of losers, but it is pointless seeking to prevent the inevitable … Many in Britain would enjoy the kind of warmer climate predicted by modellers”.

His timing was impeccable: extolling a Mediterranean climate just as the Mediterranean region goes up in flames. Amid general derision on social media, the editors changed the headline.

Heath’s column also happened to land on the day drought was declared across half of England. Nevertheless, he argued, we need universal irrigation and should construct more swimming pools. Where will the water come from? Oh, don’t get all empirical with me. He maintained we should “trust that the free market will deliver the goods on clean energy and zero-carbon transportation, but only when they are better and cheaper than existing alternatives”. But renewables are already cheaper, and better for us, than fossil fuels in almost all situations. It is only through resistance to the “free market”, led by the Trump administration – which has spent billions trying to kill clean energy and sustain coal burning – that fossil fuels retain such a share of consumption. As a result of the plunging price of renewables, far from having lost the climate war, we could be about to witness a rapid turnaround. So quick, give up now, just in case we win.

He dismissed cutting carbon emissions in the UK as a “moral act, an ethical imperative”, by which he appears to mean unhinged: “Down that road lies madness.” Yes, cutting our own emissions is a moral act and an ethical imperative. It is also pragmatic. Global action on climate breakdown depends on mutual trust. If some countries refuse to play, others are also likely to refuse, and an effective global response collapses in a circle of finger-pointing. This risk is all the greater when rich nations, which tend to have the biggest fossil fuel legacies, seek to behave as free riders. If we don’t step up, why should anyone else?

As for the “warmer climate predicted by modellers”, it could go quite the other way, as rising temperatures, some models suggest, could cause the Atlantic current system to stall, plunging Britain into extreme cold. Well, you’ll just have to learn to adapt to that instead.

Heath’s defiance of reality is so well established that it has spawned an “Allister Heath headline generator”, which pumps out bonkers statements not easily distinguishable from the originals. In a close field, I think he takes the prize for being more wrong more often than anyone else in British journalism. This, after all, is the man who described Kwasi Kwarteng’s fiscal catastrophe as “the best budget I have ever heard a British chancellor deliver, by a massive margin”. It’s a reliable rule: if Heath believes something, the opposite is likely to be true.

But it’s not just him, and it’s not just journalism. The radical right moves as a pack, and Heath is just one of many now insisting that climate catastrophe is something we should simply suck up. Those grammar deniers Reform UK, for example, insist: “We are better to adapt to warming, rather than pretend we can stop it.” Of course the same political tendency also defends austerity and privatisation, both of which severely hamper our ability to adapt.

To their credit, two Telegraph columnists, Ambrose Evans-Pritchard and Tim Stanley, last week broke the nihilist consensus, arguing we should rise to the challenge of climate breakdown. But they now belong to a minority, in the Telegraph and across the rightwing press.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Why? Because most of the media, most of the time, provides a platform for people who say things that have the effect of serving capital, whether or not they are true, whether or not they are coherent, whether or not they may hasten disaster. While renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels in nearly all circumstances, fossil fuels are more profitable, because useful reserves are limited and can each be monopolised by a single corporation, while prices can suddenly take flight in times of war or chaos. Almost all the very rich are heavily invested in them. The result is that any attempt to restrict the use of fossil fuels is perceived as class war. Nonsensical justifications for the status quo then follow as automatically as the Allister Heath headline generator.

So “embrace Mediterranean life”. But without the wine, which, as another Telegraph column laments, is becoming “smoke tainted” by all those fires triggered by some unmentioned and mysterious force. And without the food, whose production, thanks to the drought and heatwaves, is at grave risk in southern Europe, as it is here. And without your lovely gite, which might have been incinerated. Or the lush green landscape, also lost to the flames. Or the balmy summer temperatures, now replaced by murderous heat. Oh go on then, you know what I really mean: embrace death.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

Trump Said Qatari Jet Was Destined for His Library. That May Change.

The New York Times August 05, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A White House official says no final decision has been made about which plane will go on display at the Trump presidential library. That leaves the fate of the Qatari jet unclear.

By Maggie Haberman and Eric Lipton

Maggie Haberman reported from Las Vegas and Eric Lipton from Washington.

When Qatar donated a Boeing jet for use as a temporary Air Force One, President Trump said the luxury plane would come with him when he left office — but only as a display at his presidential library.

Those plans appear to have changed.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive subject, said on Wednesday that no final decision has been made about which plane will go to the library.

Earlier this week, Mr. Trump’s son Eric, who is heavily involved with developing the library, told NBC News in a text message that it was “not the plan at the moment” to bring the Qatari jet to the library, which is planned for downtown Miami.

One person with knowledge of the discussions said that Mr. Trump had been considering decommissioning one of the two older Air Force One jets to display at the library, but that he also planned to take the Qatari jet as well. It was unclear if that plan was still in consideration.

Mr. Trump’s decision to accept the $400 million jet has raised security and ethical concerns, about the rushed job to retrofit the plane into a presidential aircraft and about the propriety of taking such a gift from a foreign government.

The president has insisted that the plane is a gift to the U. S. Department of Defense — and not him personally — and that he would not use it after he leaves office.

Mr. Trump has spoken of the plane as a new symbol of American strength and grandeur since he first toured it in February 2025. It is also significantly newer than his own private plane, a Boeing 757 known informally as Trump Force One.

The Qatari jet has cost hundreds of millions of dollars to retrofit, although the exact cost has not been made public. After questions emerged about whether the plane has sufficient defensive capabilities to serve as Air Force One, the White House said it would be taken out of service for about one month this fall for unspecified “additional upgrades and enhancements.”

Asked in May 2025 if he planned to attempt to take the donated Qatari jet for his own personal use as a still-operating airplane once he left office, Mr. Trump said: “It would go directly to the library after I leave office. I wouldn’t be using it. No.”

The White House and the Justice Department jointly signed a memo last year, which was never made public, asserting that it was legal for the federal government to accept the gift, which would then be transferred to the Trump presidential library.

The Qatari jet has been described as a “bridge” plane for presidential travel as the Air Force awaits the two long-delayed planes that were commissioned from Boeing to replace the existing Air Force One jets.

At least inside the Air Force, no decision has been made over the fate of the Qatari plane, one Air Force official said Wednesday. The possibilities include its continued use as a third Air Force One, after Boeing delivers its two new planes starting in 2028, or it could be used by other federal government officials for government travel.

The retrofitted Qatari plane is now owned by the U. S. government, White House and Air Force officials have said.

Before either the retrofitted Qatari plane or the soon-to-be retired 747 jets flown as Air Force One since the early 1990s could be donated or transferred to an outside party, they would have to be designed officially by the government as excess property, a Pentagon official said Wednesday.

The Air Force secretary, in consultation with the office of the Secretary of Defense, then controls what happens to them, a Pentagon official said Wednesday.

Typically, that involves first offering the aircraft for use by other government agencies or even the National Guard. But eventually the plane can be donated if it is being entirely taken out of service.

The last time the Air Force formally retired one of its Air Force One official presidential planes, a request came in from the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation to donate the retired Boeing 707 jet to the Reagan library in California, which was approved in August 2001, by then Air Force Secretary James G. Roche.

The Reagan library model is one that Trump officials have referred to as the framework for what Mr. Trump had wanted.

“It’s something that was done by Ronald Reagan: they actually decommissioned the plane and they put it in his library,” Mr. Trump said in May 2025, about the possible donation to Mr. Trump’s own future library, offering his own incorrect version of this history. “It has actually made the library more successful, so it was good.”

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

El-Sayed Won a High-Stakes Michigan Primary. Now Comes the Hard Part.

The New York Times August 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate candidacy poses a critical test of Democrats’ ascendant progressive wing: Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly liberal positions, win a general election in a moderate state?

By Lisa Lerer

For months, the Democratic establishment had issued increasingly dire warnings that Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Michigan firebrand who had never won an election, would struggle to win a swing-state Senate seat that the party could not afford to lose.

The state’s governor, members of Congress and attorney general lined up behind his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, a centrist from a swing district. They argued that she could win the kind of tough races that are a hallmark of this battleground state, where voters have twice voted for Donald J. Trump and twice voted for Ronald Reagan.

On Tuesday, a slim plurality of Democratic primary voters disagreed, betting with their hearts on a candidate whose fiercely progressive message had thrilled a coalition of younger and college-educated liberals.

Now, as he heads into the general election, Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy will pose perhaps the most consequential challenge to the party’s ascendant progressive wing: Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly left-wing positions, win in a moderate state?

Dr. El-Sayed will offer the first general election test of the competing theories of electability that have been debated among Democrats for nearly a decade. Since Senator Bernie Sanders exploded onto the national stage in 2016, progressives have argued that their party’s path to victory runs through a populist economic agenda that can attract a broad coalition of working-class voters. Centrists have pushed back, saying such proposals alienate the moderate voters the party must sway to to win back areas where it has lost ground in recent years.

The narrow results hinted at the tough race ahead in November, when Dr. El- Sayed will face former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who left Congress in 2015. Dr. El-Sayed enters the general election without a strong mandate from Democrats, after more than half of primary voters cast ballots for other candidates. He performed best in wealthier, younger areas of the state, while Ms. Stevens did better in places with greater numbers of Black and working-class voters.

The close election underscored the divide between a loud, online liberal movement, which championed Dr. El-Sayed, and many of the voters who are the backbone of the party in battleground states.

In a speech to supporters early Wednesday morning, hours before the race was called in his favor, Dr. El-Sayed attempted to frame his candidacy as bigger than traditional partisan divides. And he boasted about his ability to withstand an onslaught of attacks funded by outside organizations supporting Ms. Stevens.

“We are not a purple state. We are a state in need of a movement to take our politics back,” he said, speaking at his campaign headquarters in Detroit. “When we come through this, inshallah, we’ll have taken 70 million on the chin and kept fighting back.”

The stakes extend far beyond Michigan. Democrats must hold the state to have any chance of winning back control of the Senate. With Republicans holding 53 seats, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats and keep all their own to win the majority. Michigan is the Democratic-held seat most at risk of going red.

At first glance, Dr. El-Sayed — a politically inexperienced, weight lifting, former public health official, who would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate — appeared an unlikely standard-bearer for his party. But he tapped into a sense of frustration in the primary electorate. A charismatic campaigner, he fueled his candidacy with promises to lower costs, provide universal health care and ban corporate money in politics. Fluent in podcasts and social media, he crafted a platform centered on taxing billionaires, opposition to Israel and Medicare for all.

He also embraced people and positions that strategists say carries political peril in a moderate state like Michigan.

Dr. El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker, the Marxist streamer who critics say has stoked antisemitic sentiment — a charge he denies. Throughout his campaign, Dr. El-Sayed has called Israel’s government “evil” and its actions in Gaza a “genocide.” And he supports abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“The risks with him are very obvious that he brings to the table positions that are just nonstarters with a general electorate,” said Lis Smith, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked for Mallory McMorrow, a more moderate Michigan Senate primary candidate who dropped out before Election Day. “That being said, he does connect a little bit more emotionally with the moment. He understands the anger that people across the political spectrum feel. ”

Many in the party’s liberal wing are looking even beyond November. A victory by Dr. El-Sayed would fuel their ambitions in the 2028 presidential race, providing evidence that progressive candidates can win not only in deep blue areas but also across the country. In 2028, Michigan will be among the first states to vote in the party’s presidential primaries.

“Now is an opportunity to chart a new path forward,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesman for Justice Democrats, a progressive group. “Clearly Democratic voters are on board with that new vision.”

But first, Dr. El-Sayed must win a tough race in November.

No Republican has won a U. S. Senate race in Michigan in over three decades. But Mr. Rogers has come close: Two years ago, he lost to Senator Elissa Slotkin by a razor-thin margin.

Even before the race was called on Wednesday morning, the Senate Republicans began showcasing their attacks, releasing a video ad calling Dr. El-Sayed “the most radical candidate in America.” The spot highlights his refusal to disavow a remark from his supporter Hasan Piker that “America deserved 9/11" — a comment Mr. Piker has since called “inappropriate.”

Republicans will have plenty of money to make their case.

In April, the Senate Leadership Fund, the Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, pledged to spend $45 million supporting Mr. Rogers, its largest commitment for a seat not occupied by a Republican. Another conservative group, funded in part by the DeVos family, a conservative family that has invested hundreds of millions in right-wing causes, announced a $15 million commitment to Mr. Rogers.

Still, Republicans acknowledged their own challenges in running against Dr. El-Sayed.

“He really does have a true movement and a momentum,” said Ronna McDaniel, the former chairwoman of the Republican National Committee, who is involved with conservative organizing in the state. “Republicans can’t just sit back and say, ‘Oh, he’s a socialist.’ We have to define who he is and what this actually means.”

Mr. Rogers will also have to outrun a difficult national political environment for Republicans. Mr. Trump’s approval ratings reached an all-time low this week, fueled by an unpopular war in Iran, high gas prices and economic anxiety.

And Jeff Timmer, a former executive director of the Republican Party, argued that Mr. Rogers lacks the strong support among the MAGA movement to overcome such a political drag.

“Mike Rogers doesn’t engender any enthusiasm among the die-hard party faithful,” said Mr. Timmer, who is now an independent. “He’s not the kind of candidate that anyone in the Republican Party is going to crawl across broken glass to make sure they get across the finish line.”

Dr. El-Sayed has also shown an ability to survive a barrage of attacks. His race against Ms. Stevens was the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in U. S. history, with spending topping $98 million. More than $30 million was spent in an effort to defeat him by the super PAC arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the country’s most influential pro-Israel group.

All told, Ms. Stevens had about a 9-to-1 spending advantage over Dr. El-Sayed, according to data from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The Democratic candidates traded increasingly nasty barbs in the run-up to the primary vote. Ms. Stevens and her supporters accused Dr. El-Sayed of being vain, sexist, antisemitic and encouraging “distinctly anti-American sentiment.” Dr. El-Sayed and his supporters said she was a puppet of AIPAC and unqualified, mocking her voice and appearance.

To win in November, Dr. El-Sayed must now reach beyond those voters and build a coalition that includes the moderate and independent voters who supported Ms. Stevens.

The effort to unify Democrats around his bid began in the early hours of Wednesday, even before his victory was certain.

“Tomorrow we begin to mend fences,” he said in his speech. “Whatever happens tonight, we have a responsibility to ensure that we unite to make sure that Mike Rogers never sees the inside of the U. S. Senate.”

Some of that work will depend on whether Dr. El Sayed, now the Democratic nominee, can embrace a party he has often attacked.

Ms. Smith said his eagerness to highlight the ways Democrats have failed helped fuel his primary bid. But now, she said, he must pivot.

“Sometimes he shows a little more joy in fighting Democrats than Republicans,” she said, “but hopefully that shifts in the general election.”

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

U. S. Cuts Ties With Organ Donor Group After Reports of Abuses

The New York Times August 05, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The federal government is ending its contract with a Kentucky nonprofit that it says pressured medical workers to remove organs from patients who were getting better.

By Brian M. Rosenthal

The federal government is firing the nonprofit group that coordinates organ donations in Kentucky after finding that it tried to pursue organs from critically ill people who were recovering from their injuries.

The decision, which will effectively shut down the organization, called Network for Hope, is set to be announced on Wednesday. It is part of a monthslong government effort to address unsafe and unfair practices in the United States organ transplant system.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose department oversees the transplant system, cut ties with a similar nonprofit in South Florida last year. Before that, the roughly 55 groups that have federal contracts to manage donations in the country had never faced closure.

“Americans who choose to become organ donors deserve a system that honors their gift and protects every patient,” Mr. Kennedy said in a statement ahead of the announcement, adding, “Organizations that repeatedly fail to meet federal standards and put patients at risk will be held accountable.”

Mr. Kennedy said the organization had endangered patients and failed to fix safety lapses despite numerous opportunities to improve.

Network for Hope will have a chance to appeal the government’s decision. The organization did not comment on Wednesday but has previously denied wrongdoing, saying that it has obeyed all laws and guidelines and prioritized patient safety.

An Improved System: A crackdown on problems with fairness and safety is achieving results, including a big drop in the number of sick patients being passed over for transplants.

Skipped Over in Line: The sickest patients are supposed to get priority for lifesaving transplants. But more and more, they are being skipped.

Bungled Organ Retrievals: Potential donors endured rushed or premature attempts to remove their organs. Some were gasping, crying or showing other signs of life.

Courting Overseas Patients: Despite an organ shortage, some U. S. hospitals seek out international patients, who pay as much as $2 million for a transplant. In recent years, patients from abroad have typically received organs faster than U. S. patients.

Pig Organ Transplants: The U. S. Food and Drug Administration has given the green light to two biotechnology companies for clinical trials that will transplant organs from genetically modified pigs into people with kidney failure.

In addition to Kentucky, the group also coordinates donations in more than a dozen counties in neighboring Indiana, Ohio and West Virginia. All its responsibilities will be awarded to another nonprofit.

The government’s attempts to improve the transplant system were prompted in part by a series of articles in The New York Times that detailed widespread problems, including with an increasingly common practice called donation after circulatory death.

Unlike most donors, who are brain-dead, the patients in these cases have some brain activity. But they are on life support, often in a coma, and their doctors do not expect them to recover. If donation is authorized, doctors withdraw support, wait for the patient’s heart to stop and then remove the organs. Strict rules are supposed to ensure that no retrieval begins before death or causes it.

In Kentucky, scrutiny began when a congressional committee heard testimony about the case of Anthony Thomas Hoover II, who had an overdose in 2021. After family members were told that he would not recover, they authorized donation.

As coordinators arranged for the surgery, Mr. Hoover began to stir, at one point “thrashing on the bed,” according to records reviewed by The Times. Still, Network for Hope, then called Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates, tried to move forward. Finally, on the way to the operation, Mr. Hoover cried, pulled his knees to his head and shook his head, and a hospital doctor refused to withdraw life support.

Mr. Hoover eventually recovered, although he has lingering neurological injuries.

Network for Hope initially avoided punishment. But a federal investigation last year determined that the group had similarly ignored signs of growing alertness in more than 70 other patients. Although the organ removals were eventually canceled, the investigation said multiple patients exhibited pain or distress as they were being readied for surgery.

Overall, more than 100 cases had “concerning features,” the investigators said, noting that the majority of transplants arranged by the Kentucky group were from circulatory-death patients.

Last summer, leaders of the organization testified in Congress and agreed to make changes, including increased training and regular neurology tests on potential donors. But regulators ultimately decided the group had not improved enough, leading to this week’s announcement.

Mr. Hoover is expected to attend the announcement in Lexington, Ky. His sister and legal guardian, Donna Rhorer, has publicly pushed for more safety standards. “I’m glad that something is finally being done,” she said in an interview.

In all, The Times found patients who had endured premature or bungled attempts to retrieve their organs in nine states. In some instances, hospitals, which are responsible for caring for patients before death, mistakenly concluded they would not recover. And although donation organizations are not supposed to have any role in treatment of potential donors, some groups, including the one in Kentucky, improperly pressured doctors and families while ignoring signs of recovery.

In one case in Alabama, surgeons cut into a woman’s chest before discovering she was alive. Doctors sewed her back up, and she was declared dead again 12 minutes later.

The Association of Organ Procurement Organizations, a national trade group, has emphasized that errors are rare and that donations save thousands of lives every year.

A regulatory board that runs the transplant system has been working for more than a year on a set of safety policies. The rules are expected to require potential circulatory-death donors to undergo frequent neurological testing to ensure they are not regaining awareness. The policies would also empower health workers and family members to pause the process.

Mr. Kennedy ordered all organ donation groups to hire patient safety officers after The Times’s reporting last year.

Besides addressing safety problems, government officials are working to improve fairness in the system.

After The Times reported last year that organ donation groups were regularly ignoring federal allocation rules — skipping patients at the top of waiting lists and sending organs to people who weren’t as sick and hadn’t waited as long — officials cracked down on the practice. The latest federal data shows that patients on the list were skipped about 9 percent of the time in the last quarter, down from nearly 20 percent in 2024.

And regulators recently promised renewed focus on another issue reported by The Times: how, despite America’s organ shortage, some hospitals have catered to overseas patients who pay more for transplants.

Congress has started a separate investigation into transplants for international patients. Representative Brett Guthrie, Republican of Kentucky, who chairs the committee that oversees the transplant system, applauded the government action this week.

“The American people deserve to have an organ procurement and transplantation system that they can trust,” Mr. Guthrie said. “This action takes a step forward in restoring integrity back to that system.”

Brian M. Rosenthal is an investigative reporter who has worked at The Times since 2017.

Death Renews Scrutiny of Delaney Hall. Here’s What to Know.

The New York Times August 05, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The death of a Salvadoran immigrant at the federal detention center in Newark has raised questions about the conditions there.

By Ana Ley

The death of a Salvadoran man who had been incarcerated at the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark has renewed scrutiny of the living conditions inside the federal government’s migrant holding cells.

Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, was taken from Delaney Hall to University Hospital in Newark, where he was pronounced dead on Saturday. Government officials have not said how he died, and his family members have demanded answers about the circumstances that led to his death. On Wednesday afternoon, the Department of Homeland Security said that New Jersey hospital officials and the state medical examiner would provide medical records to his relatives.

Here is what to know about Delaney Hall:

Delaney Hall opened in 2000 as a halfway house providing 250 beds for offenders serving jail terms of less than one year. From 2011 to 2017, the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency used Delaney Hall to hold up to 450 immigrant detainees. It was then used as a drug rehabilitation center and halfway house until 2023, when it was closed. It reopened in 2025 as an ICE detention center as part of President Trump’s plan to deport more migrants. Today, the center has 1,000 beds.

The detention center is run by Geo Group, one of the largest private prison operators in the United States, under a $1 billion, 15-year federal contract.

The center incarcerates immigrants who were arrested by ICE or its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security.

The people jailed inside Delaney have a broad and complex mix of immigration statuses. Some entered the United States illegally, while others overstayed their visas, which is a civil, not a criminal, offense. Many have legally applied to live in the United States and are awaiting the outcome of their cases as the Trump administration works to dissolve pathways to citizenship.

ICE officials have described the people inside Delaney Hall as killers, rapists and other criminals — “the worst of the worst.” But the federal government’s own data, including some from internal documents that The New York Times obtained in June, indicates that people with criminal convictions account for a relatively small fraction of the detainees at the center. The internal data obtained by The Times showed that of 591 people held at the time, 76 — about 13 percent — had criminal convictions, and 123 — about 21 percent — had pending criminal charges.

Health inspection reports, court filings and other public records reviewed by The Times provided some of the first documented evidence of conditions inside Delaney. Migrants had complained for months about unsafe meals, dirty living quarters and bad medical care.

The documents reviewed by The Times validated some of those complaints. Inspectors found food-preparation surfaces that had been left unsanitized. In other instances, workers had touched open garbage containers as they made meals and had not kept food at temperatures necessary to kill harmful contaminants.

Dr. Novneet Sahu, the deputy commissioner of Public Health Services at the New Jersey Health Department, received a complaint in May from a physician about a detainee with an active case of tuberculosis. The physician said that an employee at University Hospital had told her that the inmate was brought to the hospital and taken back to Delaney with no follow-up plan to contain the infection.

Dr. Sahu said that the Health Department had tried to inspect Delaney Hall’s infection-control protocols and practices but was repeatedly rebuffed. The attorney general of New Jersey sued to force the center to allow state health inspectors inside. The suit is pending.

Under federal law, members of Congress should have full access to Delaney Hall but they have sometimes been impeded by federal authorities. Democratic lawmakers have criticized ICE officials and pressed for more access.

A federal appeals court in May required the Trump administration to allow lawmakers to inspect immigration detention facilities without advance notice, ruling unanimously that the visits posed minimal problems for the government.

Representative Frank Pallone Jr., a Democrat from New Jersey, wrote a letter in July urging Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, to “take immediate action” to carry out a comprehensive review of conditions inside Delaney and to share a plan to fix the problems there.

The Department of Homeland Security has dismissed concerns about conditions at Delaney Hall and said that politicians were “inciting violent riots” by demonstrators who have gathered for weeks outside the detention center as complaints from detainees have mounted.

Days after the death of Mr. Lopez-Cornejo, his family members appeared before news cameras and said that Delaney Hall officials had refused to provide his medical records. The family demanded the documents and urged state officials to investigate Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s death.

Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s relatives have expressed concern that he might not have been getting the medication he needed to treat his diabetes and epilepsy, echoing longstanding complaints from detainees at Delaney and other detention centers about inadequate medical care.

A spokesman for Geo Group directed questions about Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s medical records to ICE, which did not respond to inquiries. The Department of Homeland Security referred questions to hospital officials and the state medical examiner, who the agency said would “release the medical record to the next of kin.”

A law firm listed in a court filing as representing Mr. Lopez-Cornejo in a case that challenged the federal government’s right to detain him did not respond to a request for comment.

The detention center has been the focus of protests for months and has renewed concerns about migrant holding cells across the United States.

Critics of Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown say that the detention centers are being used to detain too many people too hastily, leading to overcrowding, maltreatment and abuse. The White House and its supporters say the centers are essential to the effort to deport undocumented immigrants.

In New Jersey, a robust and tightly knit collection of volunteer groups has shaped a media campaign using messages from detainees, publishing their handwritten letters.

The movement has garnered support from influential religious figures, including Cardinal Joseph W. Tobin, the Roman Catholic archbishop of Newark and friend of Pope Leo XIV.

Ana Ley is a Times reporter covering immigration in New York City.

In African tech hubs, developers are picking China’s cheap, freely available artificial intelligence models over more powerful U. S. ones.

Developers built Sunflower, an artificial intelligence tool customized for Ugandan languages, using a Chinese model. Secure Muganzi, a farmer, uses Sunflower for planting information in local dialects. Credit... Video by Stuart Tibaweswa For The New York Times

Supported by

By Paul MozurAdam Satariano and Aaron Krolik

Paul Mozur and Adam Satariano reported from Nairobi, Kenya, and Aaron Krolik from New York.

When Ernest Mwebaze, a tech developer in Uganda, was building an artificial intelligence system last year tailored for his country’s many languages, he tested American and Chinese tools to see which one could help.

China’s won.

The A. I. model from the Chinese internet giant Alibaba handled Uganda’s dozens of languages better than anything from Meta or Google, Mr. Mwebaze said. It was also inexpensive, and he could customize the model with his own data.

“We want to build things as cheap as possible, yet have them work really well,” said Mr. Mwebaze, a former research scientist at Google. His system, called Sunflower, is now used across Uganda, including by farmers to receive weather information and crop advice in local dialects.

Mr. Mwebaze, 47, is one of thousands of developers across Africa who have turned to Chinese A. I. models in the past year. In Kenya, entrepreneurs are using the models to streamline legal and business services. In Nigeria, they have made educational tools that teach high school students. In Ghana, developers are building local chatbots.

China’s A. I. is surging, especially in developing countries, as people look for the best possible system at the lowest possible cost. Unlike models made by the leading American A. I. companies OpenAI and Anthropic — which are closed and charge fees — the Chinese systems are publicly available to download and modify without payment or approval.

Chinese “open-source” models account for roughly half of total A. I. use on OpenRouter, a service with 400 A. I. models for users to choose from, up from less than 25 percent a year ago, according to a New York Times analysis of data from eight million customers. Chinese models are also 19 of the 25 most downloaded open-source systems on Hugging Face, another A. I. database.

In more than two dozen interviews across Kenya, Uganda and other countries, developers, policymakers and executives described a rapidly changing A. I. market where cost, computing resources, data control and customization mattered more than where a model was made. Often they were not looking for bleeding edge A. I. They just wanted something that worked well enough on limited resources.

Using Chinese models was like owning a house while using U. S. models was like renting one, they added. Rather than spending millions to train a model from scratch, developers can download a Chinese system and build an entirely new product on top of it, paying mainly for servers. In contrast, U. S. models are a one-size fits all technology, needing subscriptions and other fees depending on the job.

“Why use an expensive Ferrari to do the school run when a Toyota hatchback can do the same?” said Moses Kemibaro, a Nairobi entrepreneur who runs a digital marketing agency, Dotsavvy, adding that Chinese models can be up to 90 percent less expensive when including costs like computing infrastructure.

Chinese officials hope their gains in Africa are a preview of things to come. Last month, powerful new Chinese A. I. systems rattled Wall Street and Silicon Valley, stoking fears in Washington that U. S. tech dominance could be undercut.

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, is using A. I. as a form of soft power. At a July conference in Shanghai, he cast Chinese models as more reliable and cheaper and warned that A. I.’s benefits must be shared or they would create “new historical injustices.” Kenya, Ethiopia, South Africa and seven other African countries signed an A. I. pact with China at the event to promote international cooperation.

Chinese firms are also courting African developers with free computing and hands-on engineering help, developers said. Many Chinese-made smartphones in Africa come with Chinese A. I. tools preinstalled.

At the same time, China’s A. I. industry faces challenges. Companies have struggled to make money from their users and face security questions about data and links to Beijing. Many African developers still pay for American A. I. models, especially for technical tasks like coding.

Yet Africa’s experience shows the global A. I. competition is now a two-horse race.

Kamal Budhabhatti, the chief executive of Craft Silicon, a Nairobi banking software company, feels the pull of both sides. He recently rebuilt his firm’s tech systems with Claude Code, Anthropic’s programming tool. A 10-person team finished in half the time a project that once took 100 engineers. The bill was high, he said, but the speed was worth it.

Huawei, the Chinese tech giant, also came calling with “some very unbelievable incentives” to switch to Chinese systems, he said, including a year of free computing and a trip to the company’s headquarters.

“It’s very hard to say no,” Mr. Budhabhatti said.

About 50 miles southeast of Nairobi, one of Kenya’s biggest collaborations with Chinese technology sits half-finished on the savanna.

Konza Technopolis, a planned city, was announced 18 years ago as Kenya’s answer to Silicon Valley. Hopefully branded the Silicon Savannah, it is now a grid of empty boulevards and skeletal buildings, watched over by a powerful Chinese surveillance system.

It would look like a failed experiment but for one slate-gray building behind an electric fence. Financed by Chinese loans and built by Huawei, the site is a data center that runs computing for Kenya’s government.

For two decades, Chinese firms have wired Africa’s telecommunications networks and paved its roads. M-Pesa, Kenya’s celebrated mobile-money system, runs on Huawei technology.

These tech ties gave China a foothold in the continent, which it is using to sell A. I. One project advertised at Konza will use technology from the Chinese A. I. firm DeepSeek to combat telecom fraud.

Locked out of advanced chips because of U. S. export controls, Chinese companies could not outspend Silicon Valley. So they gave their A. I. models away as open source, hoping to pull people from U. S. rivals.

At first, it seemed a losing bet. The United States dominated open-source A. I. Meta offered a model called Llama that developers used worldwide. But after some stumbles, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, turned more to closed models.

“It left a huge hole,” said Lucas Atkins, co-founder of Arcee A. I., an American start-up that builds open models. “It allowed the Chinese to explode into the vacuum.”

Breakthroughs came quickly. In December 2024, a DeepSeek A. I. model matched the best models at a fraction of the cost. Last month, the Chinese A. I. lab Moonshot AI released a model with coding abilities approaching the leading American systems.

In Kenya, developers embraced Chinese models.

Michael Michie builds A. I. systems for Kenyan banks and government agencies at EverseTech. His customers are price sensitive, so he makes almost everything on Chinese open-source models. Businesses want the cheapest way to use the technology, not the most advanced, he said.

“I don’t think people should worry so much about who built it,” he said. “The focus should be, does it deliver the capability you need?”

Sentai Simons, a start-up founder in Nairobi, downloaded Chinese models to build a product that turned paper legal records into searchable databases. He customized the system with about one million legal files.

His product, JibuDocs, ended up about 140 gigabytes in size — smaller than many iPhones — and cost about $25,000 to create and maintain. Using a service like Anthropic’s Claude, he said, would have cost more than $1 million.

“It’s absolutely the difference between having a business and not having a business,” he said.

Many developers said Chinese companies treated them like a priority, while U. S. firms were hardly present.

Ahmet Acar, a former principal adviser at Amazon Web Services who lives in Nairobi, said joining a developer program from Anthropic required a lengthy screening. Alibaba’s took minutes.

“With the Chinese, it was like: ‘Hey, are you able to do this? Are you located here? All right, man, go have fun,’” he said.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

In a Nairobi high-rise in June, a top Kenyan civil servant for technology said he was surprised when Anthropic pulled access to Fable, its powerful model, at the Trump administration’s behest.

It was a “wake up call” to the world, said John Tanui, the principal secretary in Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy. The abrupt move was a warning that relying on U. S. models could pose risks, he said.

A former Huawei employee who once led the Konza Technopolis project, Mr. Tanui said China and the United States had pressed Kenya to pick a side. He intends to take from both.

“We don’t lean on West or East,” he said.

Being in the middle is tricky. Developers are building systems controlled elsewhere, which means the technology can be yanked, altered or re-priced without warning. Some worry about dependence on the United States. Others do not trust China.

Mr. Budhabhatti of Craft Silicon said he was considering Huawei’s offer of generous subsidies, but was also cautious. Many of his customers are international banks that could demand their software not use Chinese hardware.

Chinese models, too, have not always been reliable. Shikoh Gitau, the founder of the Nairobi start-up Qhala, recalled when DeepSeek went dark in China before the country’s college entrance exams in 2024. It was to deter cheating, but it also disrupted African businesses like hers. Now American models could vanish because of a White House decision.

“At least with China’s models, I can download it on my computer and run it,” she said.

Others have been burned by A. I. politics. Mr. Mwebaze’s Ugandan chatbot service, Sunflower, ran into trouble when a researcher at China Media Project, an independent media research group, asked it about China. Sunflower described China as a democracy and sidestepped questions about the country’s economic and environmental impacts in Uganda.

Chinese state media praised Sunflower, and Huawei contacted Mr. Mwebaze about using its cloud services.

Mr. Mwebaze, whose nonprofit organization, Sunbird AI, is dedicated to A. I. for social good, was unnerved by the experience. He is now using Google’s open-source model, Gemma, to create a product aimed at smartphone users.

“We need to make sure we’re not on the wrong side of geopolitics,” he said.

For all of China’s momentum, much of the A. I. money in Kenya still flows to U. S. companies.

Everyday users are on U. S. systems like ChatGPT and Claude. One 2025 survey found that 42 percent of Kenya’s 23 million internet users had used ChatGPT in the previous month, among the highest rate in the world.

Even Chinese models earn Americans money. Kenyan companies often run Chinese open-source models on cloud services from Amazon and Microsoft, so the U. S. giants make money from their data centers that deliver the technology to customers.

The U. S. advantage was clear in a concrete building in Nairobi’s industrial district, where binders of paper purchase orders lined dark offices for Chandaria Industries, one of Kenya’s largest makers of toilet paper, soap and home goods.

For decades, orders arrived from supermarkets by email or on paper, and clerks keyed them in line by line. An order could take hours to process.

Chandaria recently hired Sanifu, a Kenyan start-up that uses A. I. to streamline business processes, for help. Sanifu uses OpenAI’s models for precision and reliability.

Sanifu’s digital system based on those U. S. models has transformed Chandaria. “Where an order took about two hours to process, that now takes less than 10 minutes,” said Neer Chandaria, who helps run the family firm. Four clerks who once typed in orders now audit the A. I.’s work.

But Sanifu is being courted too. On LinkedIn this year, a Singaporean employee of the Chinese internet firm ByteDance offered Sanifu’s founders access to its A. I. model.

ByteDance’s model was not accurate enough, but the courtship made an impression, said Bernard Momanyi Nyagaka, a co-founder of Sanifu. Nothing like it comes from the American labs.

And Chinese models keep improving, Mr. Nyagaka said.

“If you look at how fast they’re catching up with the American models, it’s really, really fast,” he said.

Edwin Okoth contributed reporting from Nairobi, Kenya.

Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

Adam Satariano is a technology correspondent for The Times, based in London.

Cost of Trump’s Namesake Warships Likely to Rise by 50 Percent or More

The New York Times August 05, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s goal of building a “golden fleet” of 15 battleships could cost $275 billion, according to a government estimate

By John Ismay

Reporting from Washington

A new class of warships that President Trump says will anchor a “golden fleet” for the Navy is expected to cost at least 50 percent more than estimated earlier, according to a government report released on Wednesday.

The first planned Trump-class battleship, the U. S. S. Defiant, is likely to cost $23.4 billion, $8 billion more than the Navy initially indicated.

The cost of each of the 14 additional vessels is expected to jump to slightly more than $18 billion from $10.2 billion, for a total cost of $275 billion for 15 ships.

The estimates were calculated by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, which said that the first of the battleships might take eight years or longer to build.

Mr. Trump announced in December that he expected two of the ships to be constructed over the next two and a half years.

“They’ll help maintain American military supremacy, revive the American shipbuilding industry and inspire fear in America’s enemies all over the world,” Mr. Trump said at the time, alongside renderings of the new ships.

Months after the announcement, Mr. Trump decided that the ships would be powered by nuclear reactors instead of the gas turbine engines used in destroyers and cruisers, a move that adds significantly to the costs.

“New ship types and new ship classes invariably cost more than is estimated at the start of construction,” said Norman Polmar, a naval analyst and author.

The term battleship usually refers to an earlier era of much larger armored warships that had multiple turrets armed with major-caliber guns. The last U. S. battleship was launched in 1944.

The ships Mr. Trump envisions are significantly smaller and would have guided missiles as their primary armament instead.

Some of the additional weapons the Navy has said will arm the new ships, like an electromagnetic gun, were canceled after the spending of billions on decades of failed research and development. Others, like a defensive laser weapon, do not yet exist.

Mr. Trump has said he may want to build as many as 25 nuclear-powered battleships, which he called the “golden fleet.”

Building 25 of the larger warships would cost roughly $455 billion, according to the figures provided by the report.

Senator Jeff Merkley, Democrat of Oregon and the ranking member of the Budget Committee, requested that the Congressional Budget Office study the new battleship program.

“At a time when families are struggling to afford groceries, gas, health care and child care, Congress cannot throw hundreds of billions of dollars at Trump’s ‘Golden Fleet,’ including plastering his name across a new battleship,” the senator said in a statement.

In April, Mr. Trump fired his Navy secretary for not moving quickly enough on building the battleship of his dreams.

On Tuesday, Senator Patty Murray, Democrat of Washington, said in a statement that funds for the new fleet were removed from the continuing resolution that is advancing through the Senate and would fund the government through Dec. 11.

Whether any of the ships will ever actually be built is not certain, as the Navy in recent years has tried and failed to build new types of warships on time and on budget. One such program, the Constellation-class frigate, was canceled just a month before Mr. Trump announced his namesake vessel. Another, called the littoral combat ship, has been plagued by problems and the Navy has already begun decommissioning some of them.

The Ford-class aircraft carriers have been bedeviled by mechanical and electrical problems since the lead ship of the class was commissioned. Only one is currently in service, and the delivery of the next two has been delayed by years.

The president’s fixation on new ships also extends to the Coast Guard, with his recent decision to order $7 billion in no-bid contracts to build 11 new icebreakers for use in the Arctic and Antarctic.

In a speech to military leaders last September, Mr. Trump cited the 1950s documentary television series “Victory at Sea,” which touted the role that battleships and other Navy vessels played in World War II.

“I think we should maybe start thinking about battleships,” the president said. “I used to watch ‘Victory at Sea.’ I love ‘Victory at Sea.’”

But battleships played a diminished role during battles in the Pacific during World War II as newer aircraft carriers proved more versatile and effective in fighting the Japanese at sea.

Since then, the Navy has sought to build smaller but far more capable warships that can carry out different kinds of missions.

Mr. Trump is not the first president to want to bring battleships back into service, after they were decommissioned following World War II and placed back into commission intermittently for service in the Korean and Vietnam Wars. President Ronald Reagan made them a centerpiece of his “600-ship Navy” concept when he personally recommissioned the battleship U. S. S. New Jersey in 1982.

The last of those battleships, the U. S. S. Missouri, was decommissioned in 1992 after seeing combat during the Persian Gulf War and was turned into a floating museum in Pearl Harbor.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

No one doubted the intensity of Lobga Rangzen’s commitment to a Tibet free of Chinese control. But they were not prepared for what he did next.

Credit...

Supported by

By Vivian Wang

Visuals by Vincent Alban

It was 91 degrees in Manhattan and even hotter on the pavement, but the Tibetans gathered as planned outside the Chinese Consulate. Amid the waving flags and synchronized chants, one of the protesters, Ngawang Tashi, looked for his friend Lobga Rangzen.

Lobga Rangzen was a stalwart of events like this. His friends joked that he was happier at protests than on his birthday. At protests, he felt most useful to the cause of Tibetan independence from China — a cause to which he was so devoted, he had even put it in his name: Rangzen means “independence” in Tibetan.

Ngawang Tashi scanned the crowd once, then again. It was strange that Lobga Rangzen wasn’t there.

The next evening, July 2, he was at Costco when another friend called.

“Come to the United Nations right now,” the friend said. “He is in front of there and burning.”

Around the world, many people had already seen what Ngawang Tashi was just learning: Lobga Rangzen, 52, had set himself on fire in front of the United Nations headquarters in Manhattan, streaming the act live on Facebook. He had planted a Tibetan flag on the pavement and taken out fliers that demanded FREE TIBET and CHINA OUT OF TIBET. Then he lit his chuba, or Tibetan robe, on fire.

Ngawang Tashi couldn’t make sense of the news. He had just seen Lobga Rangzen a few days earlier, at their weekly Tibetan dance group. Hadn’t Lobga Rangzen just promised to make his famous Tibetan sausages for a party a few days later? Surely, he reassured himself, his friend would be fine.

But when he arrived at the hospital where firefighters had taken Lobga Rangzen, a nurse told him that he was too late. He could go in just to pay his last respects.

Since then, Ngawang Tashi has been grieving. But as politicians, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, issued statements of mourning and major media outlets wrote about his friend’s death, he, and many Tibetan activists, have also struggled with a grim realization. Lobga Rangzen’s unthinkable act — the first known self-immolation by a Tibetan in the United States — may have achieved one of his greatest goals, however briefly: He made the world pay attention to Tibet.

“The other activities we Tibetans were doing, nobody is going to care about that,” Ngawang Tashi said. “Now everybody is talking.”

A week after Lobga Rangzen’s death, Ngawang Tashi sat inside his friend’s bedroom on the third floor of a narrow house in Queens. The two had shared the place for several years. Beside Ngawang Tashi was Lobga Rangzen’s niece, Sonam Choedon, who had lived there for several months after moving to the United States from India last year.

All around them were reminders of the time they had spent with Lobga Rangzen, and how closely it had been intertwined with protest. On the dresser was a snapshot of Lobga Rangzen with friends, including Ngawang Tashi, during a 13-day walk they made from New York to Washington in 2014 for Tibetan rights. On a table, there was a framed photograph of Sonam waving a Tibetan flag at a protest her uncle had taken her to last summer.

A tangle of plastic badges hung from the curtain rod, showcasing volunteer stints over the years: as a security guard when the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader, visited New York; as a videographer for an advocacy event. Awards from Tibetan activism groups covered the walls. A brightly colored tapestry of the Potala Palace, the former residence of the Dalai Lamas, was pinned over his bed. The only non-Tibetan element was a vibrating exercise machine, with a few shirts neatly draped over the arms.

“I used to dance with him in this room,” Ngawang Tashi said, gesturing to the narrow strip of floor between the table and the bed, where they had followed along with Tibetan music videos.

Sonam smiled. Sometimes, when her uncle walked toward his friends on the street, she said, “you could see him come dancing.”

Lobga Rangzen’s room was a shrine to a homeland he hadn’t seen in more than 30 years. He was born in a remote part of eastern Tibet, as Lobsang Palden. (Tibetans usually do not have family names, only given names.) China had occupied Tibet since the 1950s, and he grew up hearing about how his family had resisted that occupation, Sonam said. Three of his uncles fought the Chinese Army in the 1950s, with one killed in combat and another dying in prison.

As a child, Lobga Rangzen was sent to a monastery for education. But the Chinese government allowed only one monk per family, and a relative had already taken his vows.

So in 1992, when he was 18, he and an uncle fled. The journey to escape Tibet is treacherous, often involving weeks of trekking through the Himalayas at night to avoid detection by Chinese guards. Lobga Rangzen’s parents and three siblings, unable to make the journey, stayed behind. But Lobga Rangzen and his uncle made it to a refugee center in Nepal run by the Tibetan government-in-exile.

From there, Lobga Rangzen was sent to a monastery in southern India, where he rallied other monks to attend protests against China.

In 2006, he arrived in the United States. Sonam wasn’t sure why he left India, but said that monasteries often sent members overseas to share their beliefs. In New York, Lobga Rangzen received asylum. He eventually left the monkhood, and threw himself into activism.

At the time, Tibet was drawing global attention. Ahead of the 2008 Olympics in Beijing, monks and nuns in Tibet led mass protests against Chinese rule. The Chinese government responded violently, with rights groups saying that possibly hundreds of people died. (The Chinese government said the death toll was 22.)

Leaders worldwide expressed outrage. President George W. Bush called for China to hold talks with the Dalai Lama.

In New York, Lobga Rangzen was eager to contribute to the momentum. He built floats for regular protests outside the Chinese Consulate and staged hunger strikes near the United Nations. He shared photos of himself on social media meeting with politicians — Democrats and Republicans — at the Capitol.

Initially, he had worked in construction, but his bosses wouldn’t let him take time off for protests. He turned to driving for Uber instead. He never married, which, his friends said, didn’t bother him. He could devote himself completely to the cause.

But he did occasionally acknowledge the pain of one sacrifice: Ten years ago, he cut off direct contact with his family in Tibet, fearing that his work would jeopardize their safety. He communicated with them only through a cousin in the United States, Lobsang Samdup.

Samdup said he had asked Lobga Rangzen to reconsider, telling him it was OK to think about himself more. “He said, ‘That’s not even a question,’” Samdup recalled.

For all his fervor, though, Lobga Rangzen was a cheerful figure. He always sat in the front row for performances by a stand-up comedian friend, though he knew he’d be picked for punchlines. He enjoyed hiking in upstate New York, singing as he trekked.

After late-night Uber shifts, he would meet up around 3 a. m. with other Tibetan driver friends at Indian restaurants in Midtown Manhattan, regaling them with gossip or folk tales.

“Sometimes I’d joke with him, ‘Hey, are those stories real?’” said one of those friends, Dechen Sangpo. “He would be like, ‘Doesn’t matter, you guys like it, right?’”

In recent months he was often found at the High Asia Research Center, a basement library in Queens set up by a Tibetan writer, Jamyang Norbu. Lobga Rangzen had salvaged old bookshelves from the street to help fill it.

He’d been especially enthusiastic about a pamphlet that Jamyang Norbu had written about Tibet’s history as an autonomous state. What if, Lobga Rangzen suggested, he turned the pamphlet into a slide show and drove cross-country with it playing on a screen atop his car? “He has ideas all the time,” Jamyang Norbu said. Even if some didn’t pan out, he said, “at least someone is making the effort to work things out.”

The first person to self-immolate in Tibet to protest Chinese rule was a 24-year-old monk, in 2009. That spring, when the government forbade memorials to the victims of the previous year’s protests, the monk, Tapey, set himself on fire.

Over the next decade, more than 150 other Tibetans would do the same, with 28 in November 2012 alone, according to the Tibetan exile government.

Self-immolation is, for many people, perhaps the most unfathomable of political protests. When people have chosen it as their final act — whether they were Tibetans, or Vietnamese monks protesting religious suppression in the 1960s, or more recently, American activists drawing attention to climate change or the war in Gaza — the public response has been not only horror and sympathy, but also bewilderment.

Scholars have said self-immolation can become a last resort when no other form of protest is available, at least in Tibet. (Nearly all the Tibetan self-immolations have occurred inside Tibet, with a few in India or Nepal.) “If Tibetans saw even a sliver of an opportunity to hold demonstrations, then they would not resort to self-immolation,” Tsering Woeser, a leading Tibetan poet and scholar, has written.

In New York, Lobga Rangzen protested all the time, to little apparent effect. As China’s economy grew, other countries became more reluctant to challenge it on human rights issues. Even some fellow Tibetans seemed to be resigned to Chinese rule.

The repression in Tibet, though, was unrelenting. Earlier this year, China announced that it would enact a new law to promote “ethnic unity.” The law mandates the use of Mandarin Chinese as the language of instruction in schools, and says that the Chinese government would pursue people who create “ethnic division” — the government’s label for political activism by ethnic minorities — even overseas.

Lobga Rangzen spent hours each week at the Tibetan library, talking to Jamyang Norbu about the need for new tactics. Jamyang Norbu sensed that the cross-country drive idea wasn’t satisfying him.

“But you know, other than that, what can you do now? This is the problem he faced in life. We don’t have resources,” he said. “He was running out of ideas.”

Lobga Rangzen did not raise the idea of self-immolation to his niece, cousin or any of his friends. Only Ngawang Tashi said that he once talked about it — more than 10 years ago. During the peak of the immolations in Tibet, Lobga Rangzen had asked him for advice on writing a last statement. Ngawang Tashi told him he was more useful alive. Lobga Rangzen never mentioned it again.

But in recent months the new law had weighed heavily on him. He called one friend to say the Chinese government was trying to cut out Tibetans’ tongues. He told another that Tibetans overseas might not be safe, either.

On June 30, the day before the law went into effect, he called Dechen, his friend who had also driven Ubers. Dechen had recently finished law school, and Lobga Rangzen congratulated him. But, he said, Dechen should remember not to focus only on money. “I want you to contribute for Tibetan independence,” he told him.

Dechen was surprised. Lobga Rangzen rarely offered him unsolicited advice. “I was like, ‘OK, why are you telling me this?’” Dechen said. “He was like, ‘It just came to mind, so I just wanted to share with you.’”

The next day, he called again, to say hello from a hike upstate, where he’d gone with his niece and several friends. It was July 1, the day of the demonstration against the new law at the Chinese Consulate. Lobga Rangzen didn’t mention the protest.

On July 2, he called for a third straight day. Dechen suggested grabbing lunch together, but Lobga Rangzen said it was too hot. Besides, he said, he had to take care of some things.

“Call me back when you’re done,” Dechen said. “Let’s meet.”

“All right,” Lobga Rangzen said.

Four hours later, Lobga Rangzen sat down, cross-legged, under metal scaffolding across from the United Nations building. For six minutes, he spoke into his phone camera, denouncing what he called China’s efforts at “completely erasing Tibet’s existence” and asking Tibetans in exile to unite. He spoke calmly, even as sweat beaded on his forehead from the sweltering heat.

“If I do a big action today, I want you to know it is not for any personal reason. It is not because I have nothing to eat or nothing to wear, but because I am doing this for my country,” he said.

“I don’t want you to mourn for me. I want you to continue the struggle for Tibetan independence.”

Moments later, a 911 caller reported a man on fire.

In retrospect, Lobga Rangzen’s friends realized there may have been signs. He and Dechen usually spoke a few times a month, not three days in a row. At his last dance group meeting, he had given a shirt to Ngawang Tashi, insisting he take it even when Ngawang Tashi said he had plenty.

No one could pinpoint when Lobga Rangzen had started planning but they were sure that his decision had not been spontaneous, but strategic. At the heart of activism, he knew, was the competition for attention. He had just been waiting for the moment when he thought he could have impact.

Some of his friends quietly acknowledge that his action might not make a difference with the U. S. government or the United Nations. Still, their responsibility is to try to make sure it does.

In the weeks since Lobga Rangzen’s death, hundreds of people have turned out for a stream of events in his honor. There was a 6 a. m. prayer service, a march to the Chinese Consulate and near-daily gatherings at the United Nations. Even his funeral became a protest, with attendees wearing Free Tibet baseball caps and T-shirts.

On the Wednesday after his death, about a dozen members of his dance group, including Ngawang Tashi, gathered after sunset in front of the United Nations. Metal barriers guarded the site of the immolation, where heaps of flowers and multicolored Tibetan prayer flags surrounded a photo of their friend, smiling serenely.

The group sat down on the pavement in front of the makeshift altar, heads bowed, and made a promise. In his last message, Lobga Rangzen had urged Tibetans to keep dancing, to preserve their culture. But they were too sad to dance now, Ngawang Tashi said. So for 49 days — in Tibetan Buddhism, the time it takes for the soul to be reborn — they would not, though they would carry out his wishes in other ways, including protesting.

Then, “after that,” Ngawang Tashi said, “we will keep on dancing, as you advised.”

Vivian Wang is a correspondent based in New York, where she writes about how China's global rise and ambitions are shaping the lives of people both inside and outside its borders.

Vincent Alban is a photojournalist and a member of the 2025-26 Times Fellowship class, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Why Congress Wants a Closer U. S.-Israel Defense Partnership

The New York Times August 05, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

A proposal making its way through Congress would integrate the U. S. and Israeli defense and intelligence apparatuses more tightly. Some worry that it is a bad idea.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

For decades, the United States has supported Israel’s security by providing billions of dollars a year in military assistance and by working with its close partner on intelligence, missile defense and weapons development.

Now, with U. S. political support for sending military funding to Israel dropping off sharply, Congress is considering phasing out the financial commitment and instead undertaking a far more integrated defense and technology partnership built around legally mandated defense industrial cooperation between the two nations.

Both the House and Senate have included such a proposal in the annual defense policy bill, laying the groundwork for melding U. S. and Israeli defense and intelligence capabilities in profound ways that some critics find alarming.

President Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel are pushing for the shift, which comes as lawmakers on the right and left have grown increasingly hostile to sending taxpayer dollars to Israel’s military.

Supporters argue the move would benefit the United States, allowing it to capitalize on Israel’s defense and intelligence innovations. They say it would elevate the U. S.-Israel relationship from one of donor and recipient to a strategic partnership.

But some lawmakers fear that such deep ties could blur the lines between supporting an ally and effectively allowing Israel’s military to become intertwined with the Pentagon in ways that could be dangerous and difficult to unwind.

Here is how it would work.

The United States and Israel already partner to produce defense technologies, such as the Iron Dome and David’s Sling air defense systems, with contractors including Raytheon and Rafael Advanced Defense System. The links were on display in the days following the Feb. 28 joint strikes against Iran.

The defense policy bill, which passed the House last month and is awaiting action in the Senate, would enshrine those partnerships in law.

The House measure would create an office in the Defense Department that would be legally required to facilitate cooperation between the United States and Israel. It would oversee the development of new weapons and technology, as well as the testing and rollout of new capabilities.

A separate intelligence bill that is expected to be merged with the defense legislation would call on the president and the director of national intelligence to “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the government of Israel,” except when doing so could risk U. S. national security or expose sophisticated “intelligence sources and methods.”

Proponents envision a broad collaboration on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, missile defense and cybersecurity.

The language traces back to a bipartisan bill introduced this year by Senators Ted Budd, Republican of North Carolina, and Kirsten Gillibrand, Democrat of New York. In the House, it was introduced by Representatives Ronny Jackson, Republican of Texas, and Don Davis, Democrat of North Carolina.

Separately, Representative Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican aligned with Mr. Trump’s “America First” stance, has introduced a nonbinding resolution that would call for ending the decades-old memorandum of understanding under which the United States provides billions of dollars in military aid to Israel, and for transitioning instead to “mutual defense cooperation and joint economic investment” between the two nations.

The memorandum, which mandates that the United States provide $3.8 billion a year in military aid to Israel, ends in 2028, and lawmakers in both parties have said they would oppose a new deal based on billions of dollars in direct aid to Israel.

Mr. Stutzman introduced his resolution after meetings with Israeli officials, including Mr. Netanyahu, who has endorsed it. On Tuesday, the congressman described his idea as moving “from the current status quo of giving military aid to Israel to creating a trade relationship where we can help each other militarily and economically.”

Doing so would provide extraordinarily valuable support to Israel and its military and intelligence service without explicitly requiring Congress to sign off on sending a set amount of federal money to Jerusalem each year.

The idea has gained traction as the future of traditional U. S. military assistance to Israel has become increasingly uncertain following a backlash to Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza. In a striking vote last month, nearly half of House Democrats backed an amendment that would have ended U. S. aid to Israel. The proposal failed overwhelmingly, but the vote reflected growing hostility in the Democratic Party over continuing unconditional support for Israel.

Recent polling also shows a significant split among Republicans on the matter. A New York Times/Siena poll from May found that a growing portion of younger conservative voters find aid to Israel increasingly unacceptable. Among surveyed Republican voters between 18 and 44, 63 percent said they opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel, while 72 percent of those 45 and over supported additional aid.

The push also stems from Mr. Netanyahu’s public campaign to appear less reliant on U. S. military aid as Mr. Trump urges allies to contribute more meaningfully to their own defense.

Opponents argue that the idea would give too much control over sensitive U. S. defense matters to a foreign nation.

“The U. S. government can always choose on a case-by-case basis to enter into joint production agreements,” Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, said in an interview. “What’s sort of jaw-dropping about this is that it mandates it.”

He added: “That gives the Israeli government a lot more control over the production and potentially deployment of U. S. weapons systems.”

Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, one of the few Republicans who has spoken out against the provision, called it “a betrayal of American sovereignty,” and said that it “tragically merges our military technology and supply chain with Israel’s.”

With Representative Ro Khanna, Democrat of California, Mr. Massie attempted to strip the provision from the defense bill. But the two lawmakers were blocked by Republican leaders from bringing the matter to a vote.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, warned in a social media post that the proposed partnership would “merge parts of our military with the IDF,” referring to the Israel Defense Forces. She warned that such a move would be “an existential threat to American sovereignty and democracy.”

That characterization goes further than the letter of the legislation. Neither the House nor the Senate bill would merge the U. S. and Israeli militaries or place troops under shared authority.

Backers have criticized such claims as misrepresentations aimed at limiting support for a critical ally in the Middle East.

“Despite bad-faith attempts from both sides of the political spectrum to misstate the facts, to denigrate our close ally and partner Israel,” the proposal “simply enables joint investment in research and development that will benefit Americans from both a fiscal and security perspective,” Mr. Budd said in a statement.

He said the provision would “impose zero limitations” on the U. S. military.

Defense industrial partnerships are a key feature of the U. S. relationship with close allies, including Britain, Australia, Canada and NATO partners. But the new proposals would establish one of the broadest such partnerships with Israel, with which the United States does not share any formal mutual defense treaty.

Mr. Van Hollen and other critics argue that the mandated joint production provision could constrain the United States militarily. He pointed to Israel’s repeated objections to transferring Iron Dome air defense batteries to Ukraine after Russia’s invasion, out of concern that the weapons could fall into the hands of Russia, be delivered to Iran, then used against Israel.

“The one precedent that we have is the Iron Dome co-production agreement, where the government of Israel did exercise that authority,” Mr. Van Hollen said. “That should be a very cautionary tale.”

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.
